records.name: Amerigo Vespucci
records.scaleNote: No slaving voyage of his own is documented; his ties are indirect but real: he worked inside Gianotto Berardi's Seville house (which traded in enslaved Africans), sailed on the 1499 Ojeda expedition that seized c. 232 Lucayans, and left 'five household slaves' in his 1511 will.
records.origins: Born in Florence in 1454 (some older sources say 1451), Vespucci was a commercial agent in the household of Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici. The Medici sent him to Seville around 1491–92, where he joined the business of the Florentine merchant Gianotto Berardi, Lorenzo's agent and one of Columbus's backers. He was a close friend of Columbus among the Florentines of Seville.
records.role_summary: Vespucci stands at the opening of the Atlantic system as merchant-provisioner, navigator and cartographic authority rather than as a slave trader. After Berardi's death (Dec. 1495) he executed his will and tried to complete Berardi's contract to fit out 12 ships for Hispaniola; he sailed with Alonso de Ojeda (1499–1500, Spain) and Gonçalo Coelho (1501–02, Portugal); and from 1508 he was the first Piloto Mayor of the Casa de Contratación, the agency that later administered slave licences.

roleDetail.t: Worked in a slave-trading merchant house.
roleDetail.d: Berardi, his employer and partner in Seville, had a business in African slavery and ship chandlery and invested in Columbus's first voyage; the Florentine community in Seville traded in enslaved Africans alongside textiles and dyes (Moya Pons, citing Consuelo Varela). Vespucci's personal part in Berardi's slaving is not documented.

roleDetail.t: Sailed on a voyage that took Indigenous captives.
roleDetail.d: The 1499–1500 Ojeda fleet, two of whose four ships Vespucci and his backers financed, made a slave raid in the Bahamas (c. 232 Lucayans) and Ojeda sold captives in Spain. The 'Soderini' letter attributed to Vespucci says 222 captives were sold at Cádiz, but that letter's authenticity is disputed and his individual role in the raid is not recorded.

His April 1511 will left most of his modest estate, including five household enslaved people, to his widow María Cerezo (as summarised in Wikipedia's account of the will; primary text not checked here).

roleDetail.t: Built the navigational machinery of the Atlantic.
roleDetail.d: As Piloto Mayor (appointed 22 March 1508) he trained and licensed pilots and oversaw the Padrón Real master chart at the Casa de Contratación, the institution through which the Crown later registered Atlantic shipping, including slave licences. Linking this office to the slave trade is an interpretive, structural point.

records.legacy: Two continents carry his name because Martin Waldseemüller's 1507 world map, drawing on the printed 'Mundus Novus' and Soderini letters, labelled the southern landmass 'America'. The only surviving copy of that map was bought by the US Library of Congress for $10 million (agreement 2001, purchase completed 2003) and is on permanent display. His name, more than any other, symbolises the European 'naming' of lands whose peoples were then enslaved.

legacyDetail.d: Waldseemüller's 1507 map was the first to use the name 'America'; he dropped it on later maps (1513, 1516), but it stuck.
Since the 16th century (Las Casas among the first) critics have questioned the authenticity of his letters and his claimed 1497 voyage; historians still debate how many voyages he made.

records.name: Christopher Columbus
records.scaleNote: Began the transatlantic traffic in enslaved Indigenous people: several dozen Taíno sent to Spain in 1494, then c. 500 loaded in early 1495, of whom c. 300 survived the voyage (College of Charleston LDHI).
records.origins: A Genoese navigator who had sailed to Portuguese West Africa and the Canary Islands, where the Guanche people had long been enslaved and exported to Spain. His 1492 voyage was backed by Isabella and Ferdinand, with private money from Seville's Florentine merchants, notably Gianotto Berardi.
records.role_summary: As Admiral and governor of Hispaniola, Columbus imposed tribute in gold and labour on the Taíno and organised their enslavement for sale in Spain, apparently to compensate for gold he had not found. The Crown curbed his slaving, but his rule laid the template of coerced labour that preceded mass African enslavement in the Caribbean.

roleDetail.d: In early 1495 he loaded c. 500 enslaved Taíno for Spain; only c. 300 survived the crossing (per LDHI, College of Charleston). Others captured in the same campaign were distributed to colonists.
He demanded gold tribute and labour from Hispaniola's Taíno; overwork, violence, famine and disease drove a catastrophic population collapse.
Isabella and Ferdinand quickly cut short his slaving and opposed a transatlantic trade in Indigenous people, though they permitted enslavement within the Americas.

records.legacy: Columbus was removed as governor in 1500. His legacy is fiercely contested: statues have been toppled or removed across the Americas, and in the US many places now mark Indigenous Peoples' Day instead of or alongside Columbus Day.

legacyDetail.d: The collapse of Hispaniola's Taíno population under Spanish rule was the immediate context for the Crown's turn to importing enslaved Africans after 1501.

sources.label: College of Charleston LDHI — The Spanish and New World Slavery
Wikipedia — Taíno genocide
New York Review of Books — Indians, Slaves, and Mass Murder: The Hidden History

connections.label: Ojeda sailed on his 2nd voyage, led campaigns on Hispaniola
sent Taíno captives for sale in Spain

records.name: Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici
records.scaleNote: A Florentine banker whose Seville branch (run by Berardi, later Vespucci) traded in enslaved Africans among other goods; no figures for his firm's slave dealing are documented.
records.origins: A cousin of Lorenzo 'the Magnificent' from the junior branch of the Medici, he was a wealthy patron of Botticelli and Ficino's circle. He kept commercial agents in Seville, including Gianotto Berardi and Amerigo Vespucci.
records.role_summary: Through his Seville agents he had a stake in the Florentine merchant network that supplied Columbus's fleets and dealt in enslaved Africans in Andalusia. He is best known as the addressee of Vespucci's letters, including 'Mundus Novus' (c. 1503), which announced a 'New World' to European readers.

roleDetail.d: Berardi acted as his representative in Seville; some historians speculate that Columbus indirectly drew on Medici credit via Berardi.
Vespucci's letter describing the 1501–02 Brazil voyage was addressed to him and became a European bestseller.

records.legacy: He died in 1503. His name survives chiefly through Vespucci's letters and the Renaissance art he commissioned; his branch of the Medici later produced the Grand Dukes of Tuscany.

legacyDetail.d: Letters to Florentine patrons spread knowledge of the Atlantic that fed further investment.

sources.label: John Carter Brown Library — Mundus novus
Academia Dominicana de la Historia — Moya Pons, The Italian Presence in Santo Domingo (p. 42)
Univ. of Minnesota Bell Library — Vespucci's journeys

records.name: Gianotto Berardi
records.scaleNote: Described by historians as a dealer in enslaved Africans (largely via the Portuguese trade) and as Columbus's key private financier; reported investment c. 500,000 maravedís linked to the first voyage, but no captive totals are documented.
records.origins: A Florentine merchant established in Seville from c. 1485, acting as agent for Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici. He lent money to merchants, nobles and monarchs.
records.role_summary: Berardi ran a business in African slavery and ship chandlery and was among Columbus's most important backers, investing in the first voyage and winning the contract to provision the second fleet. Vespucci worked with him and completed his affairs after his death in December 1495, which left Berardi's contract to send 12 ships to Hispaniola unfinished.

roleDetail.d: Scholarship describes him as having worked mainly in the Portuguese slave trade, from which he built much of his fortune.
Columbus's c. 500,000-maravedí share of the 1492 costs may have come from a Berardi loan (Moya Pons, citing Varela).
Held contracts to supply Columbus's second fleet and, at his death, to fit out 12 ships for Hispaniola.

records.legacy: He died insolvent-adjacent in late 1495/early 1496, leaving debts that Vespucci, as executor, had to settle. His career shows how Italian merchant capital already invested in African captives flowed directly into the first American colonies.

legacyDetail.d: His firm links the 15th-century Portuguese/Andalusian trade in Africans to Spain's first Atlantic colony.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Amerigo Vespucci (section on Berardi)

Wikisource — 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica, 'Vespucci, Amerigo'

connections.label: traded in captives via the Portuguese trade
contract to supply 12 ships to Hispaniola

records.name: Bartolomeo Marchionni
records.scaleNote: Leading trader of enslaved Africans into Lisbon in the 1480s–90s: held the crown lease for Rios dos Escravos (1486 contract) and Senegambia, and was the largest exporter of enslaved people to Valencia in the 1490s (Guidi Bruscoli).
records.origins: A Florentine merchant-banker who settled in Lisbon around 1470 and became one of the richest men in Portugal. He dominated the Madeira sugar trade and lent money to the Crown.
records.role_summary: Marchionni leased royal rights to bring captives from West Africa to Lisbon and re-exported them to Valencia, Seville and Florence. He also financed Portuguese voyages to India, including ships in Cabral's 1500 fleet, making him a pivot between African slaving, Atlantic sugar and the Asian spice route.

roleDetail.d: A 1486 contract let him import most captives from the Rios dos Escravos (Slave Rivers, Benin region) into Portugal.
Through the agent Cesare Barzi he was the largest supplier of enslaved Africans to Valencia in the 1490s, and sent captives, including women, to Florence.
Financed slave trading in and from Africa, the Madeira sugar economy and India voyages; the king considered naturalising him, probably for his loans.

records.legacy: His career, reconstructed by Francesco Guidi Bruscoli ('Bartolomeo Marchionni, homem de grossa fazenda', 2014), is a key case of Italian capital powering Portugal's early African trade.

legacyDetail.d: The crown-lease model he worked under prefigured the asiento contracts later sold by Spain.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Bartolomeo Marchionni

connections.label: captives registered/taxed via Casa dos Escravos

records.name: Crown of Castile / Spain (Ferdinand & Isabella, Charles V, Philip II…)
records.scaleNote: Licensed the whole Spanish American trade from 1501 via licences and asientos; Spanish/Uruguayan-flagged ships themselves made c. 1,116 voyages (c. 4% of the trade, per Eltis/SlaveVoyages), but the Crown's asientos drew Portuguese, Genoese, German, Dutch, French and British carriers into supplying Spanish America.
records.origins: The union of Castile and Aragon under Isabella I and Ferdinand II (1479) sponsored Columbus in 1492. Under Charles V (r. 1516–56) and Philip II (r. 1556–98) it became the first global empire.
records.role_summary: The Crown authorised the first shipments of enslaved Africans to the Americas (1501 instructions to Ovando permitting enslaved people 'born under Christian rule'), opened direct Africa-to-America shipments with Charles V's 1518 licence to Gorrevod, and then sold licences and asiento monopolies for three centuries, treating the trade as a source of revenue. It abolished slavery in Cuba only in 1886.

roleDetail.d: Instructions of 16 Sept. 1501 to Governor Ovando permitted 'black slaves or other slaves' born in Christian lands; Ferdinand later sent 100 enslaved Africans from Spain.
On 18 Aug. 1518 Charles V granted Laurent de Gorrevod a licence for 4,000 enslaved Africans direct to the colonies.

From 1595 to 1640 Portuguese asentistas (Philip II–IV ruled both crowns) held contracts for c. 4,250 captives/year paying 100,000–170,000 ducats annually; later holders included Genoese (1662), French (1701) and British (1713).
Agreed in 1817 to end the trade, yet the illegal trade to Cuba ran until c. 1867; slavery in Cuba was abolished in 1886.

records.legacy: The Spanish monarchy continues today. Spain has made no formal state apology for the slave trade; debate has centred on monuments (e.g. Antonio López in Barcelona, 2018) and museum decolonisation.

legacyDetail.d: Unlike some northern European states, Spain has not issued a formal apology for its role in Atlantic slavery.

sources.label: College of Charleston LDHI — The Early Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade: Nicolás de Ovando
College of Charleston LDHI — Emperor Charles V

records.name: Crown of Portugal (Houses of Aviz and Braganza)
records.scaleNote: Portuguese- and Brazilian-flagged ships carried c. 5.8 million of the c. 12.5 million Africans embarked, the largest national share (SlaveVoyages estimates, as charted by Statista); c. 7,310 voyages.
records.origins: Portugal's monarchs sponsored exploration down the African coast from the 1420s–40s under Prince Henry, seeking gold and a sea route to Asia. Papal bulls (1452, 1455) gave them sanction to subjugate and enslave non-Christians in Africa.
records.role_summary: The Crown taxed, licensed and monopolised the African trade: it took a royal fifth of captives (from 1444), leased trade rights (Fernão Gomes 1469), built Elmina (1482), centralised sales in Lisbon's Casa dos Escravos (1486), colonised Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola, and chartered monopoly companies. Portugal was the first and the last major European slave-trading nation.

roleDetail.d: Henry took one fifth of captives landed at Lagos in 1444; from 1512 enslaved people had to be landed only in Lisbon.
Cape Verde (1460s), São Tomé (1490s) and Luanda (1576) became embarkation hubs feeding Brazil and Spanish America.
During the Iberian Union, Portuguese contractors held the Spanish asiento 1595–1640 (Pedro Gomes Reinel first).
Trade banned by Sá da Bandeira's 1836 decree (poorly enforced); slavery abolished across Portuguese territories 25 Feb. 1869.

records.legacy: The monarchy fell in 1910, but the Portuguese Republic inherited the debate. In April 2024 President Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa said Portugal should 'pay the costs' of slavery and colonial crimes; the government rejected any reparations process.

legacyDetail.d: The President floated debt relief and financing for former colonies; the government said it would not start a reparations process.

records.name: Prince Henry "the Navigator"
records.scaleNote: Sponsor of the 1444 Lagos landing of c. 235 captives, of whom he received the royal fifth (tallies of his share differ between sources); his expeditions initiated Europe's Atlantic African slave trade.
records.origins: A son of King João I, Henry was governor of the Order of Christ and holder of the Algarve. He sponsored voyages down the West African coast in search of gold, allies against Islam and a route around Africa.
records.role_summary: Henry's licensed expeditions began seizing Africans in 1441; in August 1444 Lançarote de Freitas landed c. 235 captives at Lagos, where they were divided — separating families — with Henry taking his fifth. Zurara's chronicle, written for Henry, justified the enslavement as a route to Christian conversion.

roleDetail.d: The first large public sale of sub-Saharan Africans in Europe took place in Lagos, as described by Zurara, with Henry present on horseback receiving his share.
As sponsor he was entitled to one fifth of the captives or their value.
Zurara professed grief at the captives' suffering but justified it by their conversion — an early pro-slavery argument.

records.legacy: Henry is still celebrated in Portugal (Lagos statue inaugurated 1960; the Padrão dos Descobrimentos in Lisbon). Lagos opened a small Slave Market museum (Mercado de Escravos) in 2016 beside his statue, prompting debate over how Portugal commemorates the 'Discoveries'.

legacyDetail.d: The juxtaposition of his statue and the slave-market museum is a focus of debate about Portugal's memory of slavery.

sources.label: Miami University — Zurara, Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea (1444 excerpt)
Wikipedia — Mercado de Escravos (Lagos)
Contested Histories — Portugal: Slave Market Museum in Lagos

connections.label: took royal fifth of Lagos captives

records.name: Lançarote de Freitas
records.scaleNote: Led the 1444 expedition that landed c. 235 captives at Lagos — then the largest single seizure of Africans by Europeans.
records.origins: A squire of Henry's household and tax collector at Lagos. His 1444 expedition was the first funded by Lagos merchants rather than Henry himself.
records.role_summary: He commanded six caravels that raided islands off the Arguin coast (Mauritania) and returned to Lagos in August 1444 with c. 235 captives, who were sold in the first public slave auction of Africans in Portugal.

roleDetail.d: His voyage showed slaving could be profitable to private investors, marking a shift from exploration to commerce.
Zurara describes captives divided into lots without regard to family, separating parents, children and spouses.

records.legacy: Remembered mainly through Zurara's chronicle; the site of the 1444 sale is today commemorated by the Lagos slave-market museum.

legacyDetail.d: 1444 is often cited as the start of Europe's Atlantic slave trade from Africa.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Lançarote de Freitas
Miami University — Zurara, Chronicle (1444 excerpt)

records.name: Fernão Gomes
records.scaleNote: Held the Crown's monopoly on the Guinea trade 1469–c.1475 (rent c. 200,000 reais/year plus malagueta rights); captive totals undocumented but the lease covered trade in people as well as gold and pepper.
records.origins: A Lisbon merchant and squire, Gomes leased the Guinea trade from Afonso V after Henry's death, in return for an annual rent and an obligation to explore 100 leagues of coast a year.
records.role_summary: His captains reached the Gold Coast and found the gold trade at Elmina (1471) and the islands of the Bight of Biafra (Fernando Pó). This privatised exploration opened the regions that later supplied huge numbers of captives and led directly to the building of Elmina Castle.

roleDetail.d: The 1469 lease made exploration self-financing for the Crown; terms and dates vary between sources.
Captains including João de Santarém and Pedro Escobar reached Mina in 1471.

records.legacy: Ennobled with the name 'da Mina' and admitted to the royal council (1478). The Crown took back the trade and built Elmina in 1482.

legacyDetail.d: His lease set the pattern of royal contracts with merchants used for Marchionni and later asientos.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Fernão Gomes
Univ. NOVA Lisboa, Expansão (EVE) — D. Afonso V

connections.label: 1469 Guinea trade lease from Afonso V

records.name: Laurent de Gorrevod
records.scaleNote: Holder of Charles V's 18 Aug. 1518 licence to ship 4,000 enslaved Africans directly to Spanish America, which he resold to Genoese merchants.
records.origins: A Burgundian/Savoyard noble, governor of Bresse and a Flemish-court favourite who came to Spain with the young Charles V.
records.role_summary: As a courtier he received the 1518 licence as a royal favour, never intending to trade himself; he sold it in parts to Genoese merchants (via Adán Vivaldo and Valián de Forne to the Centurione), creating the first quasi-asiento.

roleDetail.d: The licence shows how the trade began as a tradable royal privilege granted to a courtier.

roleDetail.t: Broker of the 'asiento of the Genoese'.
roleDetail.d: His resale made Genoese houses the main importers of Africans into the Americas for over a decade.

records.legacy: The 1518 licence is widely seen as the start of the direct transatlantic slave trade; its 500th anniversary in 2018 drew renewed attention.

legacyDetail.d: His sale of rights prefigured the asiento system that lasted to 1789.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Laurent de Gorrevod
Slavery, Law & Power — Opening the transatlantic slave trade
Academia Dominicana de la Historia — The Italian Presence in Santo Domingo (p. 44)

records.name: Centurione family & Genoese merchants of Seville
records.scaleNote: Through the Casa Centuriona (Gaspar, Esteban and Jácome Centurión) they operated the 1518 licence for 4,000 Africans — the 'asiento of the Genoese' — and were the main importers into Spanish America for over a decade.
records.origins: A Genoese merchant-banking clan with branches in Seville, Cádiz, Toledo and Medina del Campo; Genoese families (Centurione, Spinola, Grimaldi, Lomellini) financed the Spanish Crown throughout the 16th century.
records.role_summary: The Centurione bought the Gorrevod licence via Adán Vivaldo and Valián de Forne and organised shipments of Africans, mainly via Portuguese suppliers in Cape Verde and São Tomé, to the Caribbean. The wider Genoese network's credit underpinned Castile's Atlantic ventures.

roleDetail.d: Britannica dates the first contract to a Genoese company in 1517–18; LDHI and Moya Pons confirm the transfer to the Centurione.
Other Genoese families such as the Grimaldi are documented as Crown financiers; their direct role in slave licences is not established in the sources consulted.

records.legacy: Genoese capital returned to the asiento in the 1660s with Grillo and Lomellini. Palazzi in Genoa built by these families survive as UNESCO sites (Strade Nuove), though the slave-trade origins of specific fortunes are rarely highlighted.

legacyDetail.d: Genoese networks financed Spanish slave contracts across two centuries.

sources.label: Academia Dominicana de la Historia — The Italian Presence in Santo Domingo (p. 44)
Dialnet — article on the Centurione family
Britannica — asiento de negros

connections.label: captives sourced via São Tomé/Cape Verde

records.name: Welser family (Augsburg)
records.scaleNote: Received a 1528 Crown contract to transport 4,000 enslaved Africans to the Spanish Caribbean and ruled Venezuela (Klein-Venedig) 1528–46; the African venture largely failed, and they profited more from enslaving Indigenous people.
records.origins: An Augsburg merchant-banking dynasty that, with the Fugger, financed Charles V's 1519 imperial election. In return they won trading concessions in the Spanish Atlantic, including a factory in Santo Domingo and the Venezuela grant.
records.role_summary: In 1528 the Welser agents (Ehinger and Sailer) contracted to deliver 4,000 enslaved Africans to the Indies and received the province of Venezuela to govern. Their governors led brutal expeditions seeking El Dorado and enslaved Indigenous people; Charles V revoked the grant after 1546.

roleDetail.d: The contract for 4,000 Africans was a licensed quota; how many were actually delivered is unclear.
Welser governors such as Ambrosius Ehinger and Nikolaus Federmann ran Venezuela from Coro, with violent slaving expeditions inland.
Scholarship (Heidelberg) concludes they profited more from enslaving Indigenous people than from the African contract.

records.legacy: The Welser trading house collapsed in 1614, but the family survives. German historians and media have re-examined their colonial role in recent years, including the 2020s debate on Germany's early colonial past.

legacyDetail.d: Klein-Venedig is often called Germany's first colonial venture.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Klein-Venedig
Heidelberg Univ. journals — article on the Welser slave-trade contract
Wikipedia — Welser family

records.name: Fugger family (Augsburg)
records.scaleNote: Britannica notes the firm entered the slave trade under Jakob Fugger; its central documented role was supplying Central European copper and brass that Portugal bartered for captives in West Africa (e.g. 4,000 ingots taken to Benin in 1515 to buy captives).
records.origins: Weavers turned merchant-bankers, the Fugger built a fortune in Tyrolean silver and Hungarian copper and became bankers to the Habsburgs, financing Charles V's election.
records.role_summary: Fugger copper and brass, shipped via Antwerp to Lisbon, became manillas and ingots used as currency to purchase captives on the West African coast. The family also financed the Iberian crowns that licensed the trade.

roleDetail.d: A Fugger-marked copper ingot from a Hungarian mine (Linden-Museum) was destined for Portugal's Upper Guinea trade; in 1505 a captive at Calabar cost 8–10 manillas.
Their loans to Charles V and Philip II sustained the monarchy that sold slave licences.

records.legacy: The family still exists (Fürst Fugger Privatbank; the Fuggerei social housing in Augsburg, founded 1516). Research projects (e.g. Global Heritage Lab, Bonn) now trace German metals in the Atlantic slave trade.

legacyDetail.d: The world's oldest social housing complex, still run by Fugger foundations, was funded from the family's 16th-century fortune.

sources.label: Britannica — Fugger family (summary)
Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek / Linden-Museum — Fugger copper ingot

metals shipped via Antwerp to Lisbon

records.name: Nicolás de Ovando
records.scaleNote: First official to oversee the import of enslaved Africans into the Americas (from 1502); requested 17 for the mines in 1505 and later c. 250 more (LDHI).
records.origins: A Knight Commander of the Order of Alcántara, appointed governor of the Indies after Columbus and Bobadilla, arriving in 1502 with c. 2,500 colonists.
records.role_summary: Ovando carried the 1501 royal instructions permitting enslaved Africans born in Christian lands. He briefly asked for a ban (1503) fearing revolts, then requested more captives for gold and copper mines. He also formalised the encomienda of Indigenous labour and ordered the Xaraguá massacre (1503).

roleDetail.d: Oversaw the earliest documented shipments from Spain to Hispaniola (from 1502).
Formalised the system granting Indigenous labour to colonists.

records.legacy: Recalled in 1509. His governorship set the model of colonial forced labour on which African slavery in the Spanish Caribbean was built.

legacyDetail.d: Enslaved Africans under his rule fled to the mountains — among the first maroons in the Americas.

sources.label: College of Charleston LDHI — The Early Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade: Nicolás de Ovando
Wikipedia — Encomienda

records.name: Alonso de Ojeda
records.scaleNote: Led the 1499–1500 voyage (with Vespucci and Juan de la Cosa) that raided the Bahamas for c. 232 Lucayans and sold captives in Spain; earlier campaigns on Hispaniola yielded c. 600 enslaved Taíno shipped to Spain.
records.origins: A Castilian hidalgo from Cuenca who sailed on Columbus's second voyage (1493) and led punitive campaigns on Hispaniola.
records.role_summary: With royal licence he led the 1499 expedition to Venezuela, on which Vespucci sailed; it ended with a slave raid and sale of captives. In 1508–10 he governed Nueva Andalucía, where his raids for captives provoked fatal resistance.

roleDetail.d: Profits were meagre (c. 15,000 maravedís shared among 55 survivors), so captives were sold to recoup costs.
Las Casas attributed his miserable end to 'all the slaves he had made'.

records.legacy: He died poor in Santo Domingo c. 1515. He is remembered in Venezuela as an early conquistador who named the region.

legacyDetail.d: His voyage is the clearest documented link between Vespucci and the taking of captives.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Alonso de Ojeda
Wikipedia — Amerigo Vespucci (1499 voyage)

records.name: Bartolomé de las Casas
records.scaleNote: Never a trader, but his 1516 proposal to replace Indigenous labour with enslaved Africans was part of the policy debate that preceded the 1518 licence; he later recanted.
records.origins: A Sevillian colonist who arrived in Hispaniola in 1502 and held an encomienda and enslaved people before renouncing them in 1514 and becoming a Dominican friar.
records.role_summary: Las Casas fought for decades against the enslavement and destruction of Indigenous Americans. In 1516 he recommended importing Africans to relieve Indigenous labour; late in life he admitted this as an error and condemned African slavery as equally unjust, in writings unpublished for c. 350 years.

roleDetail.d: Recommended African labour as a remedy for Indigenous suffering (LDHI).
Later writers blamed him for 'starting' African slavery; historians note the trade was already licensed from 1501 and his influence on the 1518 decision is debated.
In his 'History of the Indies' he wrote that enslaving Africans was as unjust as enslaving Indians.

records.legacy: Las Casas influenced the 1542 New Laws abolishing Indigenous slavery and is honoured as a founder of human-rights thought; his case is used to discuss how humanitarian reform could redirect rather than end exploitation.

legacyDetail.d: Charles V's New Laws, which he championed, banned Indigenous slavery (unevenly enforced).

sources.label: Ohio State Origins — Bartolomé de las Casas and 500 Years of Racial Injustice
ULPGC accedaCRIS — Méndez Alonzo on Las Casas and African slavery
College of Charleston LDHI — Emperor Charles V

records.name: Pedro Gomes Reinel
records.scaleNote: First holder of the general Spanish asiento (1595–1601) under Philip II; Portuguese asentistas through 1640 contracted for c. 4,250 captives a year, paying 100,000–170,000 ducats annually.
records.origins: A Portuguese merchant-financier operating during the Iberian Union (1580–1640), when Philip II ruled both Spain and Portugal, giving Portuguese traders access to Spanish America.
records.role_summary: Reinel's 1595 contract transformed licensing into a general monopoly asiento, supplied mainly from Angola and Upper Guinea to Cartagena de Indias and Veracruz. He was followed by João Rodrigues Coutinho (1601–04) and others through Cristóvão Mendes de Sousa (1631–40).

roleDetail.d: Contracted with Philip II in 1595 (Mellafe 1959, cited by CHAM, NOVA Lisbon).
Some 38 Portuguese slave ships reached Cartagena de Indias 1596–1608.

records.legacy: The Portuguese asientos made Angola the largest single source of captives for Spanish America in the early 17th century and entrenched New Christian merchant networks in Cartagena and Lima, many later persecuted by the Inquisition.

legacyDetail.d: Portugal's restoration of independence ended the Portuguese asientos.

sources.label: CHAM / NOVA FCSH — Portuguese asiento contracts 1595–1640
Revista de Estudios Americanos (CSIC) — El temprano comercio de esclavos desde Angola hacia Hispanoamérica y Brasil, 1575–1595
Britannica — asiento de negros

records.name: Domenico Grillo & Ambrosio Lomellini
records.scaleNote: Held the Spanish asiento 1662–c.1674; the contract called for 24,500 captives over seven years at 100 pesos per head to the Crown, supplied largely by Dutch and English subcontractors (Florida Slave Trade Center; García-Montón).
records.origins: Two Genoese patricians exiled from Genoa in 1647 who became financiers at the Madrid court while keeping close ties to Genoa.
records.role_summary: They turned the asiento into a monopoly that functioned like a tax farm, buying captives from the Dutch at Curaçao and the English at Jamaica rather than sending their own ships to Africa — tying Spain's trade to its rivals' slaving companies.

roleDetail.d: Signed in Madrid in July 1662 (García-Montón, Genoese Entrepreneurship and the Asiento Slave Trade, 1650–1700).
Relied on Dutch WIC and English suppliers in the Caribbean.

records.legacy: Their contract illustrates Genoese capital's long role in Spanish slaving, now the subject of recent scholarship by Alejandro García-Montón.

legacyDetail.d: Their reliance on foreign carriers foreshadowed the French (1701) and British (1713) asientos.

sources.label: Cambridge Core — review of García-Montón, Genoese Entrepreneurship and the Asiento Slave Trade
Florida Slave Trade Center — Grillo and Lomelin asiento
Univ. Pablo de Olavide — Genoese Entrepreneurship and the Asiento Slave Trade, 1650–1700

records.name: Paulo Dias de Novais
records.scaleNote: Founder (1576) and first proprietary governor of Portuguese Angola, which became the single largest source of captives in the Atlantic trade; c. 1550–1836 Luanda was the centre of the trade to Brazil.
records.origins: Grandson of Bartolomeu Dias, he led an embassy to Ndongo in 1560 and was granted Angola as a hereditary donataria by King Sebastião in 1571.
records.role_summary: He founded São Paulo de Loanda on 25 January 1576 with c. 100 settler families and 400 soldiers and began wars of conquest against Ndongo that generated captives for export to Brazil and Spanish America.

roleDetail.d: Established the port that became the main Portuguese slave-trading port until the 1836 ban.
Military campaigns into Ndongo were closely tied to slave raiding.

records.legacy: Luanda is today Angola's capital, with over 8 million people; Angola's independence came only in 1975 after a long liberation war.

legacyDetail.d: Luanda's trade created deep demographic and cultural ties between Angola and Brazil.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Luanda
BlackPast — Luanda, Angola (1576– )

connections.label: his wars against Ndongo began the conflict Nzinga later fought

records.name: Marquis of Pombal (Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo)
records.scaleNote: Created the two monopoly companies that shipped tens of thousands of Africans to Brazil: c. 25,965 to Pará and Maranhão 1757–77 (per Reis) and c. 51,806 to Pernambuco 1760–80 (ANPUH paper).
aliases: Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo
records.origins: A diplomat in London and Vienna who became chief minister to King José I (1750–77) and led the rebuilding of Lisbon after the 1755 earthquake.
records.role_summary: Pombal used state-chartered monopoly companies to expand the slave trade to northern and northeastern Brazil. His 1761 law banning the import of enslaved people into metropolitan Portugal was designed to channel captives to Brazil's mines and plantations, not to end slavery.

roleDetail.d: Grão-Pará e Maranhão (1755) and Pernambuco e Paraíba (1759).
Prohibited transporting enslaved people to Portugal itself; often misdescribed as abolition.
Ended Indigenous slavery in Brazil and expelled the Jesuits, increasing demand for African captives in the Amazon.

records.legacy: Pombal is honoured with a monumental statue in Lisbon's Marquês de Pombal square; his slave-trade companies are rarely mentioned in public commemoration.

legacyDetail.d: His 1761 decree is still sometimes cited as abolition, a framing historians reject.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo, 1st Marquis of Pombal
Wikipedia — Grão Pará and Maranhão Company
ANPUH — paper on the Companhia de Pernambuco e Paraíba slave imports

records.name: Antonio López y López, 1st Marquis of Comillas
records.scaleNote: Historian Martín Rodrigo y Alharilla documents his firms reselling enslaved people within Cuba from 1846 and a British-consul report of involvement in an illegal expedition of African captives; scale of direct trafficking uncertain.
records.origins: Born poor in Comillas (Cantabria), he emigrated to Cuba as a youth and made his fortune in Santiago de Cuba trade, partly through slavery and slave dealing, before settling in Barcelona.
records.role_summary: His firms Valdés y López and Antonio López y Hermano bought enslaved people in Santiago and sold them to western Cuba; the British consul accused the firm of joining an illegal expedition of 'bozales' from Africa after the 1817 ban. Back in Spain he founded the Compañía Trasatlántica, the Banco Hispano Colonial and the Compañía General de Tabacos de Filipinas.

roleDetail.d: Documented resale of enslaved people within Cuba from 1846 (Rodrigo y Alharilla).
British consular report of an illegal African expedition; surviving documentation is sparse because the trade was clandestine.
As a leading colonial magnate he opposed abolition in Cuba.

records.legacy: Barcelona City Council removed his statue on 4 March 2018 after long campaigns; it is stored by the Barcelona History Museum and the square was renamed after Idrissa Diallo. His family later founded the Pontifical University of Comillas.

legacyDetail.d: One of the first removals of a slave-trader monument in Spain.
Compañía Trasatlántica Española survived into the 20th century; the Comillas legacy includes the Comillas Pontifical University.

sources.label: Catalan News — Barcelona removes slave trader statue
EUI Ideas — Challenging slavery's heritage in Spain and Catalonia
Ara — Pruebas del pasado negrero de Antonio López
elDiario.es — El 'negrero' López y López gana al 'marqués' de Comillas

records.name: Pedro Martínez (Cádiz)
records.scaleNote: Called 'the largest slave trader based in Cádiz in the time of the illegal trade' (Trocadero review of Cózar Navarro, La Orca del Atlántico); his family firm traded 1817–1867.
records.origins: A Cádiz merchant whose family built a slave-trading house after Spain's 1817 treaty with Britain made the trade illegal; linked to the Partido Moderado and the Banco de Cádiz.
records.role_summary: Martínez financed and shipped illegal slaving voyages to Cuba, partnering with Pedro Blanco's Gallinas operation, which he reportedly took over after 1839; British courts pursued his ships (e.g. the Cazador, Gibraltar Vice-Admiralty appeal 1836–37).

roleDetail.d: Cádiz was Spain's leading slave port in these decades.
Barcia's biography of Blanco describes Martínez running Blanco's business after 1835–39.

records.legacy: Largely forgotten until Carmen Cózar Navarro's 2021 study; Cádiz's slaving past is now being publicly re-examined.

legacyDetail.d: His career exposes the slaving roots behind Cádiz's liberal mercantile image.

sources.label: Trocadero (Univ. Cádiz) — review on Pedro Martínez and the Cádiz slave trade
Documenta — Cózar Navarro, La Orca del Atlántico
UK National Archives — Del Campo & Martinez (ship Cazador) appeal

records.name: Josep Xifré i Casas
records.scaleNote: A Catalan-Cuban magnate (estate >120 million reales at death) documented as a slaveholder; whether he imported Africans is disputed (Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana).
records.origins: From Arenys de Mar, he fled his father's creditors to Havana in 1789 and built a business in hides and leather export.
records.role_summary: Xifré profited from the slave-based Cuban colonial economy and held enslaved people; he moved to New York (1823) and then Barcelona (1840), where he built the Porxos d'en Xifré. He is listed among Barcelona's prominent slaveholders, though not proven as a slave trader.

roleDetail.d: The Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana says he reportedly did not import Africans but did hold enslaved people.

records.legacy: The Porxos d'en Xifré still stand on Barcelona's Passeig d'Isabel II; Barcelona's municipal programme on slave-trade memory includes him.

legacyDetail.d: His colonial fortune shaped Barcelona's waterfront architecture.

sources.label: Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana — Josep Xifré i Casas
3Cat — Esclavistes a Barcelona, la recuperació d'una memòria amagada
Ara — Huir de deudas y convertirse en hombres ricos

records.name: Casa de Contratación (Seville)
records.description: Royal House of Trade founded in Seville in 1503 to register and tax all shipping, goods and passengers to the Indies, including licensed enslaved Africans. It trained and licensed pilots and kept the Padrón Real master chart; Amerigo Vespucci was its first Piloto Mayor (1508–12). It moved to Cádiz in 1717 and was abolished in 1790.

records.name: The Spanish Asiento (licence system)
records.description: From the early 16th to the mid-18th century, the Spanish Crown sold contracts (asientos) granting a private party or foreign power the monopoly on supplying enslaved Africans to Spanish America, in return for payments and a fixed quota. Holders included Genoese (1518; 1662), the Welser (1528), Portuguese merchants (1595–1640), the French Guinea Company (1701) and Britain's South Sea Company (1713, 4,800 a year for 30 years).

records.name: Charles V's 1518 licence (4,000 Africans)
records.description: On 18 August 1518 Charles V granted his courtier Laurent de Gorrevod a licence to ship 4,000 enslaved Africans to the Spanish colonies, allowing them to be taken directly from Africa rather than via Iberia. Gorrevod resold it to Genoese merchants. The first known direct voyages from Cape Verde and São Tomé reached the Caribbean in the mid-1520s.

records.name: Port of Seville
records.description: Castile's monopoly port for the Indies trade (1503–1717) and one of Europe's largest slave markets: by 1565 roughly one in fourteen inhabitants was enslaved. Florentine, Genoese and Portuguese merchants based there financed Columbus and traded in African and Indigenous captives.

records.name: Port of Lisbon
records.description: Portugal's capital and, from 1512, the only legal landing port for enslaved Africans brought to Portugal; Africans made up an estimated c. 10% of the city's 16th-century population. The Casa dos Escravos and later Casa da Guiné e da Mina handled royal taxation of captives.

records.name: Casa dos Escravos (Lisbon)
records.description: Royal institution created by King João II in 1486 to receive, assess, tax and sell all captives arriving in Lisbon; its functions later passed to the Casa da Guiné e da Mina. A 1512 order required enslaved people to be landed only at Lisbon.

records.name: Port of Luanda (Portuguese Angola)
records.description: Founded as São Paulo de Loanda in 1576 by Paulo Dias de Novais, Luanda was the main Portuguese slave-trading port until the 1836 ban and the leading single embarkation point in the Atlantic trade, chiefly to Brazil. It was occupied by the Dutch 1641–48. Today it is Angola's capital, with over 8 million people.

records.name: Elmina Castle (São Jorge da Mina)
records.description: Built by the Portuguese in 1482 on the Gold Coast, the first major European building in tropical Africa, initially for gold; it became a key slave-trading post. The Dutch captured it in 1637 and ran the slave trade there until 1814; Britain took it in 1872. A UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979 and a museum and memorial today.

records.name: Mercado de Escravos, Lagos (Algarve)
records.description: Site of the August 1444 division and sale of c. 235 captives brought by Lançarote de Freitas, often described as the first large slave market of Africans in Europe. Since 2016 a small museum occupies the building, beside a 1960 statue of Henry the Navigator.

records.name: Papal bulls Dum Diversas (1452) & Romanus Pontifex (1455)
records.description: Bulls of Pope Nicholas V authorising Afonso V of Portugal to attack, subjugate and reduce to perpetual servitude 'Saracens and pagans', and confirming Portuguese monopoly rights on the African coast. They provided religious sanction for the Portuguese slave trade and are central to the 'Doctrine of Discovery'; the Vatican formally repudiated that doctrine in 2023.

records.name: Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)
records.description: Signed 7 June 1494, it divided newly found lands along a meridian 370 leagues west of Cape Verde: Africa and Brazil fell to Portugal, most of the Americas to Castile. Because Spain had no African trading posts, it had to buy enslaved Africans from others — the structural origin of the asiento system.

connections.label: led Spain to rely on foreign suppliers

records.name: Waldseemüller world map (1507)
records.description: Printed at Saint-Dié in April 1507 by Martin Waldseemüller and Matthias Ringmann, this map first used the name 'America' in honour of Amerigo Vespucci. Of perhaps 1,000 copies, one survives; the Library of Congress agreed to buy it in 2001 for $10 million and displays it permanently.

records.name: Hispaniola (La Isabela / Santo Domingo)
records.description: Spain's first American colony, founded by Columbus in 1493. Its Taíno population collapsed under forced labour, violence and disease (from perhaps several hundred thousand to c. 11,000 by 1517), and from 1502 it received the first enslaved Africans brought to the Americas; it became an early sugar colony.

records.name: São Tomé and Cape Verde (Portuguese island entrepôts)
records.description: Portugal colonised Cape Verde in the 1460s and São Tomé and Príncipe from the 1490s. São Tomé pioneered the slave-worked sugar plantation model later transplanted to Brazil, and both islands served as collection points from which the first direct voyages to the Caribbean sailed in the 1520s.

connections.label: departure points of first direct voyages

records.name: Klein-Venedig (Welser Venezuela)
records.description: The Province of Venezuela, granted by Charles V to the Welser in 1528 and governed from Coro. Welser governors led violent expeditions searching for El Dorado and enslaved Indigenous people; the grant was revoked after the 1546 killings of Welser agents and formally ended in 1556.

records.name: Company of Cacheu (Guinea)
records.description: Portuguese company confirmed in 1676 with privileges to trade on the Guinea coast and export enslaved people to Portugal, its colonies and Spanish America; it failed to control the trade against Luso-African traders such as Bibiana Vaz and folded in 1682. Its successor, the Cacheu and Cape Verde Company (1690–1703), also held the Spanish asiento briefly (1696–1701).

records.name: Companhia Geral do Grão-Pará e Maranhão
records.description: Monopoly company founded by Pombal in 1755 to develop northern Brazil, with a 20-year monopoly on trade with Cape Verde and the West African coast (Bissau, Cacheu). It brought c. 25,965 enslaved Africans to Pará and Maranhão 1757–77 (per Reis); Queen Maria I ended it in 1778.

records.name: Companhia Geral de Pernambuco e Paraíba
records.description: Pombaline monopoly company founded 13 August 1759 for trade with Pernambuco and Paraíba, supplying enslaved people mainly from Angola to Recife; c. 51,806 captives were imported 1760–80. Its monopoly ended around 1780 under Maria I.

records.name: Anglo-Spanish Treaty of 1817 & Cuban abolition (1886)
records.description: Under British pressure Spain agreed on 23 Sept. 1817 to end its slave trade (north of the Equator at once, wholly from 1820) in exchange for £400,000. Enforcement was weak: an illegal trade to Cuba continued until c. 1867, and slavery in Cuba was abolished only in 1886.

records.name: Portuguese abolition decrees (1836–1869)
records.description: Sá da Bandeira's decree of 10 December 1836 banned the Portuguese slave trade but was poorly enforced until a treaty with Britain in 1842 and Royal Navy action; gradual emancipation laws followed, and a decree of 25 February 1869 abolished slavery throughout Portuguese territories (forced labour regimes persisted in the colonies).

records.name: Compañía Trasatlántica Española
records.description: Shipping line developed by Antonio López from his firm A. López y Cía (formally constituted 1881) with state mail contracts to Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines, built partly on capital from the Cuban slave economy.

records.name: Removal of Antonio López statue, Barcelona (2018)
records.description: On 4 March 2018 Barcelona City Council removed the statue of Antonio López from the square bearing his name, after years of campaigning by anti-racist groups; the statue is stored by the Barcelona History Museum and the square was renamed for Idrissa Diallo.

records.name: Portugal's 2024 reparations debate
records.description: In April 2024 President Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa said Portugal 'takes full responsibility' for transatlantic slavery and colonial crimes and should 'pay the costs', suggesting debt relief and financing; the government said it would not begin any reparations process, and the far-right Chega party sought to condemn his remarks.

records.name: John Hawkins
records.scaleNote: Led England's first known slaving voyages (1562–68); the first voyage alone took c. 300 Africans from the Sierra Leone coast for sale in Spanish Hispaniola, and he made three to four such voyages in all.
records.origins: Son of William Hawkins, a Plymouth merchant who had traded with the Guinea coast and Brazil. He learned of the profits of selling captives to Spanish colonists through contacts in the Canary Islands.
records.role_summary: Organised the first English slaving expeditions, seizing and buying Africans in Upper Guinea and selling them in the Spanish Caribbean in defiance of Spain's monopoly. His later voyages were backed by London investors and by Elizabeth I, who lent royal ships.

roleDetail.d: Sailed with three ships (Salomon, Swallow, Jonas) to the Sierra Leone coast, took c. 300 captives and sold them in Hispaniola.
For the 1564 voyage Elizabeth I lent the 700-ton royal ship Jesus of Lübeck, making the Crown an investor in the trade.

roleDetail.t: Defeat at San Juan de Ulúa, 1568.
roleDetail.d: His third voyage ended when a Spanish fleet attacked his ships in the Mexican harbour; most ships and many men were lost.

records.legacy: Hawkins became Treasurer of the Navy and a commander against the Spanish Armada in 1588, and was knighted. His coat of arms featured a bound African captive. His voyages are now remembered as the beginning of England's involvement in the transatlantic slave trade.

legacyDetail.d: After 1568 England's slave trade lapsed for nearly a century; Hawkins's later fame rested on reforming the navy.
Since 2020 places named after Hawkins in Plymouth have faced calls for renaming or contextualisation.

sources.label: World History Encyclopedia — John Hawkins
Encyclopedia.com — Hawkins, John
Royal Museums Greenwich — Sir John Hawkins, 1532-95
Wikipedia — John Hawkins (naval commander)

records.name: Francis Drake
records.scaleNote: Took part in Hawkins's slaving voyages of the 1560s, captaining the 50-ton Judith on the 1567–68 expedition; he did not run slaving ventures of his own.
records.origins: A Devon-born relative of the Hawkins family, he went to sea young and joined the Hawkins family's Atlantic ventures in the 1560s.
records.role_summary: Served on Hawkins's slaving voyages to West Africa and the Spanish Caribbean, commanding the Judith in 1567–68. He escaped the 1568 Spanish attack at San Juan de Ulúa, an event that shaped his later privateering against Spain.

roleDetail.d: Commanded the smallest ship of Hawkins's third slaving fleet, which raided and traded for captives on the Upper Guinea coast.
One of the few ships to escape the Spanish attack; the episode fuelled his raids on Spanish shipping.

records.legacy: Drake became famous for circumnavigating the globe (1577–80) and fighting the Armada. His early involvement in the slave trade is far less commemorated than his naval exploits, and his statues have been questioned since 2020.

legacyDetail.d: National narratives long presented Drake as a hero while omitting his slaving voyages.

sources.label: World History Encyclopedia — John Hawkins
Encyclopedia.com — Hawkins, John

records.name: Elizabeth I of England
records.scaleNote: Invested in Hawkins's slaving voyages by lending royal ships, including the Jesus of Lübeck (1564, 1567); England's trade remained small until the 1660s.
records.origins: Queen of England from 1558. Her government sought ways to break into Iberian Atlantic commerce without open war with Spain.
records.role_summary: Became a shareholder in John Hawkins's slaving expeditions by contributing royal ships. Although reported to have earlier called such trade 'detestable', she backed the voyages for their profits.

roleDetail.d: Lent the Jesus of Lübeck to Hawkins's second voyage (1564) and to the third (1567).
Established a pattern of Crown backing for slaving later formalised in royal charters under the Stuarts.

records.legacy: Her backing made the English Crown a participant in the trade from its start. The Stuart monarchy later chartered the Royal Adventurers (1660) and the Royal African Company (1672).

legacyDetail.d: Later Stuart monarchs went further, granting monopolies and holding shares in slaving companies.

sources.label: Encyclopedia.com — Hawkins, John
Wikipedia — Jesus of Lübeck

records.name: James, Duke of York (James II)
records.scaleNote: Governor and largest shareholder of the Royal African Company, which shipped more Africans than any other single institution in the trade; many captives were branded 'DY' for him.
records.origins: Younger brother of Charles II and Lord High Admiral after the 1660 Restoration. He led the royal circle that founded chartered companies to break Dutch dominance of West African trade.
records.role_summary: Headed the Company of Royal Adventurers into Africa and then the Royal African Company as governor. Captives shipped by the company were branded with 'DY' (Duke of York) or 'RAC'.

roleDetail.d: He was the company's governor and largest shareholder, keeping the post after becoming king in 1685.
Smithsonian records note many enslaved people were branded with 'DY'; others were marked 'RAC'.
English attacks on Dutch Gold Coast forts in 1664 (including Cape Coast) were part of the Royal Adventurers' war for the trade.

records.legacy: Deposed in 1688, after which Parliament opened the trade (1698). New York is named after him. His role is central to recent debates about the British monarchy's historic links to slavery.

legacyDetail.d: His RAC role is regularly cited in calls for the Royal Family to acknowledge its historic links to slavery.

sources.label: Smithsonian Transcription Center — Stock share certificate for the Royal African Company
Pepys Diary Encyclopedia — Royal African Company
Wikipedia — Royal African Company

records.name: Royal African Company
records.scaleNote: Per SlaveVoyages data cited by historian William Pettigrew, c. 187,700 Africans were carried on 653 company voyages (1672–1731), of whom c. 38,500 died at sea; Pettigrew argues it shipped more captives than any other single institution.
records.origins: Chartered in 1672 by Charles II as successor to the failed Company of Royal Adventurers into Africa, with a monopoly on English trade along the West African coast. Royal family members, courtiers and London merchants were its shareholders.
records.role_summary: Bought captives from African rulers and merchants at forts such as Cape Coast Castle and shipped them to Barbados, Jamaica and other English colonies, branding many with 'DY' or 'RAC'. It also traded gold, ivory and other goods.

roleDetail.d: Held a legal monopoly of English trade to West Africa from 1672 until Parliament opened the trade in 1698 (with a 10% duty on private traders until 1712).
Ran Cape Coast Castle as its Gold Coast headquarters and also held Bunce Island and James Island (Gambia).
Many captives were branded 'DY' for the Duke of York or 'RAC' on the chest.

records.legacy: Weakened by private competition after 1698, the company effectively stopped trading in the 1720s and was replaced in 1750–52 by the Company of Merchants Trading to Africa. Its records survive at The National Archives; its leaders' names, notably Colston's, remain contested in Bristol and London.

legacyDetail.d: The end of the monopoly let thousands of private merchants from London, Bristol and Liverpool enter the trade, greatly increasing British volumes.
Its forts passed to the Company of Merchants Trading to Africa, which ran them until 1821.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Royal African Company
Smithsonian Transcription Center — Stock share certificate for the Royal African Company
Schools History — Lifting of the Royal African Company monopoly
PBS Africans in America — The Royal African Company

records.name: Edward Colston
records.scaleNote: During his Royal African Company involvement (1680–92) the company is commonly estimated to have transported c. 80,000 Africans; the figure is an estimate and varies by source.
records.origins: Born in Bristol to a merchant family, he made his fortune as a London merchant trading to Spain, Portugal and the Mediterranean. He joined the Royal African Company in 1680.
records.role_summary: Held shares in the Royal African Company and sat on its governing court, serving as deputy governor in 1689–90. His wealth funded schools, almshouses and churches in Bristol, which commemorated him for three centuries.

roleDetail.d: Member of the RAC's Court of Assistants and its deputy governor (1689–90).
Endowed Bristol schools and almshouses; the 1895 statue presented him as a benefactor without mentioning slavery.

records.legacy: On 7 June 2020 Black Lives Matter protesters toppled his statue and pushed it into Bristol Harbour; it is now displayed, graffitied, at the M Shed museum. Colston Hall was renamed Bristol Beacon in 2020, and other Bristol institutions dropped his name.

legacyDetail.d: Four people charged with criminal damage were acquitted by a jury in January 2022.
Colston Hall became Bristol Beacon (announced 23 September 2020) after a campaign begun in 2017.

CBS News — Edward Colston statue thrown into Bristol harbor
Al Jazeera — Four charged over toppling of UK slave trader statue in Bristol

records.name: South Sea Company
records.scaleNote: Held the 1713 asiento allowing 4,800 captives a year to Spanish America for 30 years; actual deliveries fell far short, and the Church Commissioners' 2023 report cites c. 34,000 people transported, while other estimates are higher.
records.base: South Sea House, Threadneedle Street, London
aliases: The Governor and Company of the merchants of Great Britain, trading to the South Seas
records.origins: Founded in 1711 as a public–private scheme to consolidate British government debt in exchange for trading privileges in Spanish America.
records.role_summary: Under the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) it received the asiento, the contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies, plus one annual trading ship. It bought captives (often from the Royal African Company and in Jamaica) and shipped them to ports such as Cartagena, Portobelo, Veracruz and Buenos Aires.

roleDetail.d: Contract for 4,800 enslaved people a year for 30 years, plus a 'navío de permiso' for general trade.
Historians disagree on whether the slave trade was profitable or mainly a cover for smuggling; disputes fed the 1739 War of Jenkins' Ear.
Speculation in its shares produced the South Sea Bubble crash of 1720.

records.legacy: The asiento was surrendered in 1750 and the company wound up in 1853. Its shareholders included Queen Anne's Bounty (Church of England), whose stake was the main basis of the Church Commissioners' 2023 £100m commitment.

legacyDetail.d: By 1777 Queen Anne's Bounty held £406,942 of South Sea stock, per the Church Commissioners' 2023 report.

sources.label: Wikipedia — South Sea Company
Britannica — Asiento de negros
University of Southampton — South Sea Company and the asiento (working paper)
