records.name: Ouidah (Whydah)
records.description: Inland town and roadstead in present-day Benin, the second-largest embarkation point in Africa after Luanda, from which an estimated 1 million+ captives left. English (1650s/1680s), French (1704) and Portuguese (1721) forts stood there; Dahomey conquered it in 1727 and it remained active until the 1860s. In 1860 it sent the last recorded slave shipment to the United States (the Clotilda).

records.name: Fort of São João Baptista de Ajudá
records.description: Portuguese fort built at Ouidah in 1721 to serve the Bahian tobacco-for-captives trade. It remained Portuguese until Dahomey (Benin) seized it in 1961 and now houses Ouidah's history museum.

records.name: Door of No Return, Ouidah
records.description: Concrete and bronze memorial arch on Ouidah beach, inaugurated in the mid-1990s as part of the UNESCO Slave Route project, marking where captives were taken to ships. Its friezes show lines of chained people.

records.name: Route des Esclaves, Ouidah
records.description: A c.4 km memorial route from Ouidah's slave market square to the beach, with statues and sites including the Tree of Forgetting. Benin placed 'Sites marquants de la Route de l'Esclave' on its UNESCO tentative list in 1996.

records.name: Royal Palaces of Abomey
records.description: Palace complex of the Dahomean kings, whose bas-reliefs depict warfare and royal history; inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985. Treasures looted by France in 1892 were partly returned to Benin in 2021.

records.name: Fante states and Fante Confederacy
records.description: Fante coastal states (e.g. Anomabo) were major brokers of the 18th-century Gold Coast slave trade, mediating between Asante and the European castles. In 1868 Fante chiefs formed the Fante Confederacy at Mankessim, with a written constitution in 1871, before Britain dissolved it in 1873–74.

records.name: Mbanza Kongo (São Salvador)
records.description: Capital of the Kingdom of Kongo in northern Angola, renamed São Salvador after Christian conversion. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017 as a testimony to Kongo's encounter with Portugal.

records.name: Diary of Antera Duke (1785–1788)
records.description: Diary of an Efik trader of Old Calabar, written in trade English, the only surviving eyewitness account of the slave trade by an African merchant. The original was apparently destroyed in WWII bombing; extracts survive and were published by Forde (1956) and in a 2010 OUP edition.

records.name: Ibini Ukpabi (Long Juju) of Arochukwu
records.description: Oracle shrine at Arochukwu whose verdicts, consulted across Igboland, often resulted in people being sold rather than killed as believed. British forces reportedly destroyed it in the Anglo-Aro War (1901–02); the Long Juju slave route is on Nigeria's UNESCO tentative list.

records.name: Bonny (port)
records.description: Eastern Niger Delta port that became one of the largest slave-exporting ports in Africa in the late 18th century, dominated by Liverpool ships, then a palm oil port after the 1830s.

records.name: Lagos (port)
records.description: Yoruba lagoon port that became a major outlet for the illegal slave trade to Brazil and Cuba in the 1830s–40s. British bombardment in 1851 deposed Kosoko; Britain annexed Lagos in 1861.

records.name: Anglo-Lagos Treaty of 1852
records.description: Treaty signed on 1 January 1852 by Oba Akitoye, installed by British force, abolishing the slave trade at Lagos and granting British traders privileges. It paved the way to annexation in 1861.

records.name: Bamana Empire of Ségou
records.description: Bambara state founded c.1712 by Biton Kulibali at Ségou on the Niger, whose armies (tonjon) were composed largely of captives. Its wars supplied captives to Senegambian and Upper Guinea markets and European posts; it fell to Umar Tall in 1861.

records.name: Benin's 1999 apology and Cotonou reconciliation conference
records.description: In 1999 President Mathieu Kérékou apologised for Africans' role in the slave trade, including kneeling in a Baltimore church, and convened a Leaders' Reconciliation conference in Cotonou with delegates from the diaspora, Europe and the US. Benin followed in 2024–25 with a law offering citizenship to descendants of enslaved Africans.

records.name: Civil Rights Congress of Nigeria letter (2009)
records.description: In November 2009 the Lagos-based Civil Rights Congress, led by Shehu Sani, wrote to Nigeria's traditional rulers urging them to apologise for their forebears' role in raiding and selling people. A spokesman for the chiefs rejected the idea of inherited guilt.

records.name: Ghana's Year of Return (2019)
records.description: Campaign launched by President Nana Akufo-Addo in 2018 marking 400 years since enslaved Africans reached Virginia in 1619, inviting the diaspora to visit and settle; Ghana granted citizenship to around 200 diaspora members. Critics noted it focused on European castles more than on African participation.

records.name: DeWolf family of Bristol, Rhode Island
records.scaleNote: Per the Tracing Center and Brown-affiliated research, the extended family financed or commanded voyages carrying c. 10,000–12,000 enslaved Africans across the Atlantic between 1769 and 1820, making it the largest slave-trading family in US history.
records.origins: Mark Anthony DeWolf, a sailor from Guadeloupe, settled in Bristol and captained slaving voyages for the Newport merchant Simeon Potter in the 1760s. His sons, including James, John, William, Charles and later grandson George, built a family business around ships, rum distilleries, insurance and banking in Bristol.
records.role_summary: The DeWolfs ran a closed triangle: Bristol rum went to West Africa, captives were carried to Havana, Charleston and other markets, and Cuban sugar and molasses returned to the family distilleries. They kept trading after Rhode Island's 1787 ban and the federal ban of 1808, using Cuban plantations and the family's own bank and insurance company.

roleDetail.d: Estimates of c. 10,000–12,000 Africans carried on family-financed voyages (1769–1820) come from the Tracing Center and the 'Traces of the Trade' research.
The family owned ships, distilleries, the Bank of Bristol and the Mount Hope Insurance Company, and plantations in Cuba that received captives and supplied sugar.
Rhode Island outlawed the trade in 1787 and Congress in 1808, yet the DeWolfs continued to finance voyages, relying on Cuban ports and weak federal enforcement.

records.legacy: The family's wealth built Bristol's Federal-era mansions, including Linden Place (1810), now a house museum. In 2008 descendant Katrina Browne released the documentary 'Traces of the Trade: A Story from the Deep North', and the Tracing Center continues education on Northern complicity.

legacyDetail.d: Ten descendants retraced the triangle to Bristol, Ghana and Cuba in the Emmy-nominated PBS documentary; Thomas Norman DeWolf's book 'Inheriting the Trade' accompanies it.
Built for George DeWolf in 1810, later bought by James DeWolf; today a museum that interprets the family's slave-trade wealth.

sources.label: Tracing Center — James DeWolf
Providence Journal / USA Today Network — Living Off the Trade: Bristol and the DeWolfs
Linden Place — Meet the Family
Christian Science Monitor — Family confronts the North's slave-trading past

connections.label: Mark Anthony DeWolf sailed for Newport merchants

records.name: James DeWolf
records.scaleNote: Organised or financed dozens of slaving voyages from Bristol over c. 50 years; often described (Tracing Center) as the most prominent slave trader in US history.
records.origins: A son of Mark Anthony DeWolf, James went to sea young and commanded slaving voyages in the 1780s. He married into the Bradford family and invested his profits in ships, distilling, Cuban plantations and later textile mills.
records.role_summary: As captain of the Polly in 1789–90 he ordered an enslaved woman sick with smallpox thrown overboard; he was indicted but never convicted. As a shipowner he went on to finance numerous voyages into the 1810s, while serving as a Rhode Island legislator and, from 1821 to 1825, a US senator.

roleDetail.d: In 1791 a federal grand jury indicted him for murdering a woman with smallpox aboard the Polly; he left the state, and a later St. Thomas inquiry cleared him.
He served in the US Senate 1821–25 and was among the richest men in the country at his death in 1837.

records.legacy: His fortune moved into Cuban plantations and New England textile mills. His descendants include Katrina Browne, whose 2008 film 'Traces of the Trade' examined his record.

legacyDetail.d: His career shows how slave-trade wealth carried into national political office in the early republic.

sources.label: Tracing Center — James DeWolf
Wikipedia — James DeWolf

records.name: Brown family of Providence
records.scaleNote: Per Brown University's 2006 report, the family firm and individual brothers backed a handful of slaving voyages (most notoriously the Sally, 1764–65) among Rhode Island's c. 1,000; their broader fortune rested on rum, candles, iron and Caribbean trade.
aliases: Nicholas, John, Joseph and Moses Brown
records.origins: The Browns were Providence merchants; James and Obadiah Brown sent an early slaving voyage in 1736. The four brothers Nicholas, Joseph, John and Moses ran Nicholas Brown and Company, trading in rum, spermaceti candles, iron and West Indian goods.
records.role_summary: The firm sent the brigantine Sally to West Africa in 1764; of 196 Africans bought, at least 109 died. The family later split: Moses Brown became a Quaker abolitionist, while John Brown kept trading and in 1797 became the first American tried under the federal Slave Trade Act of 1794.

roleDetail.d: Captain Esek Hopkins bought 196 Africans; at least 109 died from revolt, suicide, starvation and disease before survivors were sold in Antigua.
Moses Brown freed the people he enslaved in 1773 and helped found the Providence Abolition Society; it pursued his brother John, whose ship Hope was forfeited after an 1797 federal case.
The family was the main benefactor of the College in the English Colony of Rhode Island, renamed Brown University in 1804 after Nicholas Brown Jr.'s gift.

records.legacy: Brown University carries the family name. In 2006 its Steering Committee on Slavery and Justice published a report on the family's and university's ties to slavery, which led to a memorial on campus (2014) and new research and education commitments.

legacyDetail.d: Commissioned by President Ruth Simmons, it documented the Sally voyage and recommended memorials and education programs.
The house of the Sally co-owner now hosts the Rhode Island Historical Society and has displayed the 'Sally' exhibit.

sources.label: Brown University — Slavery and Justice report (2006, PDF)
Brown University Library — Voyage of the Slave Ship Sally, 1764–1765
Providence Journal / USA Today Network — Brown vs. Brown: Brothers go head to head
Rhode Island Historical Society — John Brown papers, historical note

connections.label: hired Hopkins as master of the Sally
John Brown's Hope voyage to Havana
fellow Rhode Island merchant; candle-trade associate

records.name: Esek Hopkins
records.scaleNote: Master of the Brown family's Sally (1764–65), on which at least 109 of 196 Africans died (per Brown University).
records.origins: A Rhode Island sea captain and privateer and brother of Governor Stephen Hopkins. The Browns hired him in 1764 for their slaving venture despite his lack of experience in the African trade.
records.role_summary: Hopkins spent about nine months on the Upper Guinea coast buying 196 Africans. During the crossing captives revolted; Hopkins's crew shot or wounded several, and others died of disease, starvation and suicide. Survivors were sold in Antigua.

roleDetail.d: At least 109 of the 196 people bought died, one of the deadliest Rhode Island voyages documented.
In 1775 the Continental Congress appointed him the first commander-in-chief of the Continental Navy.

records.legacy: Hopkins is commemorated in Providence (a statue and a park), while Brown University's research has made the Sally voyage the best-known case study of Rhode Island's slave trade.

legacyDetail.d: His naval role is honoured locally, which sits uneasily with his record on the Sally.

sources.label: Brown University Library — Voyage of the Slave Ship Sally, 1764–1765
Wikipedia — Sally (1764 ship)

connections.label: sailed for Nicholas Brown and Company
Sally voyage central to Brown's 2006 report

records.name: Aaron Lopez
records.scaleNote: Took part in roughly a dozen or more slaving voyages (c. 14 by one count) between 1761 and 1774, including the Cleopatra's voyages carrying 400+ Africans to Barbados and Jamaica; slaving was a small share of his business and of Rhode Island's c. 1,000 voyages.
records.origins: Born Duarte Lopez into a converso family in Portugal, he emigrated to Newport in 1752, openly returned to Judaism and took the name Aaron. He became Newport's wealthiest merchant, trading in spermaceti candles, whaling, rum and Caribbean goods with his father-in-law Jacob Rodriguez Rivera.
records.role_summary: Lopez and Rivera co-owned or invested in slaving voyages to West Africa, with captives sold mainly in the British Caribbean. Historians, beginning with Virginia Platt (1975), document the voyages while noting they were a minor and often unprofitable part of his trade.

roleDetail.d: The Cleopatra, co-owned with Rivera, made at least three voyages (1770–74) carrying over 400 Africans to Barbados and Jamaica.
Jewish merchants were a small minority of Rhode Island and Atlantic slave traders; the great majority of Newport and Bristol voyages were sent by Christian merchants such as the DeWolfs and Browns.

records.legacy: Lopez fled Newport during the Revolution and drowned in 1782. He was a founding member of Touro Synagogue's congregation, and Newport historians now include his slaving voyages in accounts of the city's past.

legacyDetail.d: Antisemitic tracts have exaggerated Lopez's role; mainstream scholarship (Platt; Coughtry) places him as one of many Newport traders.

sources.label: RI Historical Society bibliography — 'And Don't Forget the Guinea Voyage': The Slave Trade of Aaron Lopez of Newport (Platt, WMQ 1975)
The Public's Radio — The irony of Aaron Lopez, the merchant prince of Newport
Wikipedia — Cleopatra (slave ship)

records.name: Peter Faneuil
records.scaleNote: Boston merchant who traded with the slave-based Caribbean and invested in at least one slaving venture; he enslaved at least five people in his household, valued at £620 in his estate.
records.origins: Born to a Huguenot family that fled La Rochelle for New York and Boston, Faneuil inherited the fortune of his uncle Andrew Faneuil in 1738. The family traded fish, timber and provisions to the West Indies and imported sugar and molasses.
records.role_summary: Faneuil's trade supplied Caribbean slave plantations and he took part in the triangle trade, including at least one slaving voyage. In 1740 he offered Boston a market hall; Faneuil Hall opened in 1742, built in part with profits tied to slavery.

roleDetail.d: His estate inventory listed five enslaved people; a 1738 letter refers to buying an enslaved boy.
The National Park Service acknowledges that part of the money for Faneuil Hall came from the slave trade; how central slavery was to his wealth is debated.

records.legacy: Faneuil Hall became the 'Cradle of Liberty', where colonists protested British rule. Since 2017 activists have called for renaming it; Boston has declined but considered an auction-block memorial by artist Steven Locke.

legacyDetail.d: The New Democracy Coalition proposed renaming the hall (e.g. after Crispus Attucks); Mayor Marty Walsh rejected the idea in 2017.

sources.label: History of Massachusetts — Was Faneuil Hall Built with Slave Money?
GBH — Proposed memorial at Faneuil Hall would recognize the victims of the slave trade
Wikipedia — Peter Faneuil

connections.label: fellow Boston-area elite with Caribbean slavery wealth
Huguenot merchant networks linking French and British Caribbean

records.name: Royall family (Antigua and Medford)
records.scaleNote: Among the largest slaveholding families in colonial Massachusetts; they brought 27 enslaved people from Antigua in 1737, and more than 60 people were held on the Medford estate over four decades (per the Royall House and Slave Quarters).
records.origins: Isaac Royall Sr. (c. 1677–1739) grew rich in Antigua as a sugar planter, rum distiller and slave trader. In 1732 he bought a 504-acre Medford estate and moved there in 1737 with his family and 27 enslaved Africans.
records.role_summary: The Royalls ran an Antigua sugar plantation and traded enslaved people while holding dozens in bondage at Medford. Isaac Royall Jr., a Loyalist, fled in 1775; his bequest funded Harvard's first professorship of law.

roleDetail.d: The family's Antigua sugar wealth paid for the Medford mansion and its surviving slave quarters.
In 1783 Belinda, a woman the Royalls had enslaved, successfully petitioned the Massachusetts legislature for a pension from the Royall estate.

records.legacy: The Royall House and Slave Quarters in Medford is a museum interpreting the family's enslavement of Africans. Harvard Law School's shield, based on the Royall coat of arms, was retired by the Harvard Corporation in March 2016 after student protests ('Royall Must Fall').

legacyDetail.d: The Harvard Corporation voted unanimously to retire the 80-year-old emblem.

legacyDetail.t: Only surviving freestanding slave quarters in New England.
legacyDetail.d: The 1730s building is a rare physical record of Northern slavery.

sources.label: Royall House and Slave Quarters — The Royalls
Bloomberg Law — At Harvard Law School, Battle for Inclusion Continues (2016)
Wikipedia — Royall House and Slave Quarters

records.name: Henry Laurens
records.scaleNote: His firm Austin & Laurens handled the sale of c. 8,000–10,000 Africans at Charleston between 1749 and 1762, one of the largest slave-trading houses in North America; he held c. 300 enslaved people at his death.
records.origins: The son of a Huguenot saddler in Charleston, Laurens trained in a London counting house. In 1748 he formed a partnership with merchant George Austin to export rice and import goods.
records.role_summary: Austin & Laurens received slave ships on commission (10%, double the rate for other goods), advertised and auctioned captives in Charleston, and acted as agents for British firms including Richard Oswald's, which ran Bunce Island in Sierra Leone. Laurens left the direct trade around 1763 but remained a large planter.

roleDetail.d: The firm marketed thousands of captives arriving from Senegambia, Sierra Leone and elsewhere, earning commissions per sale.
He was President of the Continental Congress (1777–78), was held in the Tower of London (1780–81), and helped negotiate the 1783 peace with Richard Oswald, his former trade partner.

records.legacy: His Mepkin plantation is now Mepkin Abbey, a Trappist monastery. Charleston's role as a principal US landing port is now interpreted at the International African American Museum (opened 2023).

legacyDetail.d: The 'Papers of Henry Laurens' are a key source for the Charleston slave market.

sources.label: World History Encyclopedia — Henry Laurens
Encyclopedia.com — Laurens, Henry (1724–1792)
Wikipedia — Henry Laurens

connections.label: agent for Oswald's Bunce Island captives
held in the Tower of London, 1780–81

records.name: Franklin & Armfield
records.scaleNote: The largest domestic slave-trading firm in the US, 1828–1836 (Encyclopedia Virginia); it shipped c. 1,000 people a year in the 1830s, and the City of Alexandria counts over 3,750 people exported.
records.origins: Isaac Franklin had traded enslaved people from the Chesapeake to Natchez since 1808; he met John Armfield in 1824 and they formed a partnership in 1828. They leased a building at 1315 Duke Street, Alexandria, and turned it into a holding pen.
records.role_summary: Armfield bought people in Maryland and Virginia, held them in Alexandria and sent them south by coastal ship or on foot in chained coffles. Franklin sold them in Natchez and New Orleans to cotton and sugar planters, profiting from the post-1808 domestic trade.

roleDetail.d: The firm ran its own vessels from Alexandria to New Orleans, as well as overland coffles to Natchez.
The firm was a major channel of the forced migration of c. 1 million people from the Upper South to the Deep South.

records.legacy: The partners retired rich in 1836. The Alexandria pen is now the Freedom House Museum, run by the City of Alexandria; historian Joshua Rothman's 'The Ledger and the Chain' (2021) reconstructs the firm's history.

legacyDetail.d: The 1315 Duke Street building is a National Historic Landmark interpreting the domestic slave trade.

sources.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — Franklin and Armfield
New York Review of Books — Partners in Brutality (on the domestic slave trade)
City of Alexandria — Freedom House Museum

connections.label: co-founder; ran New Orleans and Natchez
domestic trade boomed after 1808 import ban

records.name: Isaac Franklin
records.scaleNote: Co-head of the largest US domestic slave-trading firm; held 636 people in slavery at his death in 1846 (per Wikipedia, citing estate records).
records.origins: Born in Sumner County, Tennessee, Franklin began buying people in Baltimore and Alexandria with his brothers in 1808 and taking them down the Mississippi to Natchez and New Orleans.
records.role_summary: As partner in Franklin & Armfield he ran the selling end of the business in Natchez and New Orleans. He invested his profits in Fairvue plantation in Tennessee and several cotton plantations in West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, including Angola.

roleDetail.d: Estate records list several hundred enslaved people on his Louisiana plantations and over 100 at Fairvue.
His Angola lands later became the Louisiana State Penitentiary, where convict labour continued on the former plantation.

records.legacy: His widow Adelicia (later Acklen) used the estate to build Belmont Mansion in Nashville, now part of Belmont University. Angola remains the largest maximum-security prison in the US.

legacyDetail.d: The museum now researches and names the enslaved people of the Franklin estate.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Isaac Franklin
Belmont Mansion — Isaac Franklin
City of Alexandria — Biography of Isaac Franklin (PDF)

records.name: Lehman Brothers
records.scaleNote: A Montgomery cotton-factoring house whose business depended on slave-grown cotton; the 1860 census lists Mayer Lehman as enslaving seven people.
records.origins: Bavarian-born Henry Lehman opened a dry-goods store in Montgomery in 1844; his brothers Emanuel and Mayer joined, and by 1850 the firm was Lehman Brothers. They accepted raw cotton as payment and became cotton factors.
records.role_summary: As cotton factors the Lehmans extended credit to planters, took cotton in payment and sold it to Northern and British mills, binding the firm to plantation slavery. Mayer Lehman enslaved people in his household, and during the Civil War the firm supported the Confederacy.

roleDetail.d: Credit to planters secured on future crops linked the firm's profits directly to enslaved labour.
The firm ran blockades and supported Confederate finance; Emanuel and Mayer received pardons after the war.

records.legacy: The firm moved to New York, helped found the New York Cotton Exchange (1870), and became a major investment bank until its 2008 bankruptcy. Under Chicago's 2002 slavery-era disclosure ordinance it acknowledged its ties to slavery; its history is now taught by Harvard Business School's Baker Library.

legacyDetail.d: Lehman was among the first city contractors to disclose slavery-era ties under the ordinance.

sources.label: Harvard Business School Baker Library — Lehman Brothers: General Merchants to Commodities Brokers
New York Review of Books — The Lehman Trilogy and Wall Street's Debt to Slavery
Business Alabama — The Alabama Origin of Lehman Bros.

records.name: JPMorgan Chase
records.scaleNote: Per its 2005 disclosure, predecessor banks Citizens Bank and Canal Bank of Louisiana accepted c. 13,000 enslaved people as loan collateral (1831–1865) and came to own c. 1,250 of them through defaults.
records.origins: JPMorgan Chase absorbed Bank One in 2004, whose lineage included two antebellum New Orleans banks: Citizens Bank and Canal Bank. Louisiana's property banks raised capital and lent to planters against mortgages on land and enslaved people.
records.role_summary: The predecessor banks took enslaved men, women and children as collateral and seized many when borrowers defaulted, turning human beings into secured assets of the banking system.

roleDetail.d: c. 13,000 people pledged as collateral; c. 1,250 owned after defaults (2005 company statement to the City of Chicago).
Reporting on the 1838 Jesuit sale notes that people sold to Louisiana were mortgaged to Citizens Bank.

records.legacy: In January 2005 CEO William Harrison and President Jamie Dimon apologised and created a $5 million scholarship programme for Black students in Louisiana. Reparations advocates called it a first step.

legacyDetail.d: Prompted by Chicago's slavery-era disclosure ordinance.

sources.label: NBC News — JPMorgan: Predecessors linked to slavery
Diverse Issues in Higher Education — JPMorgan Apologizes for Predecessor Banks' Acceptance of Slaves as Collateral
New York Sun — From J.P. Morgan Chase, an Apology and $5 Million in Slavery Reparations

connections.label: successor of Citizens and Canal banks

records.name: Wachovia / Wells Fargo
records.scaleNote: Per Wachovia's 2005 report, predecessor Georgia Railroad and Banking Co. owned at least 162 enslaved people and the Bank of Charleston accepted at least 529 as loan collateral.
records.origins: Wachovia acquired descendants of the Bank of Charleston (1991) and, via its 2001 merger with First Union, the Georgia Railroad and Banking Company. Wells Fargo bought Wachovia in 2008.
records.role_summary: The Georgia railroad bank owned enslaved people who were forced to build and work the railroad; the Bank of Charleston lent on mortgages secured by enslaved people and acquired some when borrowers defaulted.

roleDetail.d: At least 162 people owned by the Georgia bank; at least 529 pledged to the Bank of Charleston (Wachovia 2005).
The bank said gaps in the records make the true numbers unknowable.

records.legacy: CEO Ken Thompson apologised in June 2005 after research required by Chicago's ordinance; Chicago officials criticised the bank for first filing an affidavit denying any ties.

legacyDetail.d: Wachovia also pledged support for African American history education.

sources.label: CNN Money — Wachovia apologizes for slavery ties (2005)
NBC News — Wachovia apologizes to black Americans
JURIST — Fourth-largest US bank apologizes for slavery ties

connections.label: Bank of Charleston loans on enslaved people

records.name: Aetna
records.scaleNote: Aetna said in 2000 that it wrote no more than about a dozen policies in the 1850s insuring enslaved people's lives for their enslavers.
records.origins: Aetna Life Insurance Company was founded in Hartford in 1853. Like several Northern insurers, it sold policies to Southern enslavers.
records.role_summary: The policies compensated enslavers financially when an insured enslaved person died, treating people as insurable property.

roleDetail.d: Discovered after researcher Deadria Farmer-Paellmann asked the company about its records in 1999–2000.

records.legacy: In March 2000 Aetna apologised but said no reparations were due. Farmer-Paellmann's work fed California's 2000 Slavery Era Insurance Registry law and later corporate reparations lawsuits.

legacyDetail.d: Among the first US corporate apologies for slavery.

sources.label: Las Vegas Sun (AP) — Apology made for slave policies (2000)
Insurance Journal — Slavery & Insurance (2000)
Democracy Now! — Aetna acknowledges issuing slave policies

records.name: New York Life (Nautilus Insurance Company)
records.scaleNote: Per its 2002 letter to California regulators, predecessor Nautilus sold slaveholder policies for about two years (1846–48); 339 of its first 1,000 policies insured enslaved people.
records.origins: Nautilus Insurance Company was chartered in New York in 1841 and began selling life policies in 1845; it renamed itself New York Life in 1849.
records.role_summary: Nautilus sold one-year policies (usually under $500) to enslavers, mostly in Virginia and Kentucky, on enslaved boatmen, carpenters, miners and labourers, paying the enslaver on death. Trustees voted to stop in April 1848.

roleDetail.d: The ledgers, now partly at the New York Public Library, name insured enslaved people — a genealogical source today.

records.legacy: New York Life has expressed 'profound regret' and funds scholarships and research; it disclosed its records under California's Slavery Era Insurance Registry.

legacyDetail.d: The company reported 15 death claims under slave policies totalling c. $7,474.

sources.label: California Department of Insurance — New York Life letter (2002, PDF)
New York Public Library Archives — Nautilus/New York Life slave policy records

records.name: Brown Brothers Harriman
records.scaleNote: Predecessor Brown Brothers & Co. was a leading financier of the antebellum cotton trade; its own history says borrowers pledged land and enslaved people to collateralise cotton finance.
records.base: New York (origins in Baltimore and Liverpool)
records.origins: Irish-born Alexander Brown founded a linen business in Baltimore in 1800; his sons opened houses in Liverpool, Philadelphia and New York (1825). The firm became one of the leading Anglo-American merchant banks.
records.role_summary: The Browns financed and shipped Southern cotton to Liverpool, advanced credit to planters and factors, and in some cases took over mortgaged plantations. A reparations lawsuit alleged the firm held Louisiana plantations with 346 enslaved people; that claim is unadjudicated.

roleDetail.d: The firm linked Southern plantations with factors, brokers, shippers and insurers on both sides of the Atlantic (per BBH's own history).
Allegations from the 2002 slavery reparations litigation; not established in court.

records.legacy: Brown Brothers merged into Brown Brothers Harriman in 1931 and remains a private bank. It now states that it regrets its predecessor's role in a cotton trade that 'relied on the abhorrent practice of slavery'.

legacyDetail.d: BBH's '200 Years of Partnership' history addresses its cotton-trade past.

sources.label: Brown Brothers Harriman — The Cotton Trade
Kirkus Reviews — Inside Money by Zachary Karabell

connections.label: plantation credit secured on enslaved people

records.name: Timothy Meaher and the Clotilda
records.scaleNote: Organised the last documented slave voyage to the US (1860), which brought 110 captives from Ouidah to Mobile.
records.origins: Maine-born Timothy Meaher became a Mobile shipbuilder, steamboat owner and planter. He reportedly bet that he could bring Africans into the US despite the 1808 ban.
records.role_summary: Meaher financed the schooner Clotilda, captained by William Foster, which bought 110 people at Ouidah from the Kingdom of Dahomey's trade. After landing in July 1860, the ship was burned and scuttled to hide the evidence, and the captives were divided among Meaher, his brothers and Foster. No one was convicted.

roleDetail.d: Federal charges were brought, but the case was dropped in 1861.
After emancipation, survivors including Cudjo Lewis (Oluale Kossola) founded Africatown near Mobile.

records.legacy: The wreck was identified in May 2019 by the Alabama Historical Commission. Meaher descendants still own much land around Africatown; in 2022 some called their ancestor's actions 'evil and unforgivable', and Clotilda descendants pursue reconciliation and community revival.

legacyDetail.d: Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2021.
A documentary film follows Africatown's Clotilda descendants and their fight over land, pollution and memory.

sources.label: Encyclopedia of Alabama — Africatown

CBS News / 60 Minutes — Descendants of Alabama slave owner say they're 'figuring out next steps'

records.name: Charles Lamar
records.scaleNote: Organised the Wanderer voyage, which landed c. 400 Africans on Jekyll Island in 1858 (estimates 409–490 per Georgia Encyclopedia and others).
records.origins: From a wealthy Savannah family, Lamar was a businessman and outspoken campaigner for reopening the African slave trade.
records.role_summary: With William Corrie of Charleston he refitted the yacht Wanderer as a slaver; it embarked captives at the Congo River and landed them at Jekyll Island in November 1858. Federal prosecutions failed, and many captives were sold across the South.

roleDetail.d: The voyage was meant to provoke and test enforcement of the 1808 ban; Southern juries declined to convict.

records.legacy: Lamar was killed in April 1865 at Columbus, Georgia, often called the last Confederate officer killed in action. A Wanderer memorial stands on Jekyll Island.

legacyDetail.d: Jekyll Island interprets the landing and the survivors' lives.

sources.label: New Georgia Encyclopedia — Wanderer
Massachusetts Historical Society — The Wanderer, the last American slave ship?

connections.label: captives embarked at the Congo River

records.name: Nathaniel Gordon
records.scaleNote: Captain of the Erie, seized in 1860 with 897 Africans aboard; the only American executed for slave trading.
records.origins: A Maine-born sea captain, Gordon made several voyages in the illegal trade in the 1850s.
records.role_summary: In August 1860 the USS Mohican captured his ship Erie near the Congo River with 897 captives, many of them children. He was convicted under the 1820 law that made slave trading piracy, and Lincoln refused clemency.

roleDetail.d: Executed in New York City on 21 February 1862.
Signalled federal resolve against the trade during the Civil War.

records.legacy: Gordon's case remains the only US execution for slave trading in more than 40 years of the piracy law.

legacyDetail.d: Earlier traders, including the DeWolfs and Lamar, went unpunished.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Nathaniel Gordon
HarpWeek — Execution of Gordon the Slave-Trader (1862)

illegal trade aimed at Cuban markets

records.name: Julián de Zulueta, Marquis of Álava
records.scaleNote: Historian Hugh Thomas calls him 'the last great slave trader of Cuba'; his ships carried 500–600 captives per voyage from Cabinda and later steamships over 1,000, during the illegal trade.
records.origins: Born in Álava (Basque Country), he arrived in Havana in 1832, worked for slave-trading relatives and married into the family of trafficker Salvador Samá.
records.role_summary: Zulueta organised illegal slaving expeditions to West Central Africa long after Spain's 1817/1820 treaty with Britain, and used the captives on his own sugar estates in Matanzas, among the most modern in Cuba. He also imported Chinese indentured labourers.

roleDetail.d: He financed voyages into the 1860s, when Cuba was the main remaining market for the Atlantic trade.
He was mayor of Havana, a senator for life and a pillar of the pro-slavery Spanish lobby; he was made Marquis of Álava in 1875.

records.legacy: A Havana street is still popularly called 'Zulueta', and his fortune helped build palaces in Vitoria-Gasteiz. Basque and Cuban researchers have recently reassessed his record.

legacyDetail.d: Calle Zulueta (officially Agramonte since 1909) still bears his name in practice.

sources.label: About Basque Country — The Havana street that still bears the name of a Basque slave trader
Wikipedia — Julián de Zulueta, 1st Marquis of Álava

records.name: Pedro Blanco
records.scaleNote: Ran slave factories at Lomboko on the Gallinas River c. 1822–1839; around 2,000 people a year were shipped from the Gallinas by the late 1830s.
records.base: Lomboko, Gallinas River (Sierra Leone) and Havana
records.origins: Born in Málaga, Blanco sailed as a slave-ship mate and captain before setting up a trading post on the Gallinas River, allied with the Vai ruler King Siaka.
records.role_summary: From fortified barracoons at Lomboko he bought captives from African suppliers and sold them to Spanish and Portuguese ships bound for Cuba and Puerto Rico. His Havana partner was Lino Carballo, with agents in Puerto Rico and elsewhere. The Amistad captives (1839) passed through Lomboko.

roleDetail.d: The Africans who later revolted aboard the Amistad were held at Lomboko before shipment to Havana in 1839.
Tales of his royal wealth are partly legend; historian María del Carmen Barcia (2018) separates myth from documents.

records.legacy: Blanco left Africa around 1839; the British Royal Navy destroyed the Gallinas factories in 1849. He has become a figure of fiction, such as Carlos Bardem's novel 'Mongo Blanco'.

legacyDetail.d: The 1849 destruction of the Gallinas barracoons was part of the West Africa Squadron's campaign.

records.name: Joaquim Pereira Marinho
records.scaleNote: Described by Brazilian historians as one of the largest traffickers of enslaved Africans into Salvador during the illegal trade (1830–1850); he died with an estate of c. 8,000 contos de réis.
records.origins: Born in Portugal, he came to Salvador as a young man and rose through trade in tobacco and goods for the African trade.
records.role_summary: He financed and shipped illegal slaving voyages from Bahia to the Bight of Benin after Brazil's 1831 ban, then invested his profits in shipping, railways, real estate and loans to sugar planters.

roleDetail.d: Brazilian historians name him among Bahia's chief smugglers of Africans in 1830–1850.
He led the Companhia Baiana de Navegação and invested in railways.

records.legacy: He was made a count and was a benefactor of the Santa Casa de Misericórdia; a statue of him stands at Salvador's Santa Izabel Hospital, debated since 2020.

legacyDetail.d: After the 2020 toppling of Colston in Bristol, Bahian journalists and activists questioned the statue.

records.name: Elias Antônio Lopes
records.scaleNote: Historian Manolo Florentino ranks him as the third-largest slave trader in the Rio de Janeiro market around 1800; he owned at least four slave ships.
records.origins: A Portuguese merchant (some accounts say of Lebanese descent) who emigrated to Rio de Janeiro, he became one of the city's richest men through trade, royal contracts and the slave trade.
records.role_summary: He financed slaving voyages to Africa, mainly to Angola and West Central Africa, which supplied Rio's market. In 1808 he gave his estate at Quinta da Boa Vista to the exiled Portuguese Prince Regent João, winning titles and favour.

roleDetail.d: His manor became the Paço de São Cristóvão, home of the Brazilian imperial family.
His vessels included the Europa, Paquete Infante, São João Americano and Deligente.

records.legacy: The palace later housed Brazil's National Museum, gutted by fire in 2018; its foundation in slave-trade wealth is now discussed by historians.

legacyDetail.d: Rebuilding is under way after the 2018 fire.

sources.label: Jornal do Brasil — Gênese da corrupção no Brasil (2019)
Wikipedia — Paço de São Cristóvão

records.name: José Bernardino de Sá
records.scaleNote: Historians attribute to him the trafficking of at least 19,000 Africans into south-eastern Brazil between 1825 and 1851, mostly illegally after 1831.
aliases: Viscount of Vila Nova do Minho
records.origins: Portuguese-born, he worked as a clerk in a Rio trading house when he organised his first known slave shipment in 1825.
records.role_summary: With Manoel Pinto da Fonseca he dominated the illegal slave trade into south-east Brazil after 1831, landing captives on secluded beaches. He invested the profits in real estate, ships and finance, becoming the largest individual shareholder of the Banco do Brasil.

roleDetail.d: Trafficked c. 19,000+ people despite the 1831 ban.
Major shareholder in the Banco do Brasil after its 1853 re-founding.

records.legacy: In September 2023 federal prosecutors opened an inquiry into the Banco do Brasil's links to slavery after historians traced Sá's investments; the bank apologised publicly on 18 November 2023.

legacyDetail.d: Prosecutors called the bank's proposed measures insufficient.

sources.label: JusticeInfo.net — Brazil bank's ties to slavery reopen wounds, reparations debate
ArtCultura (UFU) — article on José Bernardino de Sá and the São Pedro theatre

records.name: Newport, Rhode Island
records.description: Colonial Newport was the leading slaving port of British North America; Rhode Island launched c. 60% of North American slaving voyages (c. 1,000 voyages, 1700s–1807), most from Newport before the Revolution. Rum distilled from Caribbean molasses was the main trade good on the African coast.

connections.label: Mark Anthony DeWolf sailed from Newport

records.name: Bristol, Rhode Island
records.description: After the Revolution Bristol became Rhode Island's main slaving port, dominated by the DeWolf family. Local craftsmen made chains, sails and rope for slave ships, and distilleries turned Cuban molasses into rum for the African trade.

connections.label: successor to Newport as chief slaving port

records.name: Charleston, South Carolina (incl. Sullivan's Island and Gadsden's Wharf)
records.description: Charleston was the principal US landing port for African captives; scholars estimate c. 40% of enslaved Africans brought to mainland North America arrived there. Arrivals were quarantined in 'pest houses' on Sullivan's Island, and in 1806 the city required slave ships to dock at Gadsden's Wharf, where c. 100,000 people were landed, many in the 1803–07 rush before the federal ban.

records.name: International African American Museum (Charleston)
records.description: Opened in June 2023 on the site of Gadsden's Wharf, the museum interprets the forced arrival of Africans in Charleston and includes a centre for African American genealogy. Nearby, the Toni Morrison Society placed a 'Bench by the Road' on Sullivan's Island in 2008.

records.name: New Orleans
records.description: New Orleans became the largest slave market in the US during the domestic trade, receiving people shipped and marched from the Upper South to Deep South cotton and sugar plantations. Its banks lent to planters against mortgages on enslaved people.

connections.label: 1838 sale shipped people via New Orleans

records.name: Havana
records.description: Havana was the hub of Cuba's slave trade, which grew enormously after 1790 with the sugar boom. More than half of the almost one million Africans taken to Cuba arrived illegally after the 1820 Anglo-Spanish ban; the last known slave ship landed c. 1867, and slavery ended in 1886.

records.name: Lomboko and the Gallinas barracoons
records.description: Pedro Blanco's fortified slave factories on islands at the mouth of the Gallinas River (today Sierra Leone/Liberia border). The Amistad captives were held here in 1839. The Royal Navy destroyed the barracoons in 1849.

records.name: Valongo Wharf, Rio de Janeiro
records.description: Built from 1811 to land enslaved Africans, Valongo was the main point of arrival in the Americas, receiving up to c. 900,000 people (per UNESCO) before it was paved over in 1843. Rediscovered in 2011, it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 9 July 2017.

records.name: Salvador da Bahia
records.description: Colonial Brazil's capital and one of the largest slave ports in history: per SlaveVoyages, c. 1.2 million Africans disembarked in Bahia between the 1550s and 1850s, many from the Bight of Benin. The 1835 Malê revolt of enslaved Muslim Africans took place here.

records.name: Paço de São Cristóvão (Quinta da Boa Vista)
records.description: Manor built c. 1803 by slave trader Elias Antônio Lopes and given to Prince Regent João in 1808; it became the residence of Brazil's imperial family and later the National Museum, which burned in 2018.

records.name: Banco do Brasil
records.description: Brazil's state-controlled bank, re-founded in 1853 with slave trafficker José Bernardino de Sá among its largest shareholders. After federal prosecutors (MPF) opened an inquiry in September 2023, drawing on a study by 14 historians, bank president Tarciana Medeiros issued a public apology on 18 November 2023; prosecutors said an apology alone was insufficient and pressed for reparations.

records.name: Eusébio de Queirós Law (1850)
records.description: Brazilian Law No. 581 of 4 September 1850 effectively ended the transatlantic slave trade to Brazil, enforcing the unenforced 1831 ban under heavy British naval pressure after the 1845 Aberdeen Act. Landings largely ceased by 1856, though slavery continued.

records.name: Lei Áurea (Golden Law), 1888
records.description: Law No. 3,353 of 13 May 1888, signed by Princess Isabel as regent, abolished slavery in Brazil without compensation to enslavers, freeing c. 700,000 people. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery; freed people received no state support.

records.name: Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves (1807)
records.description: Signed by Thomas Jefferson on 2 March 1807 and effective 1 January 1808, the earliest date the Constitution allowed, it banned the import of enslaved people into the US. Enforcement was weak; an 1820 law made slave trading piracy punishable by death. Domestic slavery and the internal trade continued.

records.name: The Sally (1764–1765)
records.description: Brigantine owned by Nicholas Brown and Company, sailed by Esek Hopkins from Providence to the Windward Coast. Of 196 Africans bought, at least 109 died through a failed revolt, suicide, starvation and disease; survivors were sold in Antigua.

records.name: The Wanderer (1858)
records.description: A luxury racing yacht refitted as a slaver by Charles Lamar and William Corrie; it landed c. 400 Africans on Jekyll Island, Georgia, on 28 November 1858, roughly 50 years after the ban. The owners escaped conviction.

records.name: The Erie (1860)
records.description: Slave ship captained by Nathaniel Gordon, seized by USS Mohican off the Congo River in August 1860 with 897 captives aboard, many of them children. The captives were taken to Liberia.

records.name: Africatown, Mobile
records.description: Community near Mobile, Alabama founded after the Civil War by survivors of the Clotilda, including Cudjo Lewis (Oluale Kossola). Descendants still live there, and the community has worked on preservation, environmental justice and a heritage house since the 2019 wreck identification.

records.name: Royall House and Slave Quarters
records.description: Medford estate of the Royall family, with the only known surviving freestanding slave quarters in New England. A museum since 1910, it interprets the lives of the people the Royalls enslaved, including Belinda Sutton. Isaac Royall Jr.'s bequest funded Harvard Law's first professorship; the Royall-arms law school shield was retired in 2016.

records.name: Faneuil Hall, Boston
records.description: Market hall and meeting place given to Boston by Peter Faneuil and opened in 1742, known as the 'Cradle of Liberty'. Part of its funding came from Faneuil's slavery-linked trade, which has led to calls since 2017 to rename it and to plans for a memorial.

records.name: Freedom House Museum (1315 Duke Street)
records.description: The Alexandria headquarters and slave pen of Franklin & Armfield, and later of other traders, through which thousands of people were sold south. It is now a National Historic Landmark and museum run by the City of Alexandria.

records.name: Citizens Bank and Canal Bank of Louisiana
records.description: Antebellum New Orleans banks that accepted c. 13,000 enslaved people as loan collateral between 1831 and 1865 and came to own c. 1,250 through defaults, per JPMorgan Chase's 2005 disclosure. They are predecessors of JPMorgan Chase via Bank One.

connections.label: 1838 sale: people mortgaged to Citizens Bank

records.name: Chicago Slavery Era Disclosure Ordinance (2002)
records.description: City ordinance requiring companies with city contracts to research and disclose any profits from slavery or slaveholder insurance, modelled on California's 2000 Slavery Era Insurance Registry law. It led to disclosures and apologies by JPMorgan Chase, Wachovia and Lehman Brothers.

records.name: Brown University
records.description: Founded in 1764 with the Brown family as main benefactors and renamed for Nicholas Brown Jr. in 1804. Its 2006 Slavery and Justice report, commissioned by President Ruth Simmons, documented ties to the slave trade and led to a campus memorial (2014) and the Center for the Study of Slavery and Justice.

records.name: Georgetown University and the 1838 sale
records.description: In 1838 the Maryland Jesuits, led by Georgetown president Thomas Mulledy, sold 272 enslaved people to Louisiana planters Henry Johnson and Jesse Batey for $115,000, partly to pay Georgetown's debts. Georgetown apologised in 2017, renamed buildings and offers admissions preference to descendants; in 2021 the Jesuits pledged $100 million towards the Descendants Truth and Reconciliation Foundation.

records.name: Descendants Truth & Reconciliation Foundation
records.description: Partnership between the GU272 Descendants Association and the Jesuit Conference of Canada and the US, launched in 2021 with a $100 million Jesuit pledge towards a $1 billion goal. It funds descendants' education, racial-justice programmes and support for elderly descendants; some descendants have criticised the pace of funding.

records.name: CARICOM Reparations Commission and Ten Point Plan
records.description: Set up by CARICOM heads of government in 2013 and chaired by Sir Hilary Beckles of the University of the West Indies, it prepares the Caribbean case for reparatory justice from former colonial powers. Its Ten Point Action Plan (2014) calls for: a full formal apology; repatriation; an Indigenous peoples development programme; cultural institutions; action on the public health crisis; illiteracy eradication; an African knowledge programme; psychological rehabilitation; technology transfer; and debt cancellation.

records.name: Tinubu family (Lagos)
records.scaleNote: The family as a lineage was not a slave-trading house; its link to the trade runs through Madam Efunroye Tinubu (c.1805–1887), who traded captives for guns with Brazilian and Portuguese merchants and reportedly held over 360 enslaved people herself (per her biographers as summarised by Wikipedia and UFRGS).
records.origins: The name comes from Madam Efunroye Tinubu, an Egba-born trader who moved to Lagos in the 1830s and married into elite circles, including the exiled Oba Adele and later the Islamic scholar Momodu (Muhammad) Bukar/Bugara. Her biographer Oladipo Yemitan records that she had two sons by her first (Owu) husband but her later marriages produced no children.
records.role_summary: Madam Tinubu dealt in salt, tobacco, guns and enslaved people from the Abeokuta hinterland, and kept trading captives with Brazilian merchants such as Domingo José Martínez after the 1852 Anglo-Lagos treaty banned the trade. The wider 'Tinubu family' is a name-group, not a single bloodline: per Yemitan, the name is borne by Bugara's children by other wives, by her Egba relatives from Abeokuta, and by descendants of people she had enslaved.

roleDetail.t: Madam Tinubu traded captives after the 1852 ban.
roleDetail.d: Accounts based on Yemitan and British records describe her secretly exchanging enslaved people for guns with Brazilian/Portuguese merchants and a reported 1853 dispute with Domingo Martínez over the price of 20 captives.

roleDetail.t: Three lines bear the Tinubu name.
roleDetail.d: Yemitan (quoted by Prof. Siyan Oyeweso and summarised by Farooq Kperogi) says the name passed to Bugara's children by other wives (no blood tie to her), to her Abeokuta relatives, and to 'scions of her former slaves'.

roleDetail.t: The name, not wealth from slaving, is the main inheritance.
roleDetail.d: The lineage's later prominence rests on her civic fame (Iyalode of Egba, Tinubu Square) and on family land in Lagos, e.g. c.9 acres in Surulere the 'Iyalode Tinubu' family won in court (ThisDay, 2021).

records.legacy: Madam Tinubu is commemorated as a nationalist heroine at Tinubu Square, Lagos, and the family estate still litigates over her lands. Claims that Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu descends from her are widely repeated but unproven: no published genealogy links him to her line; in 2025 the estate's administrator called him a 'direct descendant' without giving evidence, while columnist Farooq Kperogi (citing Lagos historians) argues he belongs to none of the Tinubu branches. Descendants or bearers of the name carry no guilt for 19th-century acts.

legacyDetail.t: Descent of President Bola Tinubu: unproven.
legacyDetail.d: Asserted by estate administrator Chief Akindele Adamakin (Leadership, 2025) and disputed by Kperogi (2022); neither side has published documentary genealogy, and Madam Tinubu's own children are not known to have left a traceable line.
Whatever the genealogy, moral responsibility for slave trading lies with those who did it; living people who share the name or descent are not culpable.
In 2021 the Iyalode Tinubu family, headed by Garuba Bakare, took possession of c.8.99 acres with 50+ houses in Surulere after a Lagos High Court judgment.

sources.label: Farooq Kperogi — Kanuri origins of the Tinubu family in Lagos (2022)
Leadership (Nigeria) — Tinubu estate administrator decries trespass, calls for family reunification
ThisDay — Tinubu family takes possession of land with 50 houses in Surulere (2021)

records.name: Elizabeth Frazer Skelton ("Mammy Skelton")
records.scaleNote: After her husband's death she was reportedly responsible for about half of the Rio Nunez region's exports for a time (per the Dictionary of African Biography as summarised by Wikipedia); no voyage count is documented.
records.origins: Daughter of the Scottish slave trader John Frazer (1769–1813) and Phenda, an African woman who ran a slave-trading business at Bangalan on the Rio Pongo. She was schooled at the Bashia mission and in Liverpool.
records.role_summary: With her Anglo-African husband William Skelton Jr. she founded the slave fort Victoria on the Rio Nunez in 1825/26, from which captives were moved by canoe or overland to Portuguese Bissau. After his death she ran the business herself, later moving into slave-worked groundnut farming under British pressure c.1840.

roleDetail.d: Fort Victoria on the Rio Nunez (1825/26), managed jointly with William Skelton Jr.

roleDetail.t: Heir to a transatlantic slaving fortune.
roleDetail.d: Her father shipped captives to Charleston and, after 1807, to Spanish East Florida, where he held slave plantations; she won the inheritance in 1851 after decades of litigation.

roleDetail.t: Bridge between generations of Rio Pongo houses.
roleDetail.d: Her daughter Mary Ann married Joseph Richmond Lightburn in 1846, tying the Frazer–Skelton house to the Lightbourn family.

records.legacy: Her case is a leading example of the Eurafrican 'big women' traders of the Upper Guinea coast studied by Bruce Mouser and others. Her fortune passed into the intermarried Skelton, Lightburn and related houses of the Rios Nunez and Pongo.

legacyDetail.d: She features in scholarship on 'women traders and big-men' of Guinea-Conakry and in the Enslaved.org biographical database.

sources.label: Enslaved.org — Elizabeth Frazer Skelton (biography)
Wikipedia — Elizabeth Frazer Skelton (citing Dictionary of African Biography)
Mouser — Trade, Coasters, and Conflict in the Rio Pongo, 1790–1808 (J. African History)

connections.label: inland supply routes from Futa Jallon

records.name: Lightbourn family & Niara Bely (Farenya, Rio Pongo)
records.scaleNote: One of the dominant Creole slave-trading houses of the Rio Pongo c.1809–1850s (per Mouser); British naval and commission records name 'Mrs Lightbourn', but no aggregate captive count is documented.
records.origins: Stiles Edward Lightbourn, a slave trader from South Carolina, married Niara Bely (Elizabeth Bailey Gomez), daughter of Emmanuel Gomez, ruler of Bakia, in 1809. They first lived at Bangalan, then founded the trading settlement of Farenya.
records.role_summary: While Lightbourn sailed the Atlantic (he was lost at sea in 1833), Niara Bely ran Farenya, a terminus for caravan routes from Futa Jallon, as a slave-trading and storage post. She became a chief with her son Stiles Jr. in 1835 and allied with Mary Faber in regional wars.

roleDetail.d: Founded 1809; archaeology (Kenneth Kelly) suggests the village grew up around her outpost.
In 1842 she and Mary Faber helped Fula forces plunder the Susu capital Thia; after the 1852 slave-trade ban they fought the Susu until defeat in 1855.
British agent Benjamin Campbell admitted dealing with 'Mrs Lightbourn' in 1841 but claimed only legitimate goods.

records.legacy: Niara Bely was baptised Anglican in 1878 and died in 1879; her remains were re-interred in a cement grave at Farenya in 1966, now a site of archaeological and memorial interest. Her son's line and the Lightburn name persisted in the Rio Pongo.

legacyDetail.d: Excavations at Farenya and the 'Queen's graveyard' have been studied by archaeologists and visited by memorial trips (Guinéenews, 2025).

sources.label: Wikipedia — Niara Bely (citing Mouser 1980, 2013)
BlackPast — Mouser, The curious history of the Rio Pongo
Wikipedia — Farenya

records.name: Ormond family of Bangalan (John "Mongo John" Ormond)
records.scaleNote: Bangalan was a leading Rio Pongo slave factory from the 1790s into the 1840s (per Mouser and Canot's memoir); no reliable captive totals exist.
records.origins: An English trader, John Ormond, ran a factory on the Rio Pongo by the early 1790s (employing Anglo-African agents such as Bootle, killed in 1792). His Eurafrican son John Ormond Jr. inherited the Bangalan business.
records.role_summary: John Ormond Jr., called 'Mongo' ('king of the river'), bought captives from Fula and Susu caravans and sold them to visiting Spanish, Portuguese and American slavers; Théophile Conneau ('Captain Canot') described working for him in the late 1820s. A later William Ormond fought Mary Faber for control of Bangalan in 1838–40.

roleDetail.d: Canot's narrative depicts 'Jack Ormond' inspecting a captive for purchase at Bangalang (engraving, 1854).

Personal details of 'Mongo John' (his reported death c.1828, harem, wealth) come largely from Canot's sensational 1854 memoir and could not be confirmed in independent records; treat them with caution.
In 1838–40 Mary Faber waged war on her rival William Ormond at Bangalan; he was allied with Freetown interests.

records.legacy: The Ormond story entered popular culture through Canot's memoir and novels such as 'Anthony Adverse'. The family's Bangalan base was absorbed into the Lightbourn–Faber sphere by the 1840s.

legacyDetail.d: The Rio Pongo slave factories, including Ormond's, inspired Hervey Allen's 1933 novel Anthony Adverse.

sources.label: Library Company of Philadelphia (UMBRA) — engraving of 'Jack Ormond' inspecting a slave, from Captain Canot (1854)
Mouser — Trade, Coasters, and Conflict in the Rio Pongo, 1790–1808
Wikipedia — Pongo River (Guinea)

records.name: Faber family (Paul & Mary Faber, Sangha, Rio Pongo)
records.scaleNote: There were 'reportedly 6,000' enslaved people on the Faber property in 1827 (Mouser 1980, as summarised by Wikipedia); the figure is second-hand, unverified and probably inflated.
records.origins: Paul Faber, an American shipowner, set up as a slave trader in the Conakry region by 1809. In 1816 he married Mary (c.1798–after 1857), born in Freetown to Nova Scotian settler parents.
records.role_summary: Paul's ship carried captives to Cuba while Mary ran the fortified 'slave factory' at Sangha with her own private army, disguising it as a plantation to evade the Royal Navy. In 1852 she passed the business to her son William, who traded until at least 1860.

roleDetail.d: Mary Faber held most of the power at Sangha while Paul was absent; captives were described to naval patrols as 'domestics'.
Fought William Ormond (1838–40), joined the 1842 Fula raid on Thia, and fought the Susu after the 1852 ban until defeat in 1855.
A Royal Navy inquiry of 1850 still reported 'Paul Faber' active in the Pongos.

records.legacy: The Fabers are studied as an example of how descendants of freed Nova Scotian settlers in Freetown also became slave traders. The family fort was burned in 1855 and rebuilt.

legacyDetail.d: A daughter of Black Loyalist settlers became a leading slaver, complicating narratives of Sierra Leone as purely a refuge.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Mary Faber de Sanger (citing Mouser 1980; Foster 2010)
Pdavis / O'Byrne — HMS Adelaide inquiry into Paul Faber (1850)

records.name: King Siaka of the Gallinas (Vai)
records.scaleNote: Ruled the Gallinas when it was one of West Africa's busiest illegal slave markets; an 1850 missionary editorial claimed c.10,000 captives a year left the Gallinas (a contemporary estimate, not verified).
records.origins: Siaka was the Vai ruler of the Gallinas coast between the Waanji and Mano rivers in the early 19th century. His power rested on control of the river mouths where Spanish-Cuban traders set up barracoons.
records.role_summary: Siaka partnered with Pedro Blanco, allowing him to build the Lomboko barracoon complex and to post agents along the coast; the Gallinas supplied captives to Cuba, Brazil and the US. In November 1840 his son Prince Manna, acting for the ailing king, signed Joseph Denman's treaty abolishing the trade.

roleDetail.d: The alliance underpinned Blanco's Lomboko operation (1822–1838).

roleDetail.t: Signed away the trade under duress.
roleDetail.d: After Denman's raid freed 841 people and burned eight factories, Prince Manna signed the 21 Nov 1840 treaty for Siaka.
English sources call him 'King Siaka'; the Mande title 'Mansa' appears in some later accounts but is not confirmed in primary sources found.

records.legacy: The Gallinas trade revived after 1840 and the slavers sued Denman personally in the case Buron v. Denman. Gallinas royal lineages (later the Massaquoi family) remained prominent in Sierra Leone and Liberia.

legacyDetail.d: King Momulu Massaquoi's descendants form the contemporary Gallinas royal family (a later, separate ruling line).

records.name: John Kabes of Komenda
records.scaleNote: Principal African merchant to the Royal African Company at Komenda for nearly 40 years (c.1680s–1722) and a supplier of thousands of captives (per Henige 1977 and Daaku 1970); no exact count.
records.origins: Probably the son of John Cabessa, an English-employed official at Fort Amsterdam, he moved to Komenda in the Eguafo kingdom in the 1670s. By 1686 he had replaced Captain Bracon as the main African merchant to the English.
records.role_summary: Kabes supplied the Royal African Company with captives, canoe-men, food, shells and labour for building forts, and controlled who could trade at Komenda. He fought the Dutch WIC in the Komenda Wars (1694–1700) and turned his commercial power into a stool (chieftaincy) independent of Eguafo.

roleDetail.d: An English trader wrote that nothing could be done at Komenda without him; he had RAC agents removed in 1687, 1698 and 1714.
After being panyarred (seized) by the Dutch in 1688 he attacked Dutch miners in 1694 and the Dutch fort in 1694–95.
Henige shows how he founded the 'paramount stool of Komenda' — a model for trade-based states in the Niger Delta.

records.legacy: On his death in 1722 he was buried at the English fort; his son Ahenaqua inherited the trade and Komenda was governed on 'the stool of the late John Cabess' until Cape Coast eclipsed it. Historian Kwame Daaku named him one of the Gold Coast's 'merchant princes'.

legacyDetail.d: His stool passed to descendants and remained a political institution in Komenda.

records.name: John Conny (Ahanta, Brandenburg broker)
records.scaleNote: Considered one of three or four major African wholesalers dealing with Europeans on the western Gold Coast c.1700–1724, diverting trade from Dutch forts at Axim, Butre and Sekondi; no captive count documented.
records.origins: An Akan warrior-merchant from Axim who became a chief of the Ahanta; his African name is unknown (possibly 'Kenu'). He rose as the main African broker of the Brandenburg African Company.
records.role_summary: Conny channelled gold and captives to the Brandenburgers at Groß Friedrichsburg and, after they abandoned it and sold their holdings to the Dutch in 1717 without telling him, held the fort with a large armed following, repelling Dutch attacks. The Dutch finally took it in 1724 and renamed it Fort Hollandia.

roleDetail.d: His dealings hurt Dutch revenues at Axim, Butre and Sekondi.

roleDetail.t: Held a European fort for himself.
roleDetail.d: From c.1717 to 1724 he defended Groß Friedrichsburg against the WIC, reportedly with thousands of armed men.
He was defeated c.1724–25 and may have fled to Kumasi.

records.legacy: Edward Long's History of Jamaica (1774) claimed Jamaica's 'John Canoe' masquerade was begun by Akan captives who had fought for Conny; later writers connect this to the Junkanoo festival still held each December. This is one of several proposed origins (others are linguistic) and rests on a planter-historian's assertion, so it should be treated as tradition, not established fact.

legacyDetail.d: The derivation of 'John Canoe'/'Junkanoo' from John Conny is a popular tradition traced to Edward Long; it is not established by scholarship and competing etymologies exist.
