records.name: Brew family (Anomabu & Cape Coast)
records.scaleNote: Richard Brew (d.1776) was among the largest private English slave traders at Anomabu in the 1750s–70s and governor of its fort; Priestley (1969) traces his debts and dealings, but no voyage total is documented.
records.origins: Richard Brew, an Irishman, came to the Gold Coast in the 1740s and served as governor of the English fort at Anomabu (1750s–1764), continuing its construction. He had a Fante partner, and the family thereafter combined Fante matrilineal identity with an Irish surname.
records.role_summary: Brew traded captives privately on a large scale from Anomabu, the busiest English slaving beach of the period, and was reprimanded in 1763 for selling to the Dutch. He built his own fortified residence, Castle Brew (1763–64), and died bankrupt in 1776.

roleDetail.d: Combined Company office at Anomabu with his own slave trading for British and American ships.
Margaret Priestley's 'West African Trade and Coast Society' (OUP, 1969) follows the Brews from him to the 20th century.

roleDetail.t: Descendants turned to law and politics.
roleDetail.d: James Hutton Brew (1844–1915) became one of the Gold Coast's first African lawyers, drafted the 1871 Fante Confederacy constitution and founded the Gold Coast Times (1874).

records.legacy: The Brews are a well-known Ghanaian family today, prominent in law, journalism and public life; their history is one of the classic studies of coastal Afro-European society. Descendants carry no responsibility for Richard Brew's trading.

legacyDetail.d: Castle Brew at Anomabu survives as a ruin/house later known as Blankson House.
The Bodleian Library holds Margaret Bax (Priestley)'s research papers on the Brew family, c.1961–69.

sources.label: Cambridge (BSOAS review) — Priestley, West African Trade and Coast Society: A Family Study (1969)
Bodleian Archives — Margaret Bax's research papers on the Brew family
Jeffrey Green — James Hutton Brew (1844–1915) of Ghana and London
Wikipedia — Anomabu

connections.label: J. H. Brew drafted its 1871 constitution
sold to Liverpool and other British ships

records.name: Ana Joaquina dos Santos e Silva ("Dona Ana Joaquina")
records.scaleNote: One of the wealthiest Luanda slave traders of the 1820s–50s, with her own small fleet to Bahia, Recife and Rio (per Wheeler and Oliveira); voyage totals are not documented.
records.origins: Born in Luanda to a Portuguese father and mestiça mother, part of the Afro-Portuguese creole elite. She married two Portuguese merchants in succession and inherited their businesses.
records.role_summary: By the 1820s she held an extensive slave-trading portfolio, shipping captives to Bahia, Pernambuco and Rio de Janeiro in exchange for aguardente, sugar and flour, and was widely believed to keep exporting illegally after Portugal's 1836 ban. She also lent money to inland traders, financing Joaquim Rodrigues Graça's 1843 expedition to the Lunda.

roleDetail.d: Her vessels linked Luanda with Brazilian ports, Lisbon and Montevideo.
She was widely believed to continue exporting captives through Luanda after the ban.
Owned sugar estates at Ícolo e Bengo and Golungo Alto and farms at Moçâmedes.

records.legacy: She died at sea in 1859 travelling to Lisbon with eight enslaved attendants, leaving her fortune to grandchildren. Her Luanda mansion, the Palácio de Dona Ana Joaquina, was demolished in 1999 and rebuilt as a replica.

legacyDetail.d: Vanessa Oliveira stresses that the Luanda donas were not abolitionists but profited from the sale of human beings.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Ana Joaquina dos Santos e Silva (citing Wheeler; Oliveira 2021)
Oliveira — Slave Trade and Abolition: Gender, Commerce and Economic Transition in Luanda (JSTOR)
UFRGS Africanas — Ana Joaquina dos Santos Silva

records.name: Domingo José Martínez
records.scaleNote: By the late 1840s he was 'as influential in Dahomey as Francisco Félix de Souza had been a decade earlier' (Ross 1965); total captives shipped are not documented.
records.origins: A Brazilian-born merchant (often described as of mixed descent) who came to the Bight of Benin in the 1830s, starting under the Chachá de Souza at Ouidah and rising at Lagos.
records.role_summary: Martínez shipped captives from Lagos, Badagry, Ouidah and Porto-Novo to Brazil and Cuba, settling at Porto-Novo by 1846 where King Ghezo granted him privileges. After his slave cargoes were seized (1854) he switched to palm oil, still using enslaved labour, until his influence collapsed shortly before his death in 1864.

roleDetail.d: Ross (1965) shows his political influence rose and fell with his commercial fortune.
Lagos sources describe him buying captives from Madam Tinubu and the Kosoko faction.
He told missionaries he would stop buying slaves only if rivals did; he moved into palm oil in the 1850s.

records.legacy: He was buried at Ouidah; families claiming descent from him remain part of the Agudá (Afro-Brazilian) community of Benin. His career is a standard case study of the 'illegal' trade's transition to palm oil.

legacyDetail.d: A 2024 French biography by Vitoekpon Sèwanou Olivier traces his career from Ouidah to Lagos.

sources.label: Ross — The career of Domingo Martinez in the Bight of Benin, 1833–64 (J. African History 6, 1965)
Acervo Aguda — interview (Porto-Novo descendants)
Cambridge — Law, Ouidah: The Social History of a West African Slaving 'Port' (introduction)

records.name: Joaquim d'Almeida (Zoki Azata)
records.scaleNote: Named in an 1840 British consular report on illegal slave-trading agents in Bahia; after 1849 briefly Ouidah's richest resident (per Enslaved.org). No voyage totals documented.
records.origins: Born Zoki Azata in Hoko, north of Dahomey, he was enslaved as a child, shipped to Brazil, and bought and freed by the slave-ship captain Manuel Joaquim d'Almeida, whose name he took.
records.role_summary: A freed African turned slave trader, he worked between Salvador da Bahia and the Bight of Benin (1835–45), then settled at Agoué. He was the first trader outside the de Souza family to gain King Ghezo's approval and was made customs officer between Agoué and Little Popo.

roleDetail.d: Typical of returnee leaders who, per Cambridge 'History in Africa', were deeply involved in the Atlantic trade.
Gained Ghezo's licence; after 1849 the most influential man at Ouidah until British actions pushed him back to Agoué (1850).

records.legacy: He built Agoué's first Catholic chapel; his descendants credit him with bringing Catholicism, and Ouidah's Zokikomé quarter bears his name. The d'Almeida family remains a prominent Agudá lineage in Benin and Togo.

legacyDetail.d: Enslaved.org notes he is remembered as a distinguished figure in Benin's history.

sources.label: Enslaved.org — Joaquim d'Almeida (Kostiw, Dictionary of Caribbean and Afro-Latin American Biography)
Cambridge, History in Africa — Afro-Catholic baptism and the articulation of a merchant community, Agoué 1840–1860

connections.label: licensed and made customs officer by Ghezo

records.name: Amachree dynasty of New Calabar (Kalabari)
records.scaleNote: SlaveVoyages notes New Calabar was the Bight of Biafra's most important slaving and ivory site in the 1600s before Bonny overtook it by the 1730s; Kalabari remained a major entrepôt for captives bought from Igboland.
records.origins: Amachree I (dates disputed: Alagoa gives a reign of 1669–1757, other accounts a death c.1800) is remembered as founder of the modern Kalabari kingdom of Ijo traders on the New Calabar River. Most of the great trading 'houses' grew under him.
records.role_summary: Kalabari kings and house heads bought captives from the Igbo hinterland (partly via the Aro network) and sold them to European ships at the river mouth, exchanging them for cloth, metalware, guns and gunpowder. They competed with Bonny, Okrika and Nembe for the trade.

roleDetail.d: Kalabari became an entrepôt mainly selling people purchased from Igboland.
Canoe houses, absorbing purchased people as members, organised trade and war.
European records often confuse 'Calabar' (Efik) and 'New Calabar' (Kalabari) captives.

records.legacy: After a civil war (1882–84) the Amachree faction moved to Abonnema and Buguma, now the kingdom's capital. The Amachree line, today headed by the Princewill family, still holds the traditional throne; writer Victoria Princewill has discussed this ancestry in Granta (2021).

legacyDetail.d: The Amanyanabo of Kalabari remains a recognised traditional ruler in Rivers State, Nigeria.

sources.label: SlaveVoyages — Places images (New Calabar note)
Wikipedia — Kalabari Kingdom (citing Alagoa 1966)
Wikipedia — Buguma

connections.label: Liverpool ships traded at New Calabar

records.name: Damels of Cayor (Kajoor)
records.scaleNote: Cayor, the largest Wolof state, was heavily involved in the slave and horse trades for both Atlantic and Saharan markets (Seshat; Barry 1998); precise captive numbers are not documented.
records.origins: Cayor broke from the Jolof Empire at the battle of Danki (1549) under Amary Ngone Sobel Fall. Its rulers, the damel, came from the Fall lineage and controlled the coast near Cape Verde where Portuguese, Dutch and French traders first dealt with the Wolof.
records.role_summary: The damels and their tyeddo (ceddo) slave-soldiers raided neighbours and their own subjects for captives, selling them to the French at Saint-Louis and Gorée for guns, horses and cloth (Boubacar Barry). After a failed marabout revolt in 1776 many clerics were sold into slavery.

roleDetail.d: Barry argues the Atlantic trade militarised Senegambian states, with ceddo raiding for captives.
After the 1776 clerical revolt was crushed, many marabouts were sold (Colvin 1974).
Crown slaves (tyeddo) formed the damel's army and exercised political power.

records.legacy: Lat Dior, the most famous damel, resisted French railway building and died fighting in 1886; he is a national hero in Senegal. The slave-trading phase of the monarchy is less commemorated.

legacyDetail.d: National memory centres on anti-colonial resistance rather than the earlier sale of captives.

sources.label: Cambridge — Barry, Senegambia and the Atlantic Slave Trade (1998)
Seshat Global History Databank — Cayor
Wikipedia — Cayor

connections.label: sold captives to French at Gorée

records.name: Kings of Saalum (Maad / Buur Saalum)
records.scaleNote: At its height Saalum controlled four Gambia River trading ports (Barra, Iambor, Kaur, Kassang) used by European slavers; no captive totals documented.
records.origins: A Serer kingdom founded c.1494 with its capital at Kahone. Under Maad Saloum Lat Ciloor Bajaan (by 1566) it extended its power to the north bank of the Gambia.
records.role_summary: Saalum's rulers taxed and supplied the Atlantic trade on the Gambia and Saloum rivers, where captives and salt were exchanged with Portuguese, English and French traders. When the Atlantic slave trade ended, foreign trade shrank to foodstuffs and later groundnuts.

roleDetail.d: Barra (Niumi), Iambor (Baddibu), Kaur (Saalum) and Kassang (Niani) lay in its zone of influence.
After the slave trade's end the ceddo warrior class turned to preying on subjects (per Klein 1968).

records.legacy: Annexed by France in the 1860s and abolished as a monarchy in 1969, the kingship was restored in 2017 as a non-sovereign traditional title crowned at Kahone.

legacyDetail.d: Thierno Coumba Daga Ndao was crowned at Kahone on 21 May 2017.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Saloum (citing Klein 1968; Barry 1998)
Cambridge — Barry, Senegambia and the Atlantic Slave Trade (1998)

records.name: Kingdom of Kaabu (Mansaba & Nyancho)
records.scaleNote: Kaabu's wars produced a large share of the captives exported from Upper Guinea in the 17th–18th centuries; some summaries claim 'up to half', which is unverified.
records.origins: A Mandinka federation that grew out of a Mali Empire province and became independent as Mali declined (traditionally 1537). Its warrior nobility, the Nyancho, elected the mansaba at Kansala.
records.role_summary: Nyancho warriors raided for captives and sold them through Portuguese and Luso-African traders at Cacheu, Geba and Farim and through Gambia River markets, receiving cloth, beads, metalware and firearms. The slave trade dominated Kaabu's economy and enriched its war elite.

roleDetail.d: Wealth came from war captives and the kabunko cloth tax (Barry 1998; Green 2020).
By the 1640s Kaabu's province of Ganadu dominated Geba, and in 1644 the Portuguese moved merchants to Cacheu and Farim.

records.legacy: Kaabu fell when Futa Jallon forces besieged Kansala in 1867 and the mansaba blew up the gunpowder stores. It remains central to Mandinka oral tradition and griot epic across Guinea-Bissau, Gambia and Senegal.

legacyDetail.d: Kansala's fall is a major theme of Mandinka griot narrative.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Kaabu (citing Barry 1998; Green 2020; Lobban 1979)
Wikipedia — Geba, Guinea-Bissau
Durham University — Cacheu Archaeological Project

connections.label: Upper Guinea captives to Cape Verde

records.name: Pombeiros (Angolan caravan agents)
records.scaleNote: An account from c.1700 describes single pombeiro expeditions lasting a year and returning 400–600 captives (per Oliver & Atmore); collectively they fed Luanda and Benguela, the largest embarkation region of the trade.
records.origins: The term derives from Pumbo, a market near Malebo Pool. Pombeiros were African, sometimes mixed-race, agents—often themselves enslaved or freed dependants—of Portuguese officials and Luanda merchants.
records.role_summary: Because Lisbon preferred Portuguese merchants to stay on the coast, pombeiros led caravans inland on credit, buying captives ('peças') from sobas, the Imbangala and Kasanje at fortified fairs (feiras) for cloth, wine and spirits. They seldom went beyond Kasanje, which sold them captives from the Lunda.

roleDetail.d: Joseph Miller's 'Way of Death' traces debt from Brazilian and British financiers through Luanda merchants to pombeiros and inland rulers.
Fortified marketplaces; Kasanje, founded by the Imbangala c.1620, was the furthest.
In 1806 pombeiros Pedro João Baptista and Amaro José crossed from Angola to Tete in Mozambique and back.

records.legacy: In the 19th century pombeiros became caravan foremen recruiting and disciplining porters for the rubber and ivory trades. They exemplify how the Angolan trade depended on African intermediaries.

legacyDetail.d: A 2024 study describes 19th-century pombeiros commanding sections of Portuguese caravans.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Pombeiros (citing Oliver & Atmore 2005)

UNC — Miller, Way of Death: Merchant Capitalism and the Angolan Slave Trade, 1730–1830

connections.label: bought captives at the Kasanje feira
financed by Luanda merchants like her

records.name: Tinubu Square, Lagos
records.description: Public square on Lagos Island named after Madam Efunroye Tinubu, with a statue of her; formerly known as Independence Square. It commemorates her as a political figure and Iyalode, not her slave trading.

records.name: Rio Pongo slave factories (Bangalan, Sangha, Farenya)
records.description: An estuary in present-day Guinea draining from Futa Jallon, a hub of the slave trade from the early 1700s. By c.1800 Eurafrican Creole houses (Ormond, Lightbourn, Faber, Frazer) dominated it, and it remained a centre of the illegal trade to Cuba until a regional ban in 1852 (per Mouser).

records.name: Farenya (Niara Bely's settlement)
records.description: Trading settlement on the Rio Pongo founded in 1809 by Stiles Lightbourn and Niara Bely, a terminus for Futa Jallon caravans. Niara Bely lived there in a two-storey 'palace'; archaeologists have excavated the site and its early Anglican church.

records.name: English and Dutch forts at Komenda
records.description: Rival English (Royal African Company) and Dutch (WIC, Fort Vredenburg) posts at Komenda on the Gold Coast, contested during the Komenda Wars of 1694–1700. John Kabes supplied labour and materials for the English fort and was buried there in 1722.

records.name: Castle Brew, Anomabu
records.description: Private fortified house built by the Irish slave trader Richard Brew at Anomabu in 1763–64, near the English fort he had governed. It was seized for his debts after his bankruptcy; the ruin was later known as Blankson House.

connections.label: beside the Company fort at Anomabu

records.name: Palácio de Dona Ana Joaquina, Luanda
records.description: Three-storey mansion in Luanda's Bungo district that was the residence of the slave trader Ana Joaquina dos Santos e Silva. It was demolished in 1999 and replaced by a 'more or less faithful' replica.

records.name: Denman's Gallinas raid and treaty (1840)
records.description: In November 1840 Royal Navy commander Joseph Denman, sent to free Fry Norman, burned eight slave factories on the Gallinas River and freed 841 captives. On 21 November Prince Manna, for the ailing King Siaka, signed a treaty abolishing the trade; the Spanish traders later sued Denman personally (Buron v. Denman).

records.name: Agudá (Afro-Brazilian) merchant families of Ouidah, Agoué and Lagos
records.description: Brazilian slave traders and formerly enslaved Africans who returned from Bahia, settling at Ouidah, Agoué, Porto-Novo and Lagos from the late 18th century. Many leaders, though once enslaved, were active in the Atlantic slave trade; lineages such as de Souza, d'Almeida, Martins and de Medeiros (founded by Francisco José de Medeiros, mid-19th century) remain prominent in Benin, Togo and Nigeria.

records.name: Grumetes (African workers and agents) of Bance Island
records.description: Free and enslaved African employees—called grumetes or grumettas—who lived outside the walls of the British slave fort on Bance (Bunce) Island, crewing boats, trading upriver and guarding captives. Grant, Sargent & Oswald expanded this African workforce after c.1750 alongside a shipyard and fleet of small vessels that supplied Charleston and other markets.

records.name: Descendants of broker families today
records.description: Several lineages founded by African and Afro-European brokers remain prominent: the de Souza family still installs a 'Chachá' at Ouidah, the Caulkers have held Sherbro paramount chieftaincies, the Brews are a well-known Ghanaian family, and the Amachree line (Princewill family) holds the Kalabari throne. Descent confers no guilt; how families remember the trade varies.

records.name: Calvert family (Lords Baltimore; Calverts of Mount Airy and Riversdale)
records.scaleNote: As Maryland's proprietors they presided over the 1664 law making slavery lifelong and hereditary; their Riversdale descendants enslaved c. 15–32 people (1800–1806 tax lists) and Charles Benedict Calvert held 52 people in 1860, per UMD's 1856 Project.
records.base: St. Mary's City and Riversdale (Riverdale Park), Maryland
records.origins: George Calvert, 1st Baron Baltimore, sought a colonial charter; it was granted in 1632 to his son Cecil Calvert, 2nd Lord Baltimore, and Maryland was settled from 1634 as a proprietary colony. The family held proprietary power (with interruptions) until the Revolution, and an American branch descended from Benedict Swingate Calvert, son of the 5th Lord Baltimore, settled at Mount Airy (Prince George's County).
records.role_summary: Under the proprietorship, Maryland's assembly in 1664 — with Charles Calvert (later 3rd Lord Baltimore) as governor — enacted that enslaved Africans would serve 'durante vita' (for life), a foundation of Maryland's tobacco slave economy. Later Calverts were themselves planters: George Calvert (1768–1838) and Rosalie Stier Calvert ran Riversdale with enslaved labor, and their son Charles Benedict Calvert enslaved 52 people in 1860.

roleDetail.d: The 1664 Maryland act, passed under the proprietary government, made the status of enslaved Africans lifelong and extended it to their children, per the Maryland State Archives.
Tax assessments record c. 15 enslaved people at Riversdale in 1800 and 32 in 1806; diarist Adam Francis Plummer was enslaved there by George Calvert and then Charles Benedict Calvert.

roleDetail.t: Founding a university with plantation wealth.
roleDetail.d: Charles Benedict Calvert donated land from Riversdale for the Maryland Agricultural College (1856), now the University of Maryland, College Park; he held 52 people in slavery in 1860, per the 1856 Project.

roleDetail.t: Family ties across the Chesapeake gentry.
roleDetail.d: Eleanor Calvert, George Calvert's sister, married John Parke Custis (Martha Washington's son) in 1774, linking the Calverts to Mount Vernon.

records.legacy: Calvert County and the city of Baltimore carry the family's name and title. Riversdale is now a house museum run by M-NCPPC that interprets its enslaved workforce and seeks descendants of the people enslaved there; the University of Maryland's 1856 Project (2024 report) documents Calvert's role in its founding.

legacyDetail.d: The museum researches and presents the enslaved community at Riversdale and is actively seeking their descendants.
The university's 2024 report 'Reconstructing the Truth' estimates more than 500 enslaved people lived on land that became the college.

sources.label: Maryland State Archives — Blacks Before the Law in Colonial Maryland
Riversdale House Museum — The Workforce
UMD Libraries — The 1856 Project releases inaugural research report
Humanities DC — Adam Francis Plummer

connections.label: Eleanor Calvert m. John Parke Custis (1774)

records.name: Macon family (Gideon Macon of Virginia; Nathaniel Macon of North Carolina)
records.scaleNote: Nathaniel Macon's father left 3,000 acres and 25–30 enslaved people in 1761; Nathaniel held dozens at Buck Spring (c. 70 by some accounts). The family's weight lies in politics: Nathaniel was Speaker of the U.S. House 1801–1807 and a leading defender of slavery.
records.base: Buck Spring, Warren County, North Carolina
records.origins: Gideon Macon (d. 1702), a New Kent County, Virginia planter and member of the House of Burgesses (1696), founded the Virginia line; through his daughter Martha he was great-grandfather of Martha Dandridge Custis Washington. A branch moved to North Carolina, where Maj. Gideon Macon left his son Nathaniel (1757/58–1837) three enslaved people, George, Robb and Lucy, in 1761.
records.role_summary: Nathaniel Macon farmed tobacco and grain at Buck Spring with enslaved labor while serving 37 years in Congress (Speaker 1801–1807, then Senator). NCpedia describes him as a staunch advocate of states' rights and of slavery; he opposed congressional restriction of slavery in the Missouri debates of 1819–1821.

roleDetail.d: His father's 1761 estate included 3,000 acres and 25–30 enslaved people; three were bequeathed to Nathaniel.
Macon was Speaker of the House (1801–1807) when Congress passed the 1807 Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves — a ban that left the domestic trade intact.
He opposed the Missouri Compromise as conceding too much power to Congress over slavery, per NCpedia and Encyclopedia.com.

records.legacy: Macon, Georgia; Fort Macon; Macon County (NC and elsewhere); and Randolph-Macon College (chartered 1830, named for Macon and John Randolph) honor him. Buck Spring is on the National Register of Historic Places (1970); its interpretation of the enslaved community has been limited.

legacyDetail.d: A city, a fort, several counties and a Virginia college bear the Macon name.
Nathaniel Macon was a second cousin of Martha Washington through the Virginia Macons.

sources.label: NCpedia — Nathaniel Macon
Randolph-Macon College — History
Wikipedia — Buck Spring Plantation
Wikipedia — Nathaniel Macon

connections.label: Gideon Macon was Martha Washington's great-grandfather

records.name: Contee family of Prince George's County
records.scaleNote: A Prince George's/Anne Arundel tobacco-planting and mercantile family. Formerly enslaved Dennis Simms (b. 1841) recalled more than 100 enslaved people on the Contee plantation of Richard and Charles Contee (WPA interview, 1937), and Prince George's Slave Statistics (1868–69) record people declared by the administrator of John Contee's estate (per Maryland State Archives). No full count of family holdings has been published.
records.base: Nottingham and 'Contee', Prince George's County, Maryland
records.origins: Col. Thomas Contee lived at 'Brookefield' (now 'The Valley') near Nottingham on the Patuxent; his son Benjamin Contee (1755–1815), a Revolutionary officer, sat in the Confederation Congress and the first U.S. House (1789–1791), and with his brother Alexander ran stores at Nottingham, Queen Anne and Upper Marlboro. Through marriage, Capt. John Contee acquired the Snowden plantation Oaklands near Laurel.
records.role_summary: The Contees were part of southern Maryland's tobacco gentry, whose wealth rested on enslaved labor. Dennis Simms, interviewed by the Federal Writers' Project in 1937, described being enslaved on a Contee tobacco plantation (identified by the Smithsonian as Java Farm, next to Woodlawn), with frequent whippings, bans on reading and church, and secret gatherings for spirituals.

roleDetail.d: Simms's testimony describes over 100 enslaved workers on the Contee estate in the 1840s–1850s; it is a single late recollection and should be read as testimony.

Maryland State Archives' index to Prince George's freedom records lists people (e.g. Annetta Contee, 25; Walter Contee, 2) declared in the 1868–69 Slave Statistics by Daniel Clarke, administrator of John Contee's estate.
The Contee brothers' Patuxent stores linked them to the tobacco export economy that ran through Chesapeake river ports.
Oaklands (also called 'Contee'), a Snowden slave plantation that passed to Capt. John Contee by marriage, had overseers remembered as especially cruel in the mid-1800s.

records.legacy: The Prince George's County locality of Contee (near Laurel) and Contee Road preserve the name. Descendants of people enslaved on Contee land appear in Maryland's freedom records and 1867–68 slave statistics, and the Smithsonian's Woodlawn History Center (opened 2022) interprets Simms's testimony with local descendants.

legacyDetail.d: Smithsonian Environmental Research Center exhibits draw on Simms's oral history of Java Farm.
Many free and enslaved people recorded as 'Contee' appear in county records; the surname alone does not establish who enslaved them.

Smithsonian SERC — Stories from the Woodlawn History Center
Wikipedia — Benjamin Contee
Wikipedia — Oaklands (Laurel, Maryland)

connections.label: Benjamin Contee backed Potomac capital site

records.name: George Washington
records.scaleNote: Mount Vernon's June 1799 census lists 317 enslaved people on five farms: 123 owned by Washington, 153 Custis 'dower' people, and c. 40 rented from a neighbor, per Mount Vernon.
records.origins: Washington inherited ten enslaved people at age eleven on his father's death in 1743, and later Mount Vernon from his half-brother Lawrence's estate. His 1759 marriage to the widow Martha Dandridge Custis brought control of the Custis 'dower' enslaved people.
records.role_summary: Washington built Mount Vernon (8,000 acres) into a tobacco, then wheat, milling, fishing and distilling enterprise worked by enslaved people. He bought and occasionally sold people — in 1766 he shipped Tom, a foreman he called a 'Rogue & Runaway', to St. Kitts in exchange for rum, molasses and other goods — and as president signed the 1793 Fugitive Slave Act.

roleDetail.d: Washington's own census recorded every enslaved person at Mount Vernon by farm, family and task.
Washington sold Tom to the West Indies in 1766 and at least two other people to the Caribbean as punishment, per Mount Vernon.

His will freed the 123 people he owned after Martha's death (they were freed 1 January 1801); William Lee was freed outright. The 153 dower people could not be freed by him and passed to Custis heirs, splitting families.

records.legacy: Mount Vernon, owned by the Mount Vernon Ladies' Association since 1858, now interprets slavery extensively, with a Slave Memorial (1983, designed by Howard University students) and archaeology of the enslaved burial ground. The capital, a state, and countless institutions bear his name.

legacyDetail.d: Archaeology since 2014 has mapped graves at Mount Vernon's enslaved cemetery.
Mount Vernon's digital encyclopedia profiles individuals such as William Lee, Ona Judge and Tom, drawing on Washington's own records.

sources.label: Mount Vernon — Census of the Enslaved Population at Mount Vernon, 1786 and 1799
Mount Vernon — Tom (digital encyclopedia)
Mount Vernon — The Slave Memorial at Mount Vernon
Founders Online — Washington to Joseph Thompson, 2 July 1766

connections.label: married Martha Custis; managed dower people

records.name: Custis family (Martha Washington's Custis estate; Arlington)
records.scaleNote: 153 Custis 'dower' people lived at Mount Vernon in 1799; George Washington Parke Custis later owned nearly 200 people, as many as 63 at Arlington, per NPS.
records.base: Arlington House, Arlington, Virginia (also White House and Romancoke on the Pamunkey)
records.origins: Daniel Parke Custis, a wealthy Tidewater planter, died in 1757 leaving a large estate of land and enslaved people; his widow Martha's dower share went with her into her marriage to George Washington. Their grandson George Washington Parke Custis (1781–1857) inherited Custis people and built Arlington House from 1802.
records.role_summary: The Custis estate supplied much of Mount Vernon's enslaved workforce; on Martha Washington's death (1802) the dower people were divided among her grandchildren. G.W.P. Custis brought enslaved people, most born at Mount Vernon, to Arlington in 1802; his 1857 will required their freedom within five years, and his son-in-law Robert E. Lee kept them working to settle debts until filing a deed of manumission in late 1862.

roleDetail.d: Because dower people belonged to the Custis estate, Washington could not free them; in 1802 they were split among Custis heirs.
Custis owned nearly 200 people across Arlington, White House and Romancoke; NPS interprets the Syphax, Burke, Parks and Gray families.
John Parke Custis married Eleanor Calvert (1774), and Mary Custis married Robert E. Lee (1831).

records.legacy: Arlington House (NPS) now sits within Arlington National Cemetery, and the park has expanded its interpretation of the enslaved community, including restoring the slave quarters. Descendants of the Syphax family, enslaved by Custis, became prominent in Washington, D.C.

legacyDetail.d: NPS presents enslaved residents' stories and has sought to change the memorial's naming so it does not center Lee.
After federal seizure, Arlington land hosted Freedman's Village (1863) for formerly enslaved people.

sources.label: NPS — Slavery at Arlington
NPS — The Slave Quarters (Arlington House)
Mount Vernon — The Growth of Mount Vernon's Enslaved Community

connections.label: John Parke Custis m. Eleanor Calvert

records.name: Andrew Jackson
records.scaleNote: The Jackson family owned more than 300 people over the decades and about 150 at his death in 1845, per The Hermitage; he bought and sold people from 1788 to 1844, much of it in the Natchez and New Orleans markets.
records.origins: A lawyer and land speculator on the Tennessee frontier, Jackson bought his first enslaved person in 1788. In 1804 he moved to the Hermitage tract with nine enslaved people, and cotton planting there became the base of his wealth.
records.role_summary: Jackson was both a cotton planter and an active slave trader: he marketed coffles of enslaved people in the Natchez District, the Felicianas and New Orleans, writing in 1812 that his costs for 'Negroes sent to markett' rarely exceeded fifteen dollars a head. In 1811 he confronted federal Indian agent Silas Dinsmoor, who demanded passes for a coffle Jackson was driving south.

roleDetail.d: Cotton grown by enslaved people at the Hermitage made Jackson rich; roughly 150 people were enslaved there by 1845.
Historians document his buying and selling of people from 1788 to 1844, including speculative coffles sent down the Natchez Trace.
As president he backed suppression of abolitionist mailings (1835) and his Indian Removal policy opened Native lands to cotton slavery.

records.legacy: The Hermitage (Andrew Jackson Foundation) now presents the stories of the enslaved community and in December 2024 announced it had located the enslaved cemetery, with at least 28 burials; an advisory committee includes descendants. Jackson's place on the $20 bill and statues remain debated.

legacyDetail.d: Ground-penetrating radar and limited excavation confirmed the burial ground about 1,000 feet from the mansion.
The Hermitage is including descendants of the enslaved in planning interpretation of the site.

records.name: Johnson brothers of Maryland (Gov. Thomas Johnson; Catoctin Furnace)
records.scaleNote: Baker Johnson's 1809 will lists more than 80 enslaved people, many skilled ironworkers, at Catoctin Furnace, per Maryland DNR.
records.origins: Thomas Johnson (1732–1819), born in Calvert County, was a Frederick lawyer, Continental Congress delegate, Maryland's first elected governor (1777–1779) and briefly a U.S. Supreme Court justice (1791–1793). With his brothers James, Baker and Roger he founded the Catoctin ironworks in the 1770s.
records.role_summary: The Johnsons built Catoctin Furnace on the labor of enslaved African Americans, who worked as colliers, founders, forgemen, blacksmiths, farmhands and domestic servants; the furnace supplied iron during the Revolution. By mid-century hired immigrant labor replaced enslaved workers, and some enslaved workers may have been sold south.

roleDetail.d: Enslaved craftsmen held skilled posts at the furnace; named individuals in Baker Johnson's will include Collier Sam and the waggoners Henry and Harvey.
Thomas Johnson nominated Washington as commander-in-chief in 1775 and governed Maryland during the war while his family's furnace relied on enslaved labor.
As immigrant labor became cheaper, some enslaved Catoctin workers may have been sold to the Deep South.

records.legacy: The Catoctin Furnace African American Cemetery is thought to be the most complete Black cemetery tied to early American industry. A 2023 Science study (Smithsonian, Harvard, 23andMe, Catoctin Furnace Historical Society) sequenced 27 people buried there and linked nearly 42,000 living people to them; facial reconstructions were unveiled in 2021.

legacyDetail.d: The 2023 study identified five families among those buried and found the closest living relatives concentrated in Maryland.
The furnace stack and village lie in Cunningham Falls State Park, interpreted by the Historical Society.

sources.label: Maryland DNR — Catoctin Furnace (Cunningham Falls State Park)
