connections.label: Maryland ironworks run with enslaved labor

records.name: Andrew Johnson
records.scaleNote: A household enslaver, not a planter: bills of sale show he bought Sam (c. 13) for $541 in 1842 and Dolly (c. 19) for $500 in 1843; NPS says he owned at least ten people at most.
records.origins: A tailor from a poor North Carolina family, Johnson rose through Tennessee politics. As his fortunes grew he bought enslaved people for his Greeneville household.
records.role_summary: Johnson owned a small number of people — Dolly, her half-brother Sam, Dolly's children and others — and, per family tradition, freed them on 8 August 1863. As military governor of Tennessee he sought the state's exemption from the Emancipation Proclamation, and as president (1865–1869) he opposed Reconstruction measures protecting freedpeople.

roleDetail.d: NPS holds bills of sale for Sam (1842) and Dolly (1843).
8 August became Emancipation Day in East Tennessee; in 1871 Sam Johnson served as 'Officer of the Day' at Greeneville's celebration.
He vetoed the Freedmen's Bureau and Civil Rights bills of 1866; Congress overrode the latter.

records.legacy: The Andrew Johnson National Historic Site (NPS) in Greeneville interprets the people he enslaved, including Sam Johnson, who in 1867 obtained land from Johnson for a school for Black children. The question of Johnson's paternity of Dolly's children is unresolved.

legacyDetail.d: The park's 'Slaves of Andrew Johnson' history page names the enslaved household and its descendants.

sources.label: NPS — Slaves of Andrew Johnson
NPS — August 8th
American Battlefield Trust — Andrew Johnson National Historic Site

records.name: Carroll family (Charles Carroll of Carrollton; Doughoregan Manor)
records.scaleNote: A December 1773 inventory lists 330 enslaved people at Doughoregan Manor alone (Maryland Center for History and Culture); Carroll was among the largest enslavers in Maryland, with further people at Homewood and other estates.
records.origins: Charles Carroll 'the Settler' arrived in 1688 as attorney general for the Catholic proprietor Lord Baltimore and amassed land, lending and an ironworks interest. His grandson Charles Carroll of Carrollton (1737–1832) was the only Catholic signer of the Declaration and reputedly the richest man in the colonies.
records.role_summary: The Carrolls' fortune — tobacco and grain plantations, the Baltimore Iron Works, money-lending and land — rested on hundreds of enslaved people. Carroll of Carrollton wrote in favor of gradual abolition yet held some 300+ people at Doughoregan and others at Homewood (Baltimore), where enslaved gardener Izadod Conner is credited with shaping the grounds.

roleDetail.d: The family-by-family list of 330 enslaved people at Doughoregan is one of Maryland's most detailed plantation records.
At least 36 enslaved people lived and worked at Homewood, built for Carroll's son from 1801.
Carroll's cousin Archbishop John Carroll founded Georgetown (1789), whose Jesuit sponsors also held enslaved people on Maryland plantations.

records.legacy: Carroll County and many Maryland institutions bear the name; Carroll helped launch the B&O Railroad (1828). Homewood Museum at Johns Hopkins and the Maryland Center for History and Culture now research the enslaved families of Doughoregan and Homewood (e.g., the Conner family).

legacyDetail.d: Johns Hopkins' Homewood Museum has projects honoring people enslaved on the estate.
A 2022 Maryland Historical Magazine article examines Carroll and the enslaved families of Doughoregan.

sources.label: Maryland Center for History and Culture — List of negroes on Doohoregan Manor, 1773
The Cultural Landscape Foundation — Izadod Conner
WYPR — Shining a light on enslavers in Congress (Homewood)

connections.label: Settler was Lord Baltimore's attorney general

records.name: Lloyd family of Wye House
records.scaleNote: Edward Lloyd IV held 305 enslaved people in 1790 and Edward Lloyd V c. 420 in 1810 (Maryland State Archives); across generations the estate enslaved more than 1,000 people on up to 42,000 acres.
records.origins: Edward Lloyd, a Welsh Puritan, settled on the Wye River in the 1650s. Successive Edward Lloyds became one of Maryland's wealthiest landholding and enslaving dynasties; Edward Lloyd V was governor (1809–1811) and U.S. Senator (1819–1826).
records.role_summary: Wye House was the hub of a dozen outlying farms, each worked by 18–47 enslaved people under overseers, producing grain and tobacco. Frederick Douglass spent part of his childhood there in 1824 (owned by overseer Aaron Anthony) and described its brutality in his 1845 Narrative; later Lloyds moved enslaved people to new cotton plantations in the Deep South.

roleDetail.d: In 1824 c. 181 enslaved people lived at the Wye House home plantation itself, per the Frederick Douglass Papers.
Douglass's Narrative made 'Colonel Lloyd's' plantation emblematic of Chesapeake slavery.
Edward Lloyd VI acquired cotton land in Mississippi, Arkansas and Louisiana and transferred enslaved people there.

records.legacy: Wye House remains privately owned by Lloyd descendants (11th–12th generation), who have allowed University of Maryland archaeologists (from 2005) to excavate the 'Long Green' quarters and greenhouse, where African-derived protective objects were found. Exhibits and a database of hundreds of enslaved people's names have resulted.

legacyDetail.d: UMD's project, conducted with the family's permission and with descendant communities, has documented quarters, greenhouse and named individuals.

sources.label: Maryland State Archives — Aaron Anthony biography (Lloyd holdings, Douglass)
NPR — Plantation Dig Reveals Md. Town's Painful Past
Wikipedia — Wye House

connections.label: moved enslaved people to Deep South

records.name: Ridgely family of Hampton (Towson)
records.scaleNote: The Ridgelys enslaved over 500 people from the colonial era to 1864: c. 130 in 1783, more than 300 by 1790, nearly 350 in 1829, 61 in 1860, per NPS.
records.origins: Charles Ridgely bought 1,500 acres in northern Baltimore County in 1745 and opened the Northampton Ironworks in 1761. His son Captain Charles Ridgely expanded holdings to c. 24,000 acres, partly from confiscated Loyalist land, and built the Hampton mansion (completed 1790).
records.role_summary: Enslaved people — alongside convict and indentured servants — worked the ironworks, quarries, fields and mansion. Governor Charles Carnan Ridgely's 1829 will codicil freed people within set age bands, one of Maryland's largest manumissions, but it split families; his son John bought c. 60 more people and slavery continued at Hampton until Maryland abolished it in 1864.

roleDetail.d: Northampton Ironworks supplied iron, including during the Revolution, using enslaved and bound labor.
Women 25–45 and men 28–45 were freed; younger people waited, and those over 45 were bequeathed to heirs under Maryland law.
Daniel Harris was freed but his three-year-old daughter Mary was not; he bought her freedom in 1831.

records.legacy: Hampton passed to the federal government in 1948 as Hampton National Historic Site. NPS's 2020 study 'Tracing the Lives of the Enslaved' identified hundreds of living descendants of those freed in 1829, and the site interprets its quarters and enslaved community.

legacyDetail.d: The NPS Ethnographic Overview traces families freed in 1829 through generations to today.

sources.label: NPS — Chattel Slavery at Hampton
NPS — Tracing the Lives of the Enslaved study
NPS — Daniel and Mary Harris

records.name: Howard family (John Eager Howard; Belvidere)
records.scaleNote: No full count published; Howard's papers record buying, selling and manumitting enslaved people, his 1827 estate sale at Belvidere included enslaved persons, and the 1846 inventory of his son George Howard's estate at Waverly listed 25 enslaved men, women and children.
records.origins: John Eager Howard (1752–1827) inherited Baltimore County land, won fame at the Battle of Cowpens (1781), and served as governor of Maryland (1788–1791) and U.S. Senator. He became one of Baltimore's largest landowners as the city expanded over his estates.
records.role_summary: Howard's wealth was chiefly urban land, but he enslaved people on his Belvidere estate and other properties. His correspondence discusses the purchase and sale of enslaved people and deeds of manumission; his son George Howard, governor 1831–1833, enslaved people at Waverly (Marriottsville).

roleDetail.d: Letters to Virgil Maxcy (NYPL) discuss buying and selling enslaved people and signing manumission deeds.
A sale at 'Belvidere House' after Howard's death included enslaved people, per Maryland Center for History and Culture holdings.
After George Howard's death in August 1846, his estate inventory listed 25 enslaved people at Waverly.

records.legacy: Howard County, Howard and Eager Streets, and a 1904 equestrian statue in Mount Vernon Place honor him; he donated the land for Baltimore's Washington Monument. Public reckoning with his slaveholding has so far been limited.

legacyDetail.d: Mount Vernon Place was laid out on land Howard gave, with his statue in the north garden.

sources.label: NYPL Archives — John Eager Howard letters to Virgil Maxcy
Wikipedia — Waverly (Marriottsville, Maryland)
Wikipedia — John Eager Howard

records.name: Thomas Jefferson
records.scaleNote: Jefferson enslaved more than 600 (over 610) people in his lifetime, per Monticello's Getting Word project; c. 130 people were advertised for sale after his death to pay $107,000 of debt.
records.origins: Jefferson inherited land and enslaved people from his father Peter Jefferson and, through his wife Martha Wayles Skelton, from John Wayles — an inheritance that included Elizabeth Hemings and her children. Wayles had acted as an agent in slave-ship sales in Virginia.
records.role_summary: Author of the Declaration's 'all men are created equal', Jefferson ran Monticello and Poplar Forest with enslaved labor (tobacco, then wheat, a nailery and household work), bought and sold people, and freed only a handful. Most historians accept that he fathered Sally Hemings's children; as president he signed the 1807 Act ending legal imports.

roleDetail.d: Monticello's records identify more than 610 people Jefferson enslaved over his life.
After his death, nearly 100 people were sold over five days at Monticello and at least 33 more in 1829, scattering families.
Monticello and most scholars conclude Jefferson fathered six children with Hemings, whom he enslaved.
He urged and signed the ban on importing captives effective 1 January 1808.

records.legacy: Monticello (Thomas Jefferson Foundation) now centers slavery in its interpretation, including the 2018 'Life of Sally Hemings' exhibit, and its Getting Word Oral History Project (since 1993) has recorded over 200 interviews with descendants. The University of Virginia, which Jefferson founded, has built a Memorial to Enslaved Laborers.

legacyDetail.d: The project documents hundreds of descendants of Monticello's enslaved families.

sources.label: Monticello — Getting Word: About
Monticello — The 1827 dispersal sale
Monticello — Sale of Monticello

records.name: Austin Woolfolk
records.scaleNote: Baltimore's leading slave trader of the 1820s–30s, making tens of thousands of dollars a year; part of a Baltimore–New Orleans coastal trade that carried an estimated 15,000–20,000 people 1818–1860.
records.base: Pratt and Cove Streets, Baltimore, Maryland
records.origins: Woolfolk began trading in Baltimore around 1816, aged about 19, buying people in taverns and hotels; his uncle sold people he sent overland to Georgia. He belonged to a family network of traders.
records.role_summary: Woolfolk professionalised the Baltimore trade with a fixed residence and private jail on West Pratt Street, 'CASH FOR NEGROES' advertising and a network of rural agents. He marched coffles south and shipped captives from Fells Point and the Inner Harbor to New Orleans; Frederick Douglass recalled his chained gangs passing at night.

roleDetail.d: His fixed pen model was later copied by Franklin & Armfield, per Baltimore Heritage.

On 9 January 1827 he beat abolitionist editor Benjamin Lundy, who had called him a 'monster in human shape'; he pleaded guilty and Judge Nicholas Brice fined him one dollar plus costs, remarking that the trade was beneficial.
Coastwise ships carried his captives to New Orleans; one, the Decatur (1826), saw a revolt by those aboard.

records.legacy: His Pratt Street site now lies under a divided highway near MLK Boulevard; Baltimore Heritage and city historical markers document it. He retired wealthy in 1842; Joseph Donovan took over the site.

legacyDetail.d: Baltimore Heritage's 'Slave Trade in Baltimore' tour marks Woolfolk's jail.

sources.label: Baltimore Heritage — Site of Austin Woolfolk's Slave Jail
TIME — Baltimore's slavery history
AHA 2018 — Baltimore to New Orleans coastal slave trade (paper abstract)
Wikipedia — Austin Woolfolk

records.name: Hope H. Slatter
records.scaleNote: A leading Baltimore trader 1835–late 1840s, shipping captives to New Orleans and holding others in his jail at 25 cents a day; no reliable total is published.
records.base: Pratt Street (between Sharp and Howard), Baltimore, Maryland
records.origins: Born in Georgia, Slatter worked with his brother Shadrack in New Orleans before moving to Baltimore in 1835. His son Henry joined the business.
records.role_summary: From 1838 Slatter ran a private jail on Pratt Street — his house at one end, a two-storey brick prison at the other — buying Chesapeake people under 'Cash for Negroes' adverts, boarding others' captives, and shipping people south by sea. He sold the business to the Campbell brothers in the late 1840s and retired to Mobile.

roleDetail.d: Baltimore Heritage dates the jail at 224 W. Pratt Street to 1838.
1843 Baltimore Sun ads offered to hold people for 25 cents a day.
B. M. and W. L. Campbell continued the trade from the site.

records.legacy: The site, near today's Camden Yards area of Pratt Street, is marked in Baltimore Heritage's slave-trade tour. Slatter died of yellow fever in Mobile in 1853.

legacyDetail.d: Baltimore Heritage documents the 'Slatter/Campbell Slave Jail'.

sources.label: Baltimore Heritage — Site of Slatter/Campbell Slave Jail
Wikipedia — Hope H. Slatter
Afrolumens Project — Hope H. Slatter, 1843 advertisement

records.name: Ball family of South Carolina
records.scaleNote: Between 1698 and 1865 six generations owned more than twenty Cooper River rice plantations and enslaved nearly 4,000 people, per the Ball Family Slaveholder Index; Isaac Ball alone held 571.
records.base: Comingtee, Cooper River, near Charleston, South Carolina
records.origins: Elias Ball arrived from England in 1698 to claim a share of the Comingtee plantation inherited from his uncle John Coming. The family expanded across the Cooper River's tidal rice lands.
records.role_summary: The Balls bought captives directly off transatlantic ships in Charleston — in 1756 Elias Ball bought five children from the Hare, sold by Henry Laurens's firm, including a ten-year-old girl from Sierra Leone he named Priscilla. Enslaved West Africans' rice-growing knowledge and labor made the Lowcountry estates profitable.

roleDetail.d: Laurens's account book records the sale of five children from the Hare to Elias Ball on 30 June 1756.
Over twenty plantations, with surviving records for twenty-eight Ball properties.
Edward Ball linked the Hare to Bunce Island; newer research suggests most captives were bought along the Sierra Leone–Guinea coast.

records.legacy: Descendant Edward Ball's 'Slaves in the Family' (1998, National Book Award) traced both the family and descendants of the people it enslaved. Research by Ball and Joseph Opala connected Thomalind Martin Polite, Priscilla's descendant, to Sierra Leone (homecoming 2005), a story now in the International African American Museum.

legacyDetail.d: Ball's book began after a family reunion where no one mentioned the 4,000 people the family had enslaved.
Yale's Gilder Lehrman Center documented Polite's 2005 visit to Sierra Leone.

sources.label: Lowcountry Africana — Ball Family Slaveholder Index
Yale Macmillan Center — Priscilla's Story
Edward Ball — Slaves in the Family
Charleston City Paper — Polite: My family's link to West Africa is told in IAAM exhibit

connections.label: Hare voyage linked to Sierra Leone

records.name: Hampton family (Wade Hampton I, II, III)
records.scaleNote: Wade Hampton I 'may have owned as many as 900' enslaved people by 1820 (South Carolina Encyclopedia), and at his 1835 death was said to hold c. 3,000 (a contemporary claim, unverified). In 1860 the Hamptons' Issaquena County, Mississippi, plantations held 335 people per the slave schedules, while Digital History credits Wade Hampton III with c. 900 in the Delta — counts vary by source and date.
records.base: Columbia, South Carolina (Millwood); The Houmas, Louisiana; Mississippi
records.origins: Wade Hampton I (1752–1835), a Revolutionary officer and land speculator, became a cotton planter in the South Carolina midlands and in 1811 bought Louisiana land (The Houmas) that he made the state's largest sugar operation, selling c. $100,000 a year by 1827.
records.role_summary: Three generations built one of the antebellum South's largest slaveholding fortunes in cotton and sugar across South Carolina, Louisiana and Mississippi. Wade Hampton III, a Confederate general, became governor in 1876 after a campaign marked by Red Shirt violence that ended Reconstruction in South Carolina.

roleDetail.d: The Houmas, worked by enslaved people, made Hampton I Louisiana's largest sugar producer by 1827.
Hampton II and III held plantations in South Carolina and the Mississippi Delta (Hampton II's own Walnut Ridge tract was 2,529 acres).
Hampton III's 1876 election, backed by armed Red Shirts, restored white minority rule.

records.legacy: A Wade Hampton III equestrian statue stands on the South Carolina State House grounds, and his name remains on schools and places, some renamed after 2020 debates. Houmas House is a Louisiana museum; Millwood's ruins survive near Columbia.

legacyDetail.d: Hampton monuments and names have been debated as part of Confederate memorial reviews.

sources.label: South Carolina Encyclopedia — Hampton, Wade I
South Carolina Encyclopedia — Hampton, Wade II
Wikipedia — Wade Hampton III
Digital History (University of Houston) — Biographical sidebar: Wade Hampton

connections.label: War of 1812 era (Hampton I a U.S. general)

records.name: Middleton family of South Carolina
records.scaleNote: The Middleton Place Foundation identifies some 2,800 people enslaved by the Middleton family between 1738 and 1865 across their rice plantations.
records.base: Middleton Place, Ashley River, South Carolina
records.origins: The Middletons arrived in Carolina from Barbados in the late 1600s. Henry Middleton acquired the Ashley River estate by marriage in 1741 and later presided over the First Continental Congress; his son Arthur signed the Declaration of Independence.
records.role_summary: Enslaved Africans and their descendants built and worked the Middletons' rice fields, terraced gardens and house; the family's wealth and political leadership — from Congress to the 1860 Ordinance of Secession, which Williams Middleton signed — rested on their labor.

roleDetail.d: The Ashley River rice fields were likely built by enslaved people brought from West Africa.
Williams Middleton signed South Carolina's Ordinance of Secession (1860); Union troops burned the house in 1865.

records.legacy: Middleton Place (Foundation-owned, a National Historic Landmark) runs the 'Beyond the Fields' exhibit and tours on its enslaved people, and since 2006 has hosted joint reunions of Black and white Middleton descendants (c. 300 attended in 2016), which led to a tuition assistance program.

legacyDetail.d: Begun in 2006 at the suggestion of an African American descendant.
A freedmen's dwelling on site interprets enslaved and post-emancipation lives.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Middleton Place
Suffolk University — Reinterpreting Life on a Southern Plantation
The Cultural Landscape Foundation — Middleton Place

records.name: Pinckney family of South Carolina
records.scaleNote: Charles Cotesworth Pinckney enslaved c. 250 people, per NPS; Charles Pinckney's Snee Farm (715 acres) and other estates were worked by enslaved people producing rice and indigo.
records.base: Charleston and Snee Farm, Mount Pleasant, South Carolina
records.origins: Eliza Lucas Pinckney developed indigo as a South Carolina export crop in the 1740s using enslaved labor and expertise. Her sons Charles Cotesworth and Thomas Pinckney and their cousin Charles Pinckney became leading Federalist-era statesmen.
records.role_summary: At the 1787 Constitutional Convention C. C. Pinckney and Charles Pinckney insisted South Carolina would reject a Constitution that empowered Congress to ban the Atlantic slave trade, helping secure the clause protecting imports until 1808.

roleDetail.d: NPS's convention chronicle records C. C. Pinckney's 22 August 1787 argument for protecting slave imports.
Charles Pinckney inherited Snee Farm in 1782 and grew rice and indigo with enslaved workers; a 1787 inventory lists them by name.

records.legacy: Charles Pinckney National Historic Site (est. 1988) preserves 28 acres of Snee Farm and uses archaeology to interpret the enslaved community there.

legacyDetail.d: The park's 'Enslaved Community of Snee Farm' presents archaeology of quarters and daily life.

sources.label: NPS — Enslaved Community of Snee Farm
NPS — Constitutional Convention, August 22
NPS — Charles Pinckney

connections.label: C. C. Pinckney served in Washington administration

records.name: Port of Baltimore (Fells Point and Inner Harbor)
records.description: Baltimore grew as an export port for Chesapeake tobacco and grain produced largely by enslaved people, and became a hub of the domestic slave trade: slave jails clustered between the Inner Harbor and Fells Point, and an estimated 15,000–20,000 people were shipped by sea to New Orleans between 1818 and 1860 (AHA 2018 paper; NARA M1895 manifests). Baltimore also had the largest free Black population of any U.S. city by 1860.

records.name: Pratt Street slave jails, Baltimore
records.description: Private jails on West Pratt Street held people bought in the Chesapeake before sale south: Austin Woolfolk's at Pratt and Cove (by 1821), Hope H. Slatter's at 224 W. Pratt (1838, later the Campbells'), and Joseph Donovan's. Sites are marked by Baltimore Heritage; most lie under modern roads near Camden Yards and MLK Boulevard.

records.name: Mount Vernon
records.description: George Washington's 8,000-acre, five-farm plantation on the Potomac, where 317 enslaved people lived in 1799. Owned since 1858 by the Mount Vernon Ladies' Association, it now interprets slavery extensively, including the 1983 Slave Memorial and ongoing burial-ground archaeology.

records.name: Monticello
records.description: Thomas Jefferson's Albemarle County plantation, where hundreds of enslaved people worked fields, a nailery and the household. Most of the enslaved community was sold in 1827 to pay his debts; today the Thomas Jefferson Foundation interprets Mulberry Row, Sally Hemings's life and descendant histories through Getting Word.

records.name: The Hermitage (Nashville)
records.description: Andrew Jackson's cotton plantation, where about 150 people were enslaved at his death in 1845. The Andrew Jackson Foundation located its enslaved cemetery (at least 28 burials) in 2024 and is forming a descendant advisory committee.

records.name: Riversdale (Riverdale Park, Maryland)
records.description: Plantation house completed by Rosalie Stier Calvert and George Calvert in the early 1800s, worked by enslaved people including diarist Adam Francis Plummer; part of its land became the University of Maryland campus. Now a National Historic Landmark house museum run by M-NCPPC that interprets its enslaved workforce.

records.name: Wye House
records.description: Seat of the Lloyd family on Maryland's Eastern Shore since the 1650s, hub of farms that enslaved hundreds; Frederick Douglass lived there as an enslaved child in 1824. Still privately owned by Lloyd descendants; UMD archaeology since 2005 has uncovered quarters and African-derived ritual objects.

records.name: Hampton National Historic Site (Towson)
records.description: The Ridgely family's Baltimore County plantation and ironworks estate, with a mansion completed in 1790 and surviving stone slave quarters; nearly 350 people were enslaved there in 1829. NPS has operated it since 1948 and researches descendants of the enslaved.

records.name: Doughoregan Manor
records.description: The Carroll family's c. 10,000-acre Howard County estate, where a 1773 inventory listed 330 enslaved people by family. It remained in Carroll family hands long after Charles Carroll of Carrollton's death in 1832 and is a National Historic Landmark.

records.name: Catoctin Furnace
records.description: Iron furnace founded in 1776 by Thomas Johnson and three of his brothers in Frederick County and worked by enslaved African American ironworkers; it made iron for the Continental Army. Its African American cemetery (c. 100 graves; donated to Cunningham Falls State Park in 2026) is the subject of a 2023 Science ancient-DNA study linking nearly 42,000 living people to 27 individuals buried there.

records.name: Maryland Act of 1664 (lifelong slavery)
records.description: Act of the Maryland assembly, under the Calverts' proprietary government, declaring that enslaved Africans in the province and those imported later would serve 'durante vita' (for life), with their children enslaved as well. It gave legislative sanction to slavery practiced since the 1640s and anchored the Chesapeake tobacco economy.

records.name: Maryland Constitution of 1864 (abolition)
records.description: Maryland's third constitution, ratified narrowly by referendum on 12–13 October 1864 (soldiers' votes provided the margin) and effective 1 November 1864, abolished slavery in the state a year before the 13th Amendment. 1 November is now marked as Maryland Emancipation Day.

records.name: Philipse family (Frederick & Adolph Philipse)
records.scaleNote: Per Historic Hudson Valley, Philipse ships made at least five Madagascar voyages in 1693–1699 buying 1,100+ captives, and carried 809 captives to Barbados in 1720–1725; 23 enslaved people were listed at Philipsburg Manor in 1750.
records.base: New York (Manhattan) and Philipsburg Manor, Westchester
records.origins: Frederick Philipse (1626–1702) arrived in New Amsterdam from Friesland as a carpenter for the Dutch West India Company and became the colony's richest merchant through marriage, trade and land. He kept his fortune through the English takeover of 1664 and assembled the vast Philipsburg manor on the Hudson.
records.role_summary: Frederick and his son Adolph (1664–1750) ran a merchant fleet to Europe, the Caribbean and Africa that carried African captives from c.1680. In the 1690s they bought captives from pirate brokers on Madagascar to evade the Royal African Company monopoly, and they held enslaved people on their Westchester and Manhattan properties.

roleDetail.d: Per Historic Hudson Valley, at least five Philipse voyages (1693–1699) bought more than 1,100 captives off Madagascar, partly from the pirate broker Adam Baldridge on Île Sainte-Marie.

roleDetail.t: 'It is by negroes that I finde my cheivest Proffitt.'
roleDetail.d: Frederick Philipse's own 1695 statement, quoted by Historic Hudson Valley, describes captives as his main source of profit.
Per Historic Hudson Valley, 809 captives were carried to Barbados on Philipse ships between 1720 and 1725.

roleDetail.t: Enslaved community at the Upper Mills.
roleDetail.d: Adolph's 1750 probate inventory lists 23 enslaved men, women and children by name at Philipsburg Manor, placed first among his assets; several were sold after his death.

records.legacy: The family's Loyalist heirs lost the manor when New York confiscated it after the Revolution. Today Historic Hudson Valley runs Philipsburg Manor in Sleepy Hollow as a site interpreting northern colonial slavery, built around the named enslaved people of the 1750 inventory.

legacyDetail.t: Museum reinterpreted as a heritage site of slavery.
legacyDetail.d: Historic Hudson Valley's 'People Not Property' project and the Philipsburg Manor interpretation centre the enslaved millers and farmworkers rather than the Philipse family.
The Philipse records are widely used to show that slavery and slave trading were central to the economy of colonial New York, not only to the plantation South.

sources.label: Historic Hudson Valley — The Philipse Family and the Slave Trade
Historic Hudson Valley — The Philipsburg Manor Inventory
SlaveVoyages — Voyage 36998 (Philipse-owned voyage)

connections.label: rose as WIC-era merchant in New Amsterdam

records.name: Peter Stuyvesant
records.scaleNote: As WIC director in Curaçao and director-general of New Netherland (1647–1664) he expanded slave imports; per the Museum of the City of New York, the WIC ship Witte Paert brought almost 300 captives in 1655 and c.700 enslaved Africans lived in New Netherland by the mid-1660s.
records.origins: A Frisian minister's son, Stuyvesant entered Dutch West India Company service in Brazil and then Curaçao, where he became director and lost a leg attacking Spanish St Martin in 1644. The WIC appointed him director-general of New Netherland in 1645; he arrived in 1647.
records.role_summary: Stuyvesant worked with the WIC to turn New Amsterdam into a port for the Atlantic trade in enslaved Africans and to link it to the Curaçao slave depot. He personally held enslaved people on his Manhattan bouwerij (farm).

roleDetail.d: Per MCNY, in the late 1650s he worked with the WIC to raise annual imports of captives; in 1655 the Witte Paert anchored in the East River with almost 300 Africans for sale.
He sought to make New Netherland a supplier of Curaçao, which would return salt, horses and enslaved people; the scheme had limited success because merchants preferred other markets.
Some forty enslaved Africans are recorded as working his bouwerij, the site of today's St Mark's Church and his statue.

records.legacy: His name survives across New York (Stuyvesant High School, Bedford-Stuyvesant, Stuyvesant Square) and his 1941 statue by Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney stands near his old farm. Calls to remove his memorials—over antisemitism in 2017 and over slaveholding in a 2023 City Council hearing—remain unresolved.

legacyDetail.d: A 2023 NYC Council Cultural Affairs hearing considered removing statues of figures including Stuyvesant, citing his slaveholding; critics called it 'cancel culture'.
Historians at the Gotham Center argue the statue site should also tell the story of the enslaved Africans who worked the bouwerij for over a century.

sources.label: Museum of the City of New York — Petrus Stuyvesant
Gotham Center — Monuments of Colonial New York: Stuyvesant and Hudson
amNY — New York and Curaçao: the Dutch connection

connections.label: surrendered colony to Duke of York's fleet 1664

records.name: Van Cortlandt family
records.scaleNote: Merchants and manor lords of Dutch origin who held enslaved people across several generations and traded captives on consignment; per NESRI/CUNY Stephanus traded illegally with Madagascar and Frederick owned a slave ship.
records.base: New York City and Westchester (Van Cortlandt Manor, Croton)
records.origins: Oloff Stevense Van Cortlandt came to New Amsterdam as a WIC soldier in 1638 and became a brewer and burgomaster. His sons Stephanus and Jacobus became leading merchants, Stephanus receiving the royal patent for Van Cortlandt Manor in 1697.
records.role_summary: Stephanus was a business partner of the slave trader Robert Livingston and was involved in illegal Madagascar trade; Jacobus sold enslaved people on consignment in New York. The family's Bronx plantation and Westchester manor ran on enslaved labour into the early 19th century.

roleDetail.d: Per the Van Cortlandt House Museum, Jacobus and Frederick both took part in slave trading; NESRI/CUNY research records Frederick owning a slave ship.
Enslaved people likely helped build the Van Cortlandt House (1748–49) in today's Bronx and farmed wheat and ran mills there.
Historic Hudson Valley names enslaved people such as Titus and Bridget held by Pierre Van Cortlandt at Croton.

records.legacy: Van Cortlandt Park and two museum houses keep the name; both now interpret enslavement. The Van Cortlandt House Museum runs an enslaved-Africans tour, and Historic Hudson Valley's Van Cortlandt Manor presents the named people held there.

legacyDetail.d: The Van Cortlandt House Museum documents enslaved household servants from 1748 to at least 1821, when Augustus Van Cortlandt freed a woman named Dinah.

sources.label: Van Cortlandt House Museum — Enslaved Africans tour
Historic Hudson Valley — Van Cortlandt Manor
NESRI/CUNY — Stephanus Van Cortlandt

connections.label: Catharina Van Cortlandt married Frederick Philipse

records.name: Willem Gideon Deutz
records.scaleNote: Per the Amsterdam Museum he held a financial stake in more than a hundred plantations; his 'negotiatie' model spawned at least 240 plantation funds (per Itinerario/Cambridge).
records.origins: An Amsterdam merchant-banker from a regent family, Deutz traded in plantation produce from Suriname. Governor Jan Jacob Mauricius is thought to have encouraged him, around 1751, to extend credit to Surinamese planters.
records.role_summary: From his 'Surinam office' on the Herengracht, Deutz pioneered the plantation 'negotiatie': a fund pooling money from many Dutch investors and lending it to planters against mortgages on plantations—and thus on the enslaved people who were counted as plantation property.

roleDetail.d: The negotiatie bundled capital from a broad range of investors as credit for plantations, with land and enslaved people as collateral (Amsterdam Museum; Leiden research).
Per the Amsterdam Museum, Deutz held a financial stake in more than a hundred plantations.

roleDetail.t: Fed a credit boom and crash.
roleDetail.d: The model was copied in dozens of funds; easy credit drove expansion and speculation in Suriname, followed by mass defaults after the 1773 Amsterdam crisis.

records.legacy: His former house, Huis Willet-Holthuysen (Amsterdam Museum), hosts the 2026–27 exhibition 'Plantation along the Canal' on how canal-house wealth financed Surinamese plantations. Amsterdam's 2021 apology explicitly covered the city's regent elite of which Deutz was part.

legacyDetail.d: The Amsterdam Museum exhibition examines Deutz and Fredrik Berewout (owner of Jagtlust) alongside the named enslaved people of Jagtlust.

sources.label: Amsterdam Museum — Plantage aan de gracht (Plantation along the Canal)
Cultureel Persbureau — Exhibition at Huis Willet-Holthuysen exposes financing of Surinamese plantations
Itinerario (Cambridge) — Debunking Debts: Suriname at the end of the 18th century

records.name: Coopstad & Rochussen (Rotterdam)
records.scaleNote: More than 80% of the 68 slave ships that left Rotterdam in 1750–1780 were fitted out by the firm (c. 55+ voyages, per the Rotterdam research as reviewed by Kardux, 2022); SlaveVoyages lists individual voyages (e.g. Maas, Publicola, Nicolaas Theodorus, Willemina Aletta). It was Rotterdam's leading slaving house in the later 18th century.
records.origins: A Rotterdam merchant partnership of Herman Coopstad and Isaac Jacobus Rochussen. After the WIC lost its monopoly (1730), private Dutch firms could fit out slaving voyages on payment of fees to the company.
records.role_summary: The firm owned and outfitted ships that bought captives on the Windward, Ivory and Gold Coasts (including at Elmina), Accra and Gabon, and sold them in Suriname and other Dutch colonies. Its archive survives in the Rotterdam City Archives and underpins much Dutch slave-trade data.

roleDetail.d: Per SlaveVoyages, its ships bought captives at Cape Lahou, Elmina, Accra and Gabon; one Nicolaas Theodorus voyage recorded about 35% children.
Willemina Aletta voyage 11152 landed captives in Suriname, per SlaveVoyages.

records.legacy: The firm's archive is a key source for Johannes Postma's Dutch slave-trade research. Rotterdam's KITLV-led study of city involvement led Mayor Ahmed Aboutaleb to apologise in December 2021.

legacyDetail.d: Research commissioned in 2017 found city councillors invested in the WIC and later in private slave trading and plantations; the mayor apologised on 10 December 2021.

sources.label: SlaveVoyages — Voyage 10805 (Maas, owners Coopstad & Rochussen)
SlaveVoyages — Voyage 11152 (Willemina Aletta)
Erasmus University Rotterdam — Rotterdam research at the basis of apology
New West Indian Guide — Kardux, 'Dutch cities in global slavery' (2022)

connections.label: private trade under WIC fee regime

records.name: Manuel Pinto da Fonseca
records.scaleNote: Called 'the most notorious slave dealer in all Brazil'; a British report based on his own declaration put his 1844 profits at c.£150,000.
records.origins: Born near Porto in 1804, he emigrated to Rio and rose from subordinate commercial posts after 1831, when Brazil's first anti-trafficking law made the trade illegal. With his brothers he entered slaving around 1837.
records.role_summary: He ran a mercantile house operating on four continents that trafficked captives from Angola and the Congo coast to Rio during the illegal era, using US-flagged ships and American crews to dodge British patrols. He was a principal rival of José Bernardino de Sá.

roleDetail.d: Mesquita (Anais do Museu Histórico Nacional, 2020) shows how he and Bernardino de Sá took control of the slave trade into Southeast Brazil after 1831.
He bought the brig Uncas (1844–45) and used ships such as Porpoise and Kentucky, exploiting US flags against British searches.
Recent Brazilian scholarship (ANPUH 2024) examines his ties to the Court and the Imperial government between 1837 and 1850.

records.legacy: After the 1850 Eusébio de Queirós Law he was expelled to Portugal (1851 per most English accounts; a UFF study groups him with Bernardino de Sá and Tomás da Costa Ramos among traffickers expelled in 1852) and died in Paris in 1855. His case is now central to Brazilian research on the 'contraband era', when c.750,000 Africans were landed illegally.

legacyDetail.d: He, Bernardino de Sá and Tomás da Costa Ramos were expelled rather than tried, a sign of how protected the major traffickers were.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Manuel Pinto da Fonseca (slave trader)
Anais do Museu Histórico Nacional — Mesquita, Portugueses no tráfico ilegal (2020)
ANPUH — Pinto da Fonseca and the Imperial state, 1837–1850 (2024)
UFF Polis — texto 19A, expulsions of slave traffickers after 1850

connections.label: chief rival in Rio's illegal trade

records.name: Joaquim Ferreira dos Santos, Count of Ferreira
records.scaleNote: Per the EU MANIFEST project, he traded an estimated 10,000+ captives from Luanda and Cabinda to Brazil.
records.base: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (later Porto, Portugal)
records.origins: Born in Porto in 1782, he left for Brazil in 1800 and built a consignment business in Rio de Janeiro. His network linked Rio, Lisbon and Angola.
records.role_summary: He headed a triangular network sending goods to Luanda and Cabinda, where his ships embarked captives for Brazil. He returned to Portugal in 1832 and was made Count of Ferreira in 1850.

roleDetail.d: Per MANIFEST, his ships loaded captives at Luanda and Cabinda to supply Brazil, trading an estimated 10,000+ people.
He received the Order of Christ from João VI and titles from Pedro I; Portugal made him Count in 1850.

records.legacy: Childless, he left his fortune to found Porto's Hospital Conde de Ferreira (a psychiatric hospital still operating) and 120 primary schools, about 70 of which survive. In 2023 the hospital shut part of an art installation asking 'How many enslaved people is a psychiatric hospital worth?'

legacyDetail.d: Scholars note his bequests built an image of benefactor that obscured the source of his wealth.
The hospital closed a room of Dori Nigro and Paulo Pinto's 'Vento (A)mar' on its opening day (20 May 2023).

sources.label: MANIFEST (EU) — Joaquim Ferreira dos Santos, a Portuguese trader of enslaved African peoples
Hyperallergic — Portugal hospital removes artwork about its slavery ties

records.name: João Fernandes Vieira
records.scaleNote: Brazilian scholarship (ANPUH papers citing Acioli, 1997) credits him with c.16 sugar mills in Pernambuco and Paraíba and c.2,000 enslaved people — a secondary estimate, not a documented count; he governed Angola 1658–1661.
records.origins: Born in Madeira, he rose in Dutch-ruled Pernambuco as a merchant and agent for Dutch interests, becoming the richest colonist of his era. He then led the Pernambucan Insurrection (1645–1654) that expelled the Dutch West India Company.
records.role_summary: As one of Brazil's greatest sugar planters he depended on enslaved Africans; as governor of Angola (1658–1661) he used the post to restore and expand the Luanda–Recife slave route serving his own Pernambuco interests.

roleDetail.d: About sixteen engenhos and a reported c.2,000 enslaved people (Acioli, as cited in Brazilian conference papers); the figure is an estimate.

roleDetail.t: Governor of Angola for Pernambuco's benefit.
roleDetail.d: Souza (Sankofa, 2017) shows his Angola rule was tied to his sugar and slave-trade interests and revived Luanda–Recife traffic.
Vieira and André Vidal de Negreiros pursued interests against the Kingdom of Kongo while governing Angola.

records.legacy: He is celebrated in Brazil as a hero of the Restoration of Pernambuco, and the Brazilian Army dates its origin to the Battles of Guararapes he helped lead. His slaving governorship is far less remembered.

legacyDetail.d: Popular biographies stress the insurrection; academic work stresses his Angola slave-trade interests.

sources.label: Sankofa (USP) — Souza, Conflicts and Atlantic interests in Angola: the government of João Fernandes Vieira, 1658–1661
ANPUH — João Fernandes Vieira and the Luanda–Recife trade
Canoa do Tempo (UFAM) — Vieira and Vidal de Negreiros against Congo

records.name: António Fernandes de Elvas
records.scaleNote: Held the Spanish asiento 1615–1623 and the Angola, Cape Verde and Guinea contracts; 11,328 Africans were brought to Cartagena in 1619–1624 alone (per Alencastro).
records.origins: A Portuguese New Christian (converso) merchant in the pepper trade from India, he belonged to the Lisbon networks that financed the Habsburg crown during the Iberian Union (1580–1640).
records.role_summary: He bought the asiento to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America and simultaneously the Portuguese crown contracts (contratos) for Angola, Cape Verde and Guinea, integrating supply and delivery. His son Jorge acted for him in Cartagena.

roleDetail.d: Asiento 27 Sept 1615 – 1 Apr 1623 and contratador for Angola, Cape Verde and Guinea 1615–1623.
Main destinations of his ships, with his son Jorge Fernandes de Elvas based in Cartagena.

roleDetail.t: New Christian networks under Inquisition pressure.
roleDetail.d: A USP thesis uses his family network to study tensions between New Christians, the Inquisition and the Spanish Crown; 'New Christian' labels were often accusations.

records.legacy: His tenure marked the peak of Portuguese New Christian control of the asiento, which fed the large Luanda–Cartagena flows of the 1610s–1620s. No modern institutional successor exists.

legacyDetail.d: He was succeeded by Manuel Rodrigues Lamego, continuing the converso hold on the contract until the 1640 Portuguese revolt.

sources.label: Wikipedia — António Fernandes de Elvas
Universidade de São Paulo — doctoral thesis on Elvas family New Christian network

records.name: Manuel Rodrigues Lamego
records.scaleNote: Asiento 1623–1631: 59 ships licensed for Africa and c.8,000 captives bought, mostly at Luanda (per Wikipedia summary of the scholarship); the contract envisaged c.4,250 per year.
records.origins: From a Sephardic converso family of Lamego, linked by marriage to the banker Juan Núñez Saravia and to merchants in Rouen and Amsterdam.
records.role_summary: He held the asiento for supplying enslaved Africans to Spanish America and, in 1623–1624, the Angola contract. Old Christian merchants in Seville lobbied the Inquisition against him, and his brother António was tried for 'Judaising'.

roleDetail.d: Most of the c.8,000 people bought under his contract came from Luanda.
Wikipedia gives 1 April 1623 – 25 Sept 1631; a Jesuit archive record dates the contract from 1 May 1622 for eight years.

records.legacy: His family network spread to Rouen and Amsterdam's Sephardic community. His case is studied as an example of Inquisition pressure on converso financiers of the slave trade.

legacyDetail.d: It went to Melchor Gómez Angel and Cristóvão Mendes de Sousa.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Manuel Rodrigues Lamego
Archivo Jesuitas — Asiento with Manuel Rodríguez Lamego (from 1622)

records.name: Joachim Nettelbeck
records.scaleNote: A crewman then first mate on Dutch slave ships (c.1749–50 and 1771, the Vrouwe Elisabeth of Rotterdam), who later lobbied Prussian kings for slave-worked colonies; captive numbers for his voyages are not documented in the sources used.
records.origins: A Kolberg sailor who at eleven stowed away on a Dutch slave ship from Amsterdam. He later sailed to Suriname and Sint Eustatius.
records.role_summary: In 1771 he was first mate on a Dutch slaving voyage Europe–Guinea–Suriname, commanding the longboat that bought captives along the coast for guns, powder, tobacco, spirits and textiles. He then proposed Prussian slave-plantation colonies to Frederick the Great (c.1775), Frederick William II (1786) and Gneisenau (1814).

roleDetail.t: First mate on the Vrouwe Elisabeth.
roleDetail.d: Van Oostrum (Dutch Crossing, 2025) identifies the Rotterdam ship and notes Nettelbeck narrates the voyage in his memoirs.
He cited Brandenburg's old Groß Friedrichsburg when proposing a West African slave-supply settlement in 1786; all proposals were rejected.
His 1821 autobiography is a rare first-person crew account of the Dutch slave trade.

records.legacy: Hero-worshipped for the 1807 defence of Kolberg against Napoleon, he was used in Nazi propaganda (film 'Kolberg', 1945). German cities are now renaming his streets: Berlin's Nettelbeckplatz became Martha-Ndumbe-Platz (decided 2021, completed 2025) and Dortmund's Nettelbeckstraße became May-Ayim-Straße (2024).

legacyDetail.d: Part of a wider German reckoning with colonial-era street names.

sources.label: Leiden University — den Heijer inaugural lecture (Nettelbeck on Dutch slave ships)
Wikipedia (de) — Joachim Nettelbeck (Seemann)
Projekt Gutenberg — Des Seefahrers Nettelbeck Lebensgeschichte

connections.label: sought to revive Prussian Africa trade

records.name: David de Pury
records.scaleNote: A Lisbon banker-merchant who worked for the South Sea Company from 1730 and held large shares in the slave-trading Pernambuco company; he left c.2.25 million livres to Neuchâtel (≈ CHF 600m in 2020).
records.origins: Born in Neuchâtel (then a Prussian principality), he trained in commerce and worked in London for the South Sea Company before settling in Lisbon by 1735 as a banker and merchant.
records.role_summary: His firm Pury, Mellish & Devisme held Portuguese crown monopolies on Brazilian diamonds (1757) and Brazil-wood (from 1766), commodities produced with enslaved labour. He was a large shareholder in the Companhia Geral de Pernambuco e Paraíba, which shipped enslaved Africans to northeastern Brazil.

roleDetail.d: Held large shares in the Pernambuco company (Wikipedia; HLS describes him as active in colonial and slave trade).
Diamonds and Brazil-wood monopolies drew on enslaved mining and logging labour in Brazil.
Historians still debate how directly Pury, Mellish & Devisme traded captives between Africa and Brazil.

records.legacy: His bequest built Neuchâtel's town hall, hospital and schools; a bronze statue by David d'Angers stands on Place Pury. After two petitions and a red-paint attack on the night of 12–13 July 2020, the city kept the statue but added an explanatory plaque and held an art competition (jury chaired by Pap Ndiaye); Mathias Pfund's inverted miniature 'Great in the Concrete' was installed in 2022 and stolen in August 2025.

legacyDetail.d: Two petitions sought removal or reckoning; in 2021 the city chose a plaque and an artistic contest instead.
Family member and Green politician Nicolas de Pury proposed a plaque and further research.

sources.label: Wikipedia — David de Pury
Swissinfo — Switzerland joins debate about removing controversial memorials
Historical Dictionary of Switzerland — David de Pury
Le Temps — Neuchâtel: an artwork and explanatory plaque installed facing the David de Pury statue

records.name: Burckhardt family (Christoph Burckhardt & Co., Basel)
records.scaleNote: Per the Historical Dictionary of Switzerland, family firms invested in 21 slave ships between 1783 and 1815; a Basel student map estimates c.7,350 captives shipped and at least 1,100 deaths.
records.origins: Christoph Burckhardt (1740–1812), son of a Basel merchant of the same name, ran a worldwide wholesale trade in printed cottons (indiennes) and colonial goods. He entered the slave trade through Basel-linked houses in La Rochelle (Weis) and Nantes (Benoît Bourcard).
records.role_summary: Three generations took part in slaving expeditions as investors; his son Christophe Bourcard founded Bourcard, Legrand & Cie in Nantes (1790), which fitted out slave ships such as the Intrépide and Cultivateur. For Burckhardt the trade was a sideline opening West African markets for printed cotton.

roleDetail.d: Per HLS, between 1783 and 1815, with co-investors including the Merian brothers and Paris banks Pourtalès, Perregaux, Hottinguer and Rougemont.
Indiennes were the main trade goods exchanged for people on the African coast.
HLS judges the slave trade earned him little; smuggling during the Continental Blockade paid far more.

records.legacy: The Segerhof archive, public since the 1970s, is a core source on Swiss involvement in slavery (Stettler, Haenger & Labhardt, 'Baumwolle, Sklaven und Kredite', 2004). The site features in University of Basel-linked 'Colonial Entanglements in Basel' tours.

legacyDetail.d: The Burckhardt case is central to dismantling the idea that landlocked Switzerland had no role in the slave trade.
SRF found that direct Merian participation (founders of the Christoph Merian Stiftung) cannot be proven, though a Merian banker financed the Nantes start-up.

sources.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland — Christoph Burckhardt
Visionscarto / Univ. Basel seminar — Haus Segerhof
SRF — Wie auch Schweizer mit Sklaven Geld verdienten

connections.label: invested via Weis of La Rochelle

records.name: Pourtalès family (Jacques-Louis de Pourtalès)
records.scaleNote: Per HLS, Jacques-Louis de Pourtalès co-owned Grenada plantations worked by c.350 enslaved people (1770–1797) and was a partner in the slave-trading firm Romberg, Bapst & Cie.
records.origins: Born in Geneva to a Huguenot family, Jacques-Louis de Pourtalès grew up in Neuchâtel and in 1753 founded Pourtalès & Cie, trading printed calicoes across Europe, India and the Antilles.
records.role_summary: In 1770 he bought sugar, coffee, cocoa and cotton plantations on Grenada with Basel merchant Johann Jakob Thurneysen; his son Louis went there in 1792 to run them and bought enslaved people. He also profited from slave trading through Romberg, Bapst & Cie and textile supply to slaving firms.

roleDetail.d: About 350 enslaved people; the plantations were sold in 1797.
HLS notes that c.60% of goods exchanged for captives were printed textiles, the core of Pourtalès's business.
Louis de Pourtalès's Grenada letters in the Neuchâtel archives document plantation management including smallpox vaccination of enslaved workers.

records.legacy: The fortune founded Neuchâtel's Hôpital Pourtalès (1808), which still bears the name, and the family later became prominent bankers and diplomats in Paris and Prussia. Neuchâtel's 'Colonial Footprints' trail now addresses these fortunes.

legacyDetail.d: Hôpital Pourtalès, founded 1808 as a hospital for the poor.

sources.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland — Jacques-Louis de Pourtalès
Wikipedia — Jacques-Louis de Pourtalès

records.name: Isaak Faesch
records.scaleNote: WIC governor of Curaçao, the company's slave-trade hub, 1740–1758; held enslaved people at Hato and ordered 47 executions after the 1750 revolt (per HLS).
records.origins: Born in Basel, he served as a mercenary officer in the War of the Spanish Succession, then joined his brother's Amsterdam West India trading house, which collapsed in the 1720 bubble.
records.role_summary: He became WIC governor of Sint Eustatius (1737) and Curaçao (1740), repeatedly requesting more enslaved people from Amsterdam for the island. He held enslaved people on the Hato plantation and crushed the 1750 uprising of captives newly arrived from Elmina.

roleDetail.d: Curaçao was the WIC's depot for slave trading and smuggling to Spanish America.
On his order 47 enslaved people were executed, 30 of them from his own holdings.

records.legacy: He left an estate of 121,000 guilders, shared in part by his Basel relatives. He is a key example in Swiss research on citizens serving Dutch colonial slavery.

legacyDetail.d: His case appears in the Historical Dictionary of Switzerland's coverage of Swiss involvement in slavery.

sources.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland — Isaak Faesch
Wikipedia — Isaak Faesch

records.name: Leu & Co. (Zinskommission, Zurich)
records.scaleNote: Per the 2020 University of Zurich study, Zurich's investments (via Leu & Co.) in the South Sea Company, Compagnie des Indes and Danish bonds are linked to 36,494 deported Africans during its South Sea shareholding.
records.origins: A semi-state Zurich investment commission set up in 1755 (named after Johann Jakob Leu) to place public and private funds abroad; the city had bought South Sea Company shares from 1727.
records.role_summary: It invested Zurich's state and private money in the South Sea Company (asiento slave trade), the French Compagnie des Indes and Danish government bonds tied to the Danish West Indies.

roleDetail.d: During Zurich's holding the SSC carried 8,636 Africans across the Atlantic and 27,858 people from British islands to Spanish colonies.
The study links Zurich's French holdings to the company's 1720–1750 slaving, c.42,467 people.

records.legacy: Bank Leu, the successor of the Zinskommission, was privatised in 1798, became a Credit Suisse subsidiary in 1990, merged into Clariden Leu in 2007 and was absorbed into Credit Suisse in 2012; Credit Suisse was taken over by UBS in 2023. The 2020 study prompted Zurich to review its monuments and the canton to answer reparations questions.

legacyDetail.d: By Brengard, Schubert and Zürcher, commissioned by the city.
Leu & Co. (1755) → Bank Leu → Credit Suisse group (1990) → Clariden Leu (2007) → Credit Suisse (2012) → UBS (2023), per the Historical Dictionary of Switzerland and company histories.

sources.label: UZH News — Zurich's involvement in slavery (2020)
Swissinfo — Zurich's historical ties to slave trade exposed
Swiss Finance Museum — The Transatlantic Slave Trade, Part 3
Historical Dictionary of Switzerland — Leu (Bank)
Wikipedia — Bank Leu

records.name: Bern's South Sea Company shares (1719–1734)
records.description: The city-state of Bern bought c.1,300 South Sea Company shares in 1719 and held them to 1734, profiting despite the 1720 crash. The canton officially acknowledged in 2003 that the SSC ran the slave-trading asiento.

records.name: Philipsburg Manor (Upper Mills), Sleepy Hollow
records.description: The Philipse family's milling and farming complex on the Pocantico River, worked by enslaved Africans; Adolph Philipse's 1750 inventory lists 23 enslaved men, women and children by name. Historic Hudson Valley now interprets it as a heritage site of northern colonial slavery.

records.name: Plantation 'negotiaties' (Dutch plantation loan funds)
records.description: Investment funds, pioneered by Willem Gideon Deutz in the 1750s, that pooled Dutch investors' money and lent it to Caribbean and Guianese planters against mortgages on plantations and the enslaved people on them. At least 240 such funds were founded; widespread defaults followed the 1773 Amsterdam credit crisis.

records.name: Segerhof, Basel
records.description: House and office of Christoph Burckhardt & Co., built 1788–1791 on Basel's Blumenrain. Its surviving business archive, public since the early 1970s, documents the family's investment in 21 slaving voyages, and the site features in University of Basel-linked colonial walking tours.

records.name: Statue of David de Pury, Neuchâtel
records.description: Bronze statue by David d'Angers on Place Pury, inaugurated in 1855. Splashed with red paint on the night of 12–13 July 2020 after removal petitions; the city instead added a plaque and commissioned a counter-artwork, Mathias Pfund's 'Great in the Concrete' (2022), which was stolen in August 2025.

records.name: Hospital Conde de Ferreira, Porto
records.description: Psychiatric hospital in Porto funded by the will of slave trader Joaquim Ferreira dos Santos and run by the Santa Casa da Misericórdia. In May 2023 it closed part of a Porto Photography Biennial installation questioning its founder's slaving wealth. Sources give its opening as 1883 or 1893.

records.name: Hato plantation revolt, Curaçao (1750)
records.description: Uprising by enslaved people newly arrived from Elmina on the Hato plantation in Curaçao. Governor Isaak Faesch had it suppressed by militia and ordered 47 executions, 30 of them people he held himself.

records.name: University of Zurich study on Zurich and slavery (2020)
records.description: City-commissioned report by Marcel Brengard, Frank Schubert and Lukas Zürcher (September 2020) showing Zurich invested in the South Sea Company, Compagnie des Indes and Danish bonds, and that Zurich citizens owned plantations and enslaved people. It led the city to review monuments.

records.name: Amsterdam's apology for slavery (1 July 2021)
records.description: At the Keti Koti commemoration, Mayor Femke Halsema apologised for the active involvement of Amsterdam's governors in colonial slavery, based on research commissioned in 2019 that called the city's involvement 'direct, worldwide, large-scale, multifaceted and protracted'. It preceded the Dutch state's apology of December 2022.

records.name: Rotterdam's apology for slavery (10 December 2021)
records.description: Mayor Ahmed Aboutaleb apologised for city officials' role in slavery after a KITLV-led study (commissioned 2017, three volumes) found most local VOC/WIC directors sat on the city council and that the council invested in the private slave trade and plantations.

records.name: Baring family
records.scaleNote: Not slave traders themselves, but per UCL LBS the family's partners were mortgagees and compensation counter-claimants on Caribbean and Guiana estates, and Alexander Baring was reported to have received compensation for almost 500 enslaved people across four estates.
records.origins: Descended from Johann Baring, a Bremen wool merchant who settled in Exeter in 1717. His sons John and Francis founded a London merchant house in 1762 that grew into Barings Bank.
records.role_summary: Sir Francis Baring (1740–1810) built the family fortune partly through West India finance, and his son Alexander Baring (1774–1848) repeatedly opposed abolition in Parliament. Through the family firm the Barings lent to slave-owners and pursued compensation money owed to them at emancipation.

roleDetail.t: Sir Francis Baring and West India credit.
roleDetail.d: Per UCL LBS, Sir Francis had financial interests in Caribbean sugar and slavery, including the Bogue estate in Jamaica, probably as mortgagee.
MP from 1806 and later Lord Ashburton, he spoke repeatedly against emancipation; the Devon and Exeter Institution notes compensation for almost 500 enslaved people across four estates.
Partners Thomas, John and Francis Baring pursued compensation for the enslaved people of the Berbice slave-owner Wolfert Katz, a heavy debtor of the firm.

records.legacy: The family produced several peerages (Ashburton, Northbrook, Revelstoke, Cromer) and senior figures in British public life, including a Governor of the Bank of England (the 3rd Earl of Cromer). The family bank collapsed in 1995. Christ's College, Cambridge and the National Gallery now describe Baring links to slavery in their own legacy research.

legacyDetail.d: Christ's College's Legacies of Enslavement pages and the National Gallery's biography of Alexander Baring record the family's ties to slave-ownership.
The Baring Archive backs a University of Leeds PhD, funded by Baring Asset Management and ING, mapping the firm's involvement with the slave economy.

sources.label: UCL LBS — Sir Francis Baring
National Gallery — Alexander Baring, 1st Baron Ashburton
Christ's College Cambridge — Frederick Baring (Legacies of Enslavement)

records.name: Baring Brothers & Co. (Barings Bank)
records.scaleNote: One of 'the City's two dominant merchant banks' (per UCL LBS); it placed c. $2.5m in Louisiana planter-bank bonds backed by mortgages on enslaved people in 1828 and financed 60% of the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.
records.origins: Founded in London in 1762 as John and Francis Baring & Co.; renamed Baring Brothers & Co. in 1807. It became a leading financier of Atlantic trade and of the young United States.
records.role_summary: Barings did not ship captives, but its credit ran through the slave economy: it lent to Caribbean and Guiana slave-owners, collected their compensation in the 1830s, and sold bonds of Louisiana banks whose capital rested on mortgaged enslaved people. It also handled much of the Atlantic cotton trade.

roleDetail.d: With Hope & Co. of Amsterdam, Barings bought the US bonds used to pay France, taking 60% of the risk; Alexander Baring carried the bonds across the Atlantic.
Barings sold c. $2.5m of 5% bonds of the Consolidated Association of the Planters of Louisiana, whose shareholders mortgaged land and enslaved people.
Per UCL LBS, the partners successfully intercepted compensation on the Wolfert Katz estates in Berbice, British Guiana, and lent to New Orleans slave-owner Burrill Carnes against slave property.

records.legacy: Barings survived a near-collapse in 1890 with a Bank of England rescue, but failed in 1995 after rogue-trader losses and was bought by Dutch bank ING for £1. The Barings name continues in Barings LLC (asset management) and the Baring Foundation; the firm's records are held by The Baring Archive in London.

legacyDetail.d: ING absorbed the banking business in 1995; the archive and a charitable foundation survive under the Baring name.
The Baring Archive hosts a funded Leeds PhD (from 2023) on the firm's slavery links; no corporate apology had been issued as of this writing.

records.name: Lloyds Banking Group
records.scaleNote: Not to be confused with Lloyd's of London. Its documented link is through predecessor the London & Brazilian Bank (1862), which held enslaved Afro-Brazilians as loan security (per Durham research), plus slavery-derived wealth among Scottish predecessor banks (per Mullen, 2023).
records.origins: Lloyds Bank began as Taylors & Lloyds, a Birmingham Quaker bank, in 1765; it absorbed hundreds of banks, including the Bank of London & South America, and merged with HBOS (Bank of Scotland, Halifax) in 2009.
records.role_summary: Its predecessor, the London & Brazilian Bank, lent in Brazil after British emancipation and, per historian Joe Mulhern, knowingly accepted enslaved people as collateral and sometimes forced their sale to settle debts. Other predecessor banks had partners and directors who received 1830s slave-owner compensation.

roleDetail.d: Mulhern's Durham research shows the London & Brazilian Bank held mortgages secured on enslaved people in Brazil, where slavery lasted until 1888.
A 2023 University of Glasgow study by Stephen Mullen concluded that the group's commercial success was 'predicated upon' Atlantic slavery in the 18th–19th centuries.

records.legacy: Lloyds Banking Group is today one of the UK's largest retail banks (Lloyds, Halifax, Bank of Scotland). In June 2020, after the Telegraph reported predecessor-bank links in the UCL LBS database, a spokeswoman said that while 'we have much within our heritage to be proud of, we can't be proud of it all', adding 'We stand against racism, slavery and discrimination in all its forms'; it issued no formal apology or reparations scheme.

legacyDetail.d: Lloyds acknowledged it 'can't be proud of it all' and pledged to do 'more' and 'better' on diversity (as reported by the Telegraph and Leasing Life, July 2020); reparation pledges that month came from Lloyd's of London and Greene King, not Lloyds Bank.

sources.label: LSE Research Online — Mulhern, 'Human collateral: British banking's long-neglected connection with slavery in Brazil'
UCL LBS — London & Brazilian Bank (firm)
University of Glasgow Enlighten — Mullen, Corra Foundation's relationship with British banks and Atlantic slavery (2023)

records.name: NatWest Group (formerly Royal Bank of Scotland Group)
records.scaleNote: Descends from more than 100 banks founded in the 18th–early 19th centuries; its own heritage research shows predecessor partners took plantation mortgages, owned a Grenada plantation (Hankey & Co, 1767–72) and received 1830s compensation.
records.origins: NatWest began trading in 1970 from older banks including Hankey & Co (1685), Smith, Payne & Smiths (1758) and Prescott's Bank (1766); RBS took it over in 2000 and the group renamed itself NatWest Group in 2020.
records.role_summary: Predecessor banks lent to West India planters on the security of land and enslaved people; Smith, Payne & Smiths once helped fund the purchase of enslaved people for a plantation, and its partners received substantial compensation. A director of the London and Westminster Bank, John Stewart, was also a compensation recipient.

roleDetail.d: In 1766 it took a mortgage on a Grenada plantation and owned it, with its enslaved people, until 1772; four partners later received compensation.
Accepted plantation mortgages in the 1810s–20s and in one case financed the purchase of enslaved people, per NatWest's heritage hub.
RBS's 2006 report (updated 2009), prepared for US disclosure laws via its Citizens Bank subsidiary, found predecessor directors had owned enslaved people.

records.legacy: NatWest Group is a FTSE 100 bank (NatWest, Royal Bank of Scotland, Coutts). In June 2020 an RBS spokeswoman told the Telegraph these 'important and painful issues have a place in our history', said the bank had researched its slavery links 'very extensively and thoroughly' for 15 years, and that a BAME-led taskforce would consider what more it could do, including contributions to BAME groups. Its Heritage Hub publishes an 'Enslavement and Colonialism' page, but no formal apology or reparations commitment has been made.

legacyDetail.d: RBS said it was examining further action, including possible contributions to BAME groups (Fortune and Leasing Life reporting the Telegraph); no reparations programme followed.
The heritage page states there is 'no doubt' that people enriched by slavery were among predecessor banks' customers.
Three partners of its Bristol predecessor banks were founder members of Bristol's 1788 abolition committee.

sources.label: NatWest Group Heritage Hub — Enslavement and Colonialism
City of Philadelphia — Citizens Bank Slavery Era Disclosure
Leasing Life — UK bank asset finance providers' past links to slavery (July 2020)
Fortune — UK companies pressed on slavery reparations (June 2020)

records.name: Hankey family (Hankey & Co, bankers)
records.scaleNote: Per UCL LBS, Thomson Hankey alone was awarded £8,736 for 314 enslaved people on Grand Bras, Grenada (1835), and the family also claimed Grenville Vale; the bank had owned a Grenada plantation in 1767–72.
records.origins: A London banking dynasty founded by Captain Samuel Hankey in 1685. Family members became West India merchants and mortgagees, especially in Grenada and Jamaica.
records.role_summary: The Hankeys lent to Caribbean planters on the security of their estates and enslaved people and became owners when debts went unpaid. At emancipation they claimed compensation as owners and mortgagees.

roleDetail.d: Hankey & Co lent against a Grenada estate in 1766 and owned it by 1767; Thomas Hankey was also an extensive mortgagee in Jamaica (per LBS).
Thomson Hankey received £8,736 8s 9d for 314 people on Grand Bras; the family also claimed Grenville Vale (102 people) in 1837.

records.legacy: Thomson Hankey (1805–1893) later became Governor of the Bank of England, one of the figures for whom the Bank apologised in 2020. Hankey & Co passed via the Consolidated Bank and Parr's into what is now NatWest Group.

legacyDetail.t: Named in Bank of England apology.
legacyDetail.d: The 2020 apology and portrait review covered former governors and directors including Hankey.

sources.label: UCL LBS — Grenada 769 (Grand Bras Estate)
UCL LBS — Thomson Hankey
NatWest Group Heritage Hub — Enslavement and Colonialism

records.name: HSBC (Midland Bank predecessors)
records.scaleNote: HSBC's own 2020–23 review of c. 1,700 leaders of 100+ UK predecessor banks found direct slavery links at five: Leyland & Bullins, Moss & Co, City Bank, Galton & James (unconfirmed predecessor) and London Joint Stock Bank.
records.origins: HSBC was founded in Hong Kong in 1865 and bought Britain's Midland Bank in 1992. Midland had absorbed many older English banks, including two founded in Liverpool in 1807 by men enriched by the slave trade.
records.role_summary: The slavery links are through founders and leaders of predecessor banks: Thomas Leyland helped finance at least 69 slaving voyages (per HSBC), John Moss shipped and held enslaved people in the Bahamas and Demerara, and London Joint Stock Bank's first manager, George Pollard, was a trustee-awardee of £2,416 compensation for Colhoun's estate, Nevis (per UCL LBS).

roleDetail.d: Leyland & Bullins and Moss & Co were both founded in 1807, the year Britain banned the slave trade, by men whose wealth came partly from it.
HSBC counted investing in voyages, owning enslaved people or receiving compensation; other investigations were said to be ongoing.

records.legacy: HSBC is one of the world's largest banks. On its history site it states that it 'regrets the past actions and activities of individuals associated with these predecessor banks and the harm they caused', but it has made no reparations commitment.

legacyDetail.d: The research concluded in the first half of 2023 and is published on history.hsbc.com under 'Lessons from history'.

sources.label: HSBC History — Lessons from history
HSBC History — Leyland and Bullins
HSBC History — Moss and Co, later North Western Bank
UCL LBS — George Pollard

records.name: Moss family of Liverpool (John Moss)
records.scaleNote: Per UCL LBS, the Moss brothers inherited c. 1,000 enslaved people in the Bahamas in 1820, moved 603 of them to Demerara in 1821–25, and John Moss was awarded £40,353 for Anna Regina estate.
records.origins: A Liverpool merchant family partly enriched by the transatlantic slave trade. John Moss joined his father's firm and in 1807 founded the bank Moss, Dales & Rogers.
records.role_summary: John and his brothers inherited enslaved people from their uncle James Moss and, under licence, forcibly moved hundreds of them from the Bahamas to cotton and sugar estates in Demerara, where an intra-Caribbean transfer still separated families. John Moss was paid one of the larger compensation awards.

roleDetail.d: Of 1,762 people imported under licence into Demerara–Essequibo in 1821–25, 603 were sent from the Bahamas by John, Henry and James Moss (per LBS).
John Moss was awardee of £40,353 18s 3d for Anna Regina, British Guiana.
A biography says Moss worked with Sir John Gladstone on the planters' compensation campaign.

records.legacy: John Moss became first chairman of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, an early icon of industrial Britain. His bank became the North Western Bank, then part of Midland Bank, now HSBC UK, which in 2023 publicly listed his slavery links.

legacyDetail.d: Moss & Co (1826) → North Western Bank (1864) → London and Midland Bank (1897) → HSBC (1992).

sources.label: UCL LBS — John Moss
HSBC History — Moss and Co, later North Western Bank
Grace's Guide — John Moss

records.name: Drax family (Drax Hall, Barbados)
records.scaleNote: James Drax pioneered large-scale sugar in Barbados in the 1640s with c. 200 enslaved Africans by the early 1650s; at abolition the family claimed £4,293 for 189 people on Drax Hall (per UCL LBS); the family still owns the estate.
records.base: Drax Hall, St George, Barbados / Charborough, Dorset
records.origins: James Drax was an English settler who arrived in Barbados in the 1620s. He was among the first planters to make sugar work on a large scale there, and he bought African captives to do it.
records.role_summary: The Draxes created one of the earliest and longest-lived English slave plantations, holding enslaved people at Drax Hall from the 1640s until 1834, plus a large Jamaica estate. Historian Hilary Beckles has called Drax Hall a 'killing field' where tens of thousands died, though death-toll figures are estimates.

roleDetail.d: Drax Hall (c. 1650) is one of the oldest surviving houses in the Americas and the site where the gang-labour sugar system took shape in Barbados.
J.S.W.S. Erle-Drax claimed £4,293 12s 6d for 189 enslaved people at Drax Hall (LBS claim Barbados 3784).
Beckles's estimate of up to 30,000 deaths is widely quoted; other accounts give 'thousands'.

records.legacy: Richard Drax, Conservative MP for South Dorset 2010–2024, inherited the 617-acre Drax Hall estate in 2017 and the family seat at Charborough. Barbados's government considered seeking reparations from him in 2022; a 2024 plan to buy 50 acres for housing (reportedly c. £3m) was paused after public outcry. He has called his ancestors' role 'deeply regrettable' but says no one today can be held responsible.

legacyDetail.t: First individual reparations claim by a state.
legacyDetail.d: A 2022 Barbados cabinet paper reportedly proposed asking Drax to contribute land for a museum and housing, with legal action as an option.
No settlement had been announced as of 2025 reporting.

sources.label: UCL LBS — Barbados 3784 (Drax Hall)
The Conversation — Tracing the Drax family's millions
