records.name: General Sir James Duff
records.scaleNote: Owner of the Grange sugar estate, Hanover, Jamaica (1832–39), for which £4,101 0s 1d was awarded (claim Jamaica Hanover 455, per UCL LBS); LBS registers 211–221 enslaved people there in 1830–32.
records.origins: A Scottish army officer and MP for Banffshire, of the family of the Earls Fife. Like many Scottish gentry he held Jamaican plantation property.
records.role_summary: Duff owned the Grange sugar estate in Jamaica and was compensated as its owner when slavery ended. He is a direct example of how 1830s compensation money flowed into the British landed and political class.

roleDetail.d: £4,101 awarded on claim Jamaica Hanover 455 for the Grange estate, where c. 210–220 people were enslaved in the early 1830s (per LBS).

records.legacy: UCL's Legacies of British Slavery project identified Duff as a first cousin six times removed of Prime Minister David Cameron. When Cameron visited Jamaica in September 2015, Jamaican reparations campaigners cited the link and asked for an apology; Cameron rejected reparations and offered aid, including £25m for a prison.

legacyDetail.d: Some reports call Duff Cameron's cousin through the Earls Fife; UCL used 'first cousin six times removed'. Cameron is not accused of wrongdoing.

sources.label: UCL LBS — Grange Sugar Estate, Hanover, Jamaica
UCL News — David Cameron faces demands for slavery reparation on Jamaica visit (2015)
Jamaica Gleaner — Reparations committee wants David Cameron to say sorry
Channel 4 News — Jamaica calls for Britain to pay slave trade reparations

records.name: Cumberbatch family (Cleland estate, Barbados)
records.scaleNote: An 1804 Barbados list credits Abraham Parry Cumberbatch with 292 enslaved people; his will records £5,388 10s 2d received as slave compensation (per UCL LBS).
records.origins: Abraham Cumberbatch came to Barbados as a young man in the early 1700s and built the Cleland sugar plantation. The estates passed down to Abraham Parry Cumberbatch (1784–1840).
records.role_summary: Abraham Parry Cumberbatch was an absentee owner living in England who claimed compensation for enslaved people on the Cleland and Farm estates. The award went to trustees to fund an annuity for his second wife.

roleDetail.d: Held Cleland and Farm estates from England; trustees included his brother-in-law Robert Chaloner MP.
His will set aside £5,388 10s 2d received as compensation; press reports giving £6,000 are approximate.

records.legacy: The actor Benedict Cumberbatch is a descendant; he has said his mother advised him not to use the name professionally. In 2024 reports suggested Barbados might seek reparations from the family, but a Barbados National Task Force on Reparations member said it was not doing so. No wrongdoing by living descendants is alleged.

legacyDetail.d: The plantation's history has been revisited in Barbadian reparations debates alongside Drax Hall.

sources.label: UCL LBS — Abraham Parry Cumberbatch
AOL / USA Today — Is Benedict Cumberbatch facing slavery reparations in Barbados? Official says no

records.name: Charles McGarel and the Hogg family (Viscounts Hailsham)
records.scaleNote: Charles McGarel was among the largest compensation beneficiaries: e.g. £9,751 for 184 people on Nouvelle Flandres, Demerara; partners in Hall, McGarel received almost £100,000 for nearly 1,000 people (per UCL LBS / Wikipedia).
records.origins: Charles McGarel, from Larne in Ulster, became a Demerara merchant and slave-owner. He married into the Hogg family; his brother-in-law Quintin Hogg entered the West India sugar trade through him.
records.role_summary: McGarel owned and mortgaged estates in Demerara and Berbice, petitioned in 1826 against compulsory manumission, and collected large compensation sums. Quintin Hogg later ran Demerara sugar estates worked by indentured labourers after emancipation.

roleDetail.d: McGarel was one of 65 absentee owners and mortgagees petitioning the Privy Council in 1826 against compulsory manumission in Demerara and Berbice.
McGarel left his estate to brother-in-law James Hogg on condition he added 'McGarel' to his name; the name passed into the Hailsham line.

records.legacy: McGarel's money built Larne Town Hall, which Amnesty International asked to be renamed in 2020. Quintin Hogg founded the Regent Street Polytechnic (now University of Westminster); his son and grandson were the 1st and 2nd Viscounts Hailsham, both Lord Chancellors. How far McGarel wealth funded the Polytechnic is debated.

legacyDetail.d: Amnesty called for McGarel Town Hall to be renamed over his slavery links.
Connections between slavery-derived money and later philanthropy are drawn by LBS but not quantified.

sources.label: UCL LBS — Charles McGarel
UCL LBS — Quintin Hogg
Irish Post — Amnesty calls on Larne to rename McGarel Town Hall

records.name: Moses Taylor
records.scaleNote: By the Civil War his firm's network covered at least 24 Cuban estates that profited from the labour of thousands of enslaved people (per Princeton & Slavery Project).
records.origins: A New York clerk with the Howland shipping firm, he set up as a sugar broker in 1832, aged 26, handling Cuban growers' sugar.
records.role_summary: Taylor sold Cuban sugar in New York, extended credit and investment advice to Cuban planters, and banked their money in the US, while Cuba still imported African captives illegally. His partners and clients included Drake Brothers of Havana and Tomás Terry, men tied to the slave trade.

roleDetail.d: Historian Roland Ely showed that Taylor acted as banker and agent for slave-owning Cuban sugar planters (1833–1868).
He led City Bank of New York from 1856 to 1882; his businesses held accounts there, which Citi says let the bank profit indirectly from enslaved labour.

records.legacy: City Bank became National City Bank and then Citigroup. Taylor's grandson Moses Taylor Pyne was one of Princeton University's leading benefactors, a link documented by the Princeton & Slavery Project. His papers are held by the New York Public Library.

legacyDetail.d: Pyne's gifts to Princeton derived in part from the Taylor sugar fortune.

sources.label: Princeton Alumni Weekly — Moses Taylor Pyne and the Sugar Plantations of the Americas
Citigroup — Re-examining Citi's historical connections to slavery in the U.S. (2023)
NYPL — Moses Taylor papers

records.name: Citigroup (City Bank of New York)
records.scaleNote: Citi's 2023 review found no record that it directly bought, sold or held enslaved people, but concluded predecessors likely profited indirectly before 1866, chiefly via Moses Taylor's Cuban sugar business.
records.origins: Chartered in 1812 as City Bank of New York, it grew under Moses Taylor into one of the largest US banks.
records.role_summary: Its slavery links run through clients and leaders: Taylor's sugar firms, which imported slave-grown Cuban sugar, banked there, and Citi says some founding or early directors likely owned enslaved people.

roleDetail.d: Citi's 2022–23 review, by an independent research firm, found likely indirect profits through transactions with Taylor and others.

records.legacy: Citigroup is one of the largest US banks. In July 2023 it published its findings and tied them to its $1bn 'Action for Racial Equity' programme (2020), saying 'None of this changes the past but it can help make for a more equitable future.' No apology or direct reparations were made.

legacyDetail.d: An earlier study about two decades before had found no direct involvement; critics say the framing is narrow.

sources.label: Citigroup — Re-examining Citi's historical connections to slavery in the U.S. (2023)
Fortune — Citigroup says predecessor companies likely saw indirect financial benefits from slavery

records.name: Bank of America (FleetBoston / Providence Bank)
records.scaleNote: Its 2005 disclosure found two predecessors (Boatmen's Savings Institution and Southern Bank of St. Louis) dealt in transactions involving enslaved people as collateral; via Fleet it descends from the Providence Bank founded in 1791 by slave-trader John Brown.
records.origins: Today's bank combines NationsBank, BankAmerica, Boatmen's of St. Louis and FleetBoston (acquired 2004), whose oldest strand was the Providence Bank of Rhode Island.
records.role_summary: The Providence Bank was founded by John Brown, a slave-ship owner, and served Rhode Island merchants. The bank's 2005 Heritage Research Center report found two slave-related transactions by predecessor banks in St. Louis, though it said neither bank took possession of enslaved people.

roleDetail.d: FleetBoston was sued with Aetna and CSX in the Farmer-Paellmann case as successor of John Brown's Providence Bank; the case was dismissed.
A Heritage Research Center report for Chicago's ordinance found two slave-related transactions by predecessors.

records.legacy: Bank of America is the second-largest US bank. In June 2005 CEO Kenneth Lewis expressed regret for predecessor institutions that supported or tolerated slavery, calling its legacy a shameful mark (Chicago Sun-Times), and the bank pledged support for Black communities.

legacyDetail.d: The disclosure was made to satisfy Chicago's Slavery Era Business Disclosure Ordinance; JPMorgan Chase and Wachovia had made similar disclosures earlier in 2005.

sources.label: City of Philadelphia — Bank of America Slavery Era Disclosure
Chicago Sun-Times (via insideARM) — Bank of America admits ties to slavery (2005)
Business & Human Rights Resource Centre — Lawsuit chases companies tied to slavery

records.name: CSX Corporation (predecessor railroads)
records.scaleNote: Successor to numerous Southern railroads that were built or run partly with enslaved labour, usually hired from enslavers, according to the 2002 lawsuit and USA Today reporting; no total count is documented.
records.origins: CSX was formed in 1980 from the Chessie System and Seaboard Coast Line, which absorbed many antebellum Southern railroads.
records.role_summary: Before 1865 Southern railroad companies commonly rented enslaved men from their owners, and some bought people outright, to grade track and run lines. CSX inherited several such lines.

roleDetail.d: Named with Aetna and FleetBoston in Deadria Farmer-Paellmann's federal suit as 'successor in interest to numerous predecessor railroad lines that were constructed or run, at least in part, by slave labor'.
CSX called slavery a 'tragic chapter' but said the suit was 'wholly without merit'.

records.legacy: CSX is a major US freight railroad. The 2002 case was consolidated and dismissed in 2004–05 as a 'political question'; CSX has not issued an apology.

legacyDetail.d: USA Today (2002) reported that all four big North American rail networks own lines built and operated with slave labour.

sources.label: Business & Human Rights Resource Centre — Lawsuit chases companies tied to slavery
Business & Human Rights Resource Centre — Rail networks own lines built with slave labor (USA Today, 2002)

records.name: Norfolk Southern (predecessor railroads)
records.scaleNote: Successor to Southern Railway and Norfolk & Western lines, some of whose antebellum predecessors leased and purchased enslaved workers; lawsuits in 2002 alleged this but no total is documented.
records.origins: Formed in 1982 from the Southern Railway and the Norfolk & Western, which had absorbed dozens of pre-Civil War Southern lines.
records.role_summary: Antebellum predecessor lines in the South rented enslaved men for construction and maintenance, and some owned enslaved workers. Norfolk Southern was named in 2002 suits as their successor.

roleDetail.d: A class action led by former NAACP official Richard Barber Sr. named Norfolk Southern, New York Life and Brown Brothers Harriman.
Precise numbers for NS predecessor lines are not established in sources found here.

records.legacy: Norfolk Southern is a major US freight railroad. The reparations suits against it were dismissed with the consolidated 2004–05 rulings; the company has issued no apology.

legacyDetail.d: Railroad slavery is now studied by historians, but no company-commissioned report like the banks' exists.

sources.label: BLET — NS sued for slavery reparations (2002)
Business & Human Rights Resource Centre — Rail networks own lines built with slave labor (USA Today, 2002)

records.name: Brooks Brothers
records.scaleNote: Made livery for enslaved coachmen and footmen in Southern households; a surviving coat worn by a young man enslaved by Dr William Newton Mercer is held by The Historic New Orleans Collection. The volume of this trade is unknown because company records are private.
records.origins: Founded in New York in 1818 by Henry Sands Brooks; it became America's oldest clothing brand.
records.role_summary: Brooks Brothers sold livery made for enslaved domestic workers, including coats with family-crest buttons, to wealthy Southern planters. Historian Jonathan Michael Square calls livery an extensive part of its 19th-century business.

roleDetail.d: Two Brooks Brothers livery coats from the Mercer household (Mississippi/New Orleans), sold through the firm's livery department c. 1857–65 and acquired by The Historic New Orleans Collection in 2013, survive as rare material evidence.

records.legacy: Brooks Brothers still trades (bought out of bankruptcy in 2020 by SPARC Group). Researchers note it has not publicly acknowledged this history, and its archive remains closed to them.

legacyDetail.d: Square's research into the scale of the trade has been limited by lack of access to company records.

sources.label: Vestoj — A Stain on an All-American Brand (Jonathan Michael Square)
The Historic New Orleans Collection — Enslaved servant's coat loan to the Met

records.name: Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations
records.scaleNote: Received and managed Haiti's 1825 indemnity (150m francs, reduced to 90m in 1838) for former colonists for about a century; the NYT (2022) estimated c. 112m francs was actually paid, c. $560m today.
records.origins: A French state financial institution founded in 1816 to hold public and legal deposits.
records.role_summary: Under Charles X's 1825 ordinance Haiti had to pay its indemnity into the Caisse, which distributed it to former Saint-Domingue colonists as compensation for lost property, including enslaved people. Haiti borrowed from French banks such as CIC to keep paying.

roleDetail.d: The Caisse administered the indemnity from 1825 to c. 1925, per a 2025 French civil-society letter citing its archives.
2025 research in the Caisse's archives suggests the French Treasury may itself have gained from the payments.

records.legacy: The Caisse des Dépôts is today France's public financial institution, managing hundreds of billions of euros. On the 200th anniversary in 2025 President Macron announced a joint French–Haitian commission of historians to examine the indemnity; France has not agreed to restitution.

legacyDetail.d: Campaigners, including France's Foundation for the Memory of Slavery, urged France to recognise and repair the indemnity's injustice.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Haitian independence debt
Le Nouvelliste — Double Debt: Did the French State Benefit from the Sum Paid by Haiti?
Collège de France — Haiti 1825: from independence to debt (symposium)

connections.label: Haiti's loans paid into the system

records.name: Royal Exchange Assurance
records.scaleNote: One of only two chartered corporate marine insurers (with London Assurance) from 1720 to 1824, though Lloyd's held c. 75–90% of the market; the slave and West India trades made up c. 41% of British marine insurance in the 1790s (per Pearson & Richardson, Journal of Economic History, 2019).
records.origins: Chartered by Act of Parliament in 1720, the same Bubble Act year as the South Sea scheme, together with London Assurance, to sell marine and fire insurance.
records.role_summary: As a marine insurer during the peak of the British slave trade it sold cover in a market where slave voyages and slave-grown produce were major lines of business. Its fire business also insured Caribbean plantation property, including dwellings of the enslaved.

roleDetail.d: A surviving 1773 Royal Exchange policy for a Barbados property lists slave dwellings among insured buildings.
Historians (Pearson & Richardson) document chartered insurers' role, but the company's own share of slaving cover is not quantified.

records.legacy: Royal Exchange merged with Guardian Assurance in 1968 to form Guardian Royal Exchange, which French insurer AXA bought in 1999. UCL's LBS database links several of its directors and a deputy governor to slavery; unlike Lloyd's of London in 2020, no specific apology for Royal Exchange Assurance has been found.

legacyDetail.d: Now part of AXA's UK business.

sources.label: Journal of Economic History — Pearson & Richardson, 'Insuring the Transatlantic Slave Trade'
Rock Library — Royal Exchange Assurance policy made out to John Turner, 1773
Global Trade Review — Insurance giants apologise over slave trade ties (2020)

records.name: Elihu Yale
records.scaleNote: As President of Madras for the East India Company (1687–92) he oversaw a port where the Company sanctioned and regulated an Indian Ocean slave trade; how much his own fortune came from it is disputed.
records.origins: Born in Boston and raised in London, he joined the East India Company as a clerk and rose to govern Fort St George, Madras, where he grew rich through private trade.
records.role_summary: This is the Indian Ocean, not the Atlantic, trade: Yale's administration in Madras sanctioned the sale and shipment of enslaved people, and David Blight's 2024 history argues part of his fortune came from trafficking. His 1718 gift of goods funded the college that took his name.

roleDetail.d: Blight's Yale and Slavery (2024) argues the Company's Madras office 'sanctioned and regulated' the Indian Ocean slave trade, that Yale played a 'key leadership role' in it, and that part of his fortune came from buying and selling people.
Some historians argue the evidence does not show Yale was personally a slave trader.

records.legacy: Yale University, named for him in 1718, apologised in February 2024 for its early leaders' ties to slavery. A 1708 portrait of Yale with an enslaved child in a silver collar was removed from a Yale boardroom in 2007.

legacyDetail.d: Yale kept the name while publishing the history.

sources.label: Boston Globe — Yale apologizes for its connections to slavery (2024)
Yale News — Yale vows new actions to address past ties to slavery, issues apology
Yale and Slavery Research Project — Yale and Slavery: A History (2024, PDF)

records.name: London & Brazilian Bank
records.description: British bank formed in London in 1862 to lend in Brazil, where slavery lasted until 1888. Historian Joe Mulhern showed it knowingly held enslaved Afro-Brazilians as security for loans and sometimes forced their sale; through the Bank of London & South America it is a predecessor of Lloyds Banking Group.

records.name: Farmer-Paellmann reparations lawsuits (2002–2006)
records.description: In March 2002 activist Deadria Farmer-Paellmann sued Aetna, FleetBoston and CSX in federal court in Brooklyn on behalf of descendants of the enslaved; similar suits named Lehman, New York Life, Norfolk Southern and others. The cases were consolidated in Chicago and dismissed in 2004–05 as raising a 'political question', a ruling largely upheld on appeal in 2006.

records.name: Harvard & the Legacy of Slavery report and fund (2022)
records.description: Report published 26 April 2022 finding that Harvard leaders, faculty and staff enslaved more than 70 people from 1636 until Massachusetts abolition, and that donors' fortunes came from slavery and slave-produced goods. President Lawrence Bacow committed $100 million to a Legacy of Slavery Fund for descendant outreach, education and memorials, but not direct payments.

connections.label: Isaac Royall Jr. endowed first law professorship

records.name: Yale and Slavery Research Project (2020–2024)
records.description: Launched in 2020 and led by historian David Blight; its 2024 book 'Yale and Slavery: A History' found that founders and early leaders enslaved over 200 people and that Connecticut Hall was partly built with enslaved labour. Yale formally apologised on 16 February 2024 and funded free copies and local programmes in New Haven.

records.name: University of Glasgow reparative justice programme
records.description: A September 2018 report by Simon Newman and Stephen Mullen found Glasgow received gifts from slavery-derived wealth worth c. £16.7m–£198m today, though it never owned enslaved people. In August 2019 it signed an agreement with the University of the West Indies to raise £20m over 20 years for a Glasgow-Caribbean Centre for Development Research, widely called the first such UK university commitment.

connections.label: agreement backed by Sir Hilary Beckles (UWI)

records.name: University of Cambridge Legacies of Enslavement inquiry (2019–2022)
records.description: Set up in 2019; its report of 22 September 2022 found Cambridge gained 'significant benefits' from slavery through investments in the South Sea Company, donations from investors in slave-trading companies, and fellows' roles, while finding no evidence it owned enslaved people or plantations. Colleges such as Jesus and Christ's ran their own inquiries.

records.name: Princeton & Slavery Project (2017)
records.description: Research project led by historian Martha Sandweiss, launched publicly in November 2017, which found that Princeton's first nine presidents all owned enslaved people at some point, documented a 1766 slave auction on campus, and traced donor wealth such as Moses Taylor Pyne's Cuban-sugar inheritance.

records.name: Evanston, Illinois, local reparations programme (2021)
records.description: In March 2021 Evanston's council voted 8–1 to begin the first US city reparations programme, funded by a 3% cannabis tax pledged in 2019 (target $10m over ten years). It gives eligible Black residents or descendants who suffered housing discrimination between 1919 and 1969 $25,000 for housing costs; it addresses housing discrimination rather than slavery directly.

records.name: California Reparations Task Force (AB 3121)
records.description: Created by California's AB 3121 (2020), the first US state task force on reparations. Its c. 1,100-page final report of 29 June 2023 made more than 115 recommendations, including a formal apology and methods for calculating compensation for descendants of enslaved people; the legislature has since enacted only some measures.

records.name: H.R. 40 — Commission to Study and Develop Reparation Proposals
records.description: Bill first introduced by Rep. John Conyers in 1989 and reintroduced every Congress since, to create a 13-member commission studying slavery and its legacy and recommending remedies. On 14 April 2021 the House Judiciary Committee approved it 25–17, its first-ever committee vote; it has not passed the full House.

connections.label: courts called reparations a political question

events.title: Lagos slave sale
events.text: Lançarote de Freitas lands c. 235 captives at Lagos; Henry the Navigator takes the royal fifth.

source.label: Wikipedia — Mercado de Escravos

events.title: Portuguese reach Kongo
events.text: Diogo Cão's fleet reached the Congo estuary, opening diplomatic and commercial relations that soon included trade in captives.

source.label: Britannica — History of Angola

events.title: Vespucci in Seville; Columbus sails
events.text: Amerigo Vespucci, Medici agent, is settled in Gianotto Berardi's Seville house as Berardi helps finance Columbus's first voyage.

source.label: Wikipedia — Amerigo Vespucci

events.title: Treaty of Tordesillas
events.text: Castile and Portugal divide the Atlantic world; Africa goes to Portugal, leaving Spain dependent on foreign suppliers of captives.

source.label: New World Encyclopedia — Treaty of Tordesillas

events.title: Columbus ships Taíno captives
events.text: Columbus loads c. 500 enslaved Taíno for Spain; c. 300 survive. Berardi dies in December and Vespucci takes over his affairs.

source.label: College of Charleston LDHI — The Spanish and New World Slavery

events.title: Ojeda–Vespucci voyage
events.text: Alonso de Ojeda's expedition, with Vespucci aboard, ends with a slave raid in the Bahamas and sale of captives in Spain.

source.label: Wikipedia — Alonso de Ojeda

events.title: First Africans licensed to the Americas
events.text: Ferdinand and Isabella's instructions to Ovando permit enslaved Africans born under Christian rule to be taken to Hispaniola.

source.label: College of Charleston LDHI — Nicolás de Ovando

events.title: 'America' named
events.text: Waldseemüller's world map names the New World 'America' after Vespucci.

source.label: Library of Congress — 1507 Waldseemüller map

events.title: Vespucci named Piloto Mayor
events.text: Vespucci becomes the first chief pilot of the Casa de Contratación, training pilots and keeping the Padrón Real until his death in 1512.

source.label: Wikipedia — Pilot Major of Spain

events.title: Direct Africa–Americas licence
events.text: Charles V licenses Laurent de Gorrevod to ship 4,000 Africans directly to the colonies; the licence passes to Genoese merchants.

source.label: Slavery, Law & Power — 1518 charter

events.title: Afonso I protests to João III
events.text: Afonso I of Kongo wrote to the king of Portugal that traders were seizing free Kongolese and nobles, asking him to curb the trade; he regulated rather than ended it.

source.label: World History Commons — Afonso I letters to the King of Portugal (primary source)

events.title: Welser contract
events.text: The Augsburg Welser receive a contract for 4,000 enslaved Africans and the governorship of Venezuela.

source.label: Wikipedia — Klein-Venedig

events.title: Hawkins's first English slaving voyage
events.text: John Hawkins took c. 300 Africans from the Sierra Leone coast and sold them in Spanish Hispaniola, beginning England's transatlantic slave trade.

source.label: World History Encyclopedia — John Hawkins

events.title: Elizabeth I invests in slaving
events.text: The Queen lent the royal ship Jesus of Lübeck to Hawkins's second slaving voyage.

source.label: Encyclopedia.com — Hawkins, John

events.title: Defeat at San Juan de Ulúa
events.text: A Spanish fleet attacked Hawkins's third slaving expedition in Mexico; Hawkins and Drake escaped but most ships were lost.

source.label: World History Encyclopedia — John Hawkins

events.title: First Portuguese asiento
events.text: Pedro Gomes Reinel contracts with Philip II, opening 45 years of Portuguese asientos.

source.label: CHAM / NOVA FCSH — Portuguese asientos

events.title: Elvas takes the asiento
events.text: Portuguese New Christian António Fernandes de Elvas takes the Spanish slave-supply asiento and the Angola, Cape Verde and Guinea contracts.

source.label: Wikipedia — António Fernandes de Elvas

events.title: Dutch West India Company chartered
events.text: The States General gave the WIC a monopoly on Dutch Atlantic trade and war, the vehicle for the Dutch slave trade.

source.label: Canon van Nederland — Slavernij

events.title: Njinga's embassy to Luanda
events.text: Njinga negotiated peace with the Portuguese governor in Luanda on behalf of Ndongo and was baptised Ana de Sousa.

source.label: Wikipedia — Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba

events.title: Lamego succeeds to the asiento
events.text: Manuel Rodrigues Lamego holds the asiento to 1631; c.8,000 captives are bought, mostly at Luanda.

source.label: Wikipedia — Manuel Rodrigues Lamego

events.title: WIC seizes Elmina
events.text: Dutch forces took Elmina from Portugal; between 1637 and 1641 they also took São Tomé and Luanda.

source.label: Project MANIFEST — The United Provinces and the Transatlantic Slave Trade

events.title: Portuguese move Geba merchants to Cacheu
events.text: With Geba dominated by Kaabu's province of Ganadu, Portuguese authorities forced its traders to relocate to Cacheu and Farim.

source.label: Wikipedia — Geba, Guinea-Bissau

events.title: Swedes build Carolusborg at Cape Coast
events.text: Hendrik Carloff, for the Swedish Africa Company, built the fort that later became Cape Coast Castle.

source.label: Wikipedia — Swedish Gold Coast

events.title: Witte Paert lands captives at New Amsterdam
events.text: Under Stuyvesant, the WIC ship Witte Paert arrives with almost 300 enslaved Africans for sale to colonists.

source.label: Museum of the City of New York — Petrus Stuyvesant

events.title: Fernandes Vieira governs Angola
events.text: Pernambuco planter João Fernandes Vieira becomes governor of Angola (1658–1661) and revives the Luanda–Recife slave route.

source.label: Sankofa (USP) — Souza 2017

events.title: Company of Royal Adventurers chartered
events.text: Charles II chartered the company under the Duke of York; its 1663 charter explicitly included the slave trade.

source.label: Wikipedia — Royal African Company

events.title: Maryland makes slavery lifelong
events.text: Under the Calvert proprietorship, Maryland's assembly declared that enslaved Africans would serve 'durante vita' and their children would be enslaved.

source.label: Maryland State Archives — Blacks Before the Law in Colonial Maryland

events.title: Royal African Company founded
events.text: The RAC received a monopoly of English trade to West Africa and became the largest single shipper of enslaved Africans in the trade's history.

source.label: PBS Africans in America — The Royal African Company

events.title: Groß Friedrichsburg founded
events.text: Brandenburg built its Gold Coast fort; gold proved scarce and the trade turned to captives.

source.label: Wikipedia — Brandenburger Gold Coast

events.title: Code Noir and the Coymans asiento
events.text: Louis XIV issued the Code Noir governing slavery in French colonies; the same year Dutchman Balthasar Coymans won the Spanish asiento.

source.label: BnF — « Code Noir » (The Black Code)

events.title: Akwamu seizes Christiansborg
events.text: Asameni of Akwamu and some 80 men posing as traders captured the Danish castle at Accra and traded from it for about a year.

source.label: The Conversation — Resistance and collaboration: Asameni and the keys to Christiansborg Castle

events.title: Philipse Madagascar voyages begin
events.text: Philipse ships make at least five voyages to Madagascar (1693–1699), buying 1,100+ captives from pirate brokers to evade the RAC monopoly.

source.label: Historic Hudson Valley — Philipse Family and the Slave Trade

events.title: Komenda Wars begin
events.text: John Kabes attacks Dutch miners at Komenda, opening six years of war between English- and Dutch-backed factions.

source.label: Wikipedia — Komenda Wars

events.title: Slave trade opened to all English merchants
events.text: Parliament ended the RAC monopoly, letting private traders from Bristol and later Liverpool expand the trade.

source.label: Schools History — Lifting of the Royal African Company monopoly

events.title: French Guinea Company wins the asiento
events.text: Philip V of Spain granted the Compagnie royale de Guinée the asiento to supply captives to Spanish America.

source.label: AHA — Trans-Imperial Bondage: The French Slave Trade in the Spanish Caribbean

events.title: Codrington bequest to the Church
events.text: Christopher Codrington left two Barbados plantations and their enslaved workers to the SPG, and £10,000 to All Souls College.

source.label: All Souls College — The Codrington legacy

events.title: Britain wins the asiento
events.text: Under the Treaty of Utrecht, the South Sea Company gained the contract to supply 4,800 enslaved Africans a year to Spanish America for 30 years.

source.label: Britannica — Asiento de negros

events.title: Bern buys South Sea shares
events.text: The city-state of Bern buys c.1,300 South Sea Company shares, holding them until 1734; Zurich follows from 1727.

source.label: Swiss Finance Museum — Transatlantic Slave Trade Part 2

events.title: Dutch expel John Conny from Groß Friedrichsburg
events.text: After years of resistance following Brandenburg's 1717 sale to the Dutch, Conny loses the fort, renamed Fort Hollandia.

source.label: Ghana Museums and Monuments Board — Fort Gross Frederiksburg

events.title: Dahomey conquers Whydah
events.text: King Agaja's army took the coastal kingdom of Whydah, giving Dahomey control of the Ouidah slave market.

source.label: Wikipedia — Agaja

events.title: Grant, Oswald & Co. buys Bunce Island
events.text: Richard Oswald's London firm took over the Sierra Leone fort, shipping captives to Charleston via Henry Laurens.

source.label: Yale Gilder Lehrman Center — Bunce Island history

events.title: Hato revolt crushed in Curaçao
events.text: Governor Isaak Faesch orders 47 executions after captives from Elmina rise on the Hato plantation.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland — Isaak Faesch

events.title: Pombal's slave-trade company
events.text: Pombal founds the Grão-Pará e Maranhão Company, followed by Pernambuco e Paraíba (1759).

source.label: Wikipedia — Grão Pará and Maranhão Company

events.title: Elias Ball buys 'Priscilla' off the Hare
events.text: Henry Laurens's firm sold five children from the Sierra Leone voyage of the Hare to Elias Ball, including a ten-year-old girl he named Priscilla.

source.label: Yale Macmillan Center — Priscilla's Story

events.title: Richard Brew builds Castle Brew
events.text: The Anomabu slave trader builds a private fortified house (1763–64), the year he is reprimanded for selling captives to the Dutch.

source.label: Wikipedia — Anomabu

events.title: The Sally sails from Providence
events.text: Nicholas Brown and Company's brigantine leaves for West Africa the year Brown University is founded; at least 109 of 196 captives die.

source.label: Brown University Library — Voyage of the Slave Ship Sally

events.title: Washington sells Tom to St. Kitts
events.text: George Washington shipped Tom, a Mount Vernon foreman, to the Caribbean for sale, receiving rum, sweetmeats and coin in return.

source.label: Mount Vernon — Tom

events.title: Old Calabar massacre
events.text: English captains allied with Duke Town to ambush Old Town traders; some 300 were killed and others, including two Robin John princes, were enslaved.

source.label: Wikipedia — Little Ephraim Robin John and Ancona Robin John

events.title: Slave ship Fredensborg wrecked in Norway
events.text: After landing 235 captives on St Croix, the Danish-Norwegian ship sank off Tromøy; its wreck, found in 1974, is one of very few excavated slave ships.

source.label: Cambridge — History in Africa: The slave ship Fredensborg

events.title: Pourtalès buys Grenada plantations
events.text: Neuchâtel's Jacques-Louis de Pourtalès and Basel's J.J. Thurneysen buy Grenada plantations worked by c.350 enslaved people.

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland — Jacques-Louis de Pourtalès

events.title: Bank of England's Grenada loan
events.text: The Bank lent £160,000 on two Grenada plantations; after default it came to own 599 enslaved people, selling them in 1790.

source.label: Bank of England Museum — A Story of Archival Discovery

events.title: Burckhardt's Nantes slaving house
events.text: Christophe Bourcard, son of Basel's Christoph Burckhardt, founds Bourcard, Legrand & Cie in Nantes; family firms back 21 slave ships (1783–1815).

source.label: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland — Christoph Burckhardt

events.title: Revolution in Saint-Domingue
events.text: Enslaved people rose up in August 1791 in France's richest colony, which became independent Haiti on 1 January 1804.

source.label: John Carter Brown Library — Saint-Domingue Before the Revolution

events.title: Danish slave-trade ban decreed
events.text: Christian VII signed the decree of 16 March 1792 banning the trade from 1803; imports grew during the delay.

source.label: EBSCO Research Starters — Denmark Abolishes the Slave Trade

events.title: John Brown tried under federal Slave Trade Act
events.text: John Brown of Providence becomes the first American tried under the 1794 Slave Trade Act; his ship Hope is forfeited after his brother Moses's abolition society pursues the case.

source.label: Rhode Island Historical Society — John Brown papers

events.title: Mount Vernon census: 317 people
events.text: Washington's census listed 317 enslaved people — 123 his own, 153 Custis dower people and c. 40 rented; his will freed his own after Martha's death (1801).

source.label: Mount Vernon — Census of the Enslaved Population

events.title: Barings and Hope finance the Louisiana Purchase
events.text: Barings (60%) and Hope & Co. bought the US bonds used to pay Napoleon, opening a vast territory to cotton and sugar slavery.

source.label: The Baring Archive — The Louisiana Purchase

events.title: Import ban leaves domestic trade open
events.text: Jefferson signed, and Speaker Nathaniel Macon's House passed, the ban on importing captives from 1808 — after which Chesapeake enslavers increasingly sold people south.

source.label: NCpedia — Nathaniel Macon

events.title: US ban on importing enslaved people takes effect
events.text: The 1807 Act takes effect on 1 January 1808 after a rush of arrivals at Charleston; smuggling and the domestic trade continue.

source.label: Wikipedia — Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves

events.title: Lightbourn and Niara Bely found Farenya
events.text: The South Carolina trader and his Luso-African wife establish a slaving settlement on the Rio Pongo.

source.label: Wikipedia — Niara Bely

events.title: Jackson drives a coffle on the Natchez Trace
events.text: Andrew Jackson confronted federal agent Silas Dinsmoor, who demanded passes for the enslaved people Jackson was taking south to market.

source.label: Scalawag — Ending the myth of the historic Natchez Trace

events.title: Spain agrees to end trade
events.text: Anglo-Spanish treaty bans the trade, but illegal shipments to Cuba continue for decades; Cuban slavery ends in 1886.

source.label: EBSCO Research Starters — Spain Agrees to End Slave Trade

events.title: Ghezo's coup with de Souza
events.text: Ghezo overthrew Adandozan with the help of Francisco Félix de Souza, who became Chachá and chief agent of the Ouidah trade.

source.label: Wikipedia — Francisco Félix de Souza

events.title: Osei Bonsu questions abolition
events.text: Asantehene Osei Bonsu asked British envoy Joseph Dupuis why Britain had stopped buying captives and doubted its humanitarian motives.

source.label: Bedford/St Martin's (McKay, Sources) — Osei Bonsu, An Asante King Questions British Motives (1820)

events.title: Demerara uprising begins on Gladstone estate
events.text: The large 1823 rebellion of enslaved people in Demerara began on John Gladstone's Success plantation and was violently suppressed.

source.label: AP via WSLS — Descendants of a British owner of slaves in Guyana apologize

events.title: Moss brothers move enslaved people to Demerara
events.text: John and Henry Moss bought Anna Regina and shipped hundreds of people they had inherited in the Bahamas to work it; 603 were moved under licence in 1821–25.

source.label: UCL LBS — John Moss

events.title: Haiti forced to pay 'independence debt'
events.text: Charles X's ordinance demanded 150 million francs from Haiti, under naval threat, in return for recognition.

source.label: Wikipedia — Haitian independence debt

events.title: Skeltons found Fort Victoria on the Rio Nunez
events.text: Elizabeth Frazer Skelton and William Skelton Jr. found a slave fort (1825/26) supplying captives to Portuguese Bissau.

source.label: Enslaved.org — Elizabeth Frazer Skelton

events.title: Haiti's indemnity payable to the Caisse des Dépôts
events.text: Charles X's ordinance required Haiti to pay 150 million francs into the Caisse des Dépôts for former colonists.

source.label: Wikipedia — Haitian independence debt

events.title: Monticello dispersal sale
events.text: To pay Jefferson's debts, nearly 100 enslaved people were auctioned at Monticello over five days in January, splitting families.

source.label: Monticello — 1827 dispersal sale

events.title: Franklin & Armfield founded
events.text: Isaac Franklin and John Armfield form what becomes the largest US domestic slave-trading firm, based in Alexandria.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — Franklin and Armfield

events.title: Barings sells Louisiana planter-bank bonds
events.text: Barings marketed c. $2.5m in bonds of the Consolidated Association of the Planters of Louisiana, whose capital rested on mortgaged land and enslaved people.

source.label: 64 Parishes — Consolidated Association of the Planters of Louisiana

events.title: Ridgely will frees Hampton people by age
events.text: Gov. Charles Carnan Ridgely's codicil manumitted adults in set age bands — one of Maryland's largest manumissions — while leaving others enslaved.

source.label: NPS — Chattel Slavery at Hampton

events.title: Abolition Act and £20m compensation
events.text: Parliament abolished colonial slavery from 1834 and voted £20 million to slave-owners, distributed by the Slave Compensation Commission; the 1835 £15m loan arranged by N M Rothschild and Moses Montefiore funded most of it.

source.label: The National Archives — Office of Registry of Colonial Slaves and Slave Compensation Commission records

events.title: Drax Hall compensation claim
events.text: The Erle-Drax family claimed £4,293 for 189 enslaved people at Drax Hall, Barbados.

source.label: UCL LBS — Barbados 3784 (Drax Hall)

events.title: Maryland Jesuits sell 272 people
events.text: Georgetown's Jesuit leaders sell 272 enslaved people to Louisiana planters to relieve the college's debts.

source.label: Georgetown Slavery Archive — Sale of Maryland Jesuit enslaved community, 1838

events.title: Denman destroys the Gallinas barracoons
events.text: Royal Navy forces burn eight factories and free 841 captives; Prince Manna signs an anti-slave-trade treaty for King Siaka.

source.label: Report of the Mixed Courts at Sierra Leone for 1840

events.title: Domingo Martínez settles at Porto-Novo
events.text: The Brazilian trader establishes himself at Porto-Novo with privileges from King Ghezo, becoming Dahomey's leading foreign merchant.

source.label: Ross, J. African History (1965)

events.title: Emancipation in French and Danish colonies
events.text: France abolished slavery on 27 April 1848, freeing c. 250,000 people; on 3 July enslaved people on St Croix forced emancipation in the Danish West Indies.

source.label: Wikipedia — Decree of the Abolition of Slavery of April 27, 1848

events.title: Joaquim d'Almeida becomes Ouidah's leading trader
events.text: After Francisco Félix de Souza's death, the freed African merchant becomes Ouidah's richest resident before retreating to Agoué in 1850.

source.label: Enslaved.org — Joaquim d'Almeida

events.title: Forbes fails to persuade Ghezo
events.text: Royal Navy Captain Frederick Forbes's mission failed to persuade Ghezo to abolish the trade; Ghezo gave him a captive girl, later Sarah Forbes Bonetta. A blockade followed in 1851.

source.label: Royal Collection Trust — Dahomey and the Dahomans, vol. 2, by Frederick E. Forbes

events.title: Brazil's Eusébio de Queirós Law
events.text: Under British naval pressure Brazil enforces its ban on the African trade; landings largely end by 1856.

source.label: Wikipedia — Eusébio de Queirós Law

events.title: British bombardment of Lagos
events.text: British warships attacked Lagos on 26–28 December, deposing Kosoko and installing Akitoye, who signed an anti-slave-trade treaty on 1 January 1852.

source.label: Wikipedia — Akitoye

events.title: Pinto da Fonseca expelled from Brazil
events.text: After the 1850 Eusébio de Queirós Law, Rio's leading trafficker is deported to Portugal (some sources say 1852).

source.label: Wikipedia — Manuel Pinto da Fonseca

events.title: The Wanderer lands on Jekyll Island
events.text: Charles Lamar's yacht lands c. 400 Africans in Georgia, 50 years after the ban; no one is convicted.

source.label: New Georgia Encyclopedia — Wanderer

events.title: Dona Ana Joaquina dies at sea
events.text: Luanda's best-known woman slave trader dies en route to Lisbon, accompanied by eight enslaved attendants.

source.label: Wikipedia — Ana Joaquina dos Santos e Silva

events.title: The Clotilda arrives in Mobile
events.text: Timothy Meaher's schooner brings 110 captives from Ouidah, the last documented slave voyage to the US; the ship is burned to hide the crime.

source.label: Encyclopedia of Alabama — Africatown

events.title: Nathaniel Gordon hanged
events.text: The captain of the Erie becomes the only American executed for slave trading after Lincoln refuses clemency.

source.label: HarpWeek — Execution of Gordon the Slave-Trader

events.title: London & Brazilian Bank founded
events.text: The Lloyds predecessor began lending in Brazil, where it would accept enslaved people as loan collateral until abolition in 1888.

source.label: LSE Research Online — Mulhern, 'Human collateral'

events.title: Dutch abolition (Keti Koti)
events.text: The Netherlands abolished slavery in Suriname and the Antilles on 1 July 1863, compensating enslavers; forced 'state supervision' labour lasted to 1873.

source.label: DNB — DNB apologises for its historical links to slavery

events.title: Maryland abolishes slavery
events.text: Maryland's new constitution, narrowly ratified by referendum, ended slavery in the state on 1 November 1864.

source.label: Maryland State Archives — Constitutional Convention of 1864

events.title: Fall of Kansala
events.text: Futa Jallon forces besiege Kaabu's capital; the mansaba fires the powder stores, ending Mandinka hegemony.

source.label: Wikipedia — Kaabu

events.title: Amachree faction moves to Buguma
events.text: After the 1882–84 Kalabari civil war the Amachree line resettles at Abonnema and Buguma, today's capital.

source.label: Wikipedia — Kalabari Kingdom

events.title: Cuba abolishes slavery
events.text: Spain ends the patronato system, completing gradual emancipation in Cuba begun by the 1870 Moret Law.

source.label: Hispanic American Historical Review — Rebecca Scott, Gradual Abolition and the Dynamics of Slave Emancipation in Cuba, 1868–86

events.title: Jaja of Opobo deported
events.text: Vice-Consul Harry Johnston lured Jaja aboard a British ship; tried in Accra, he was exiled to the West Indies.

source.label: NOW Grenada — This day in history: 8 June 1888 (Jaja arrives in Grenada)

events.title: Lei Áurea abolishes slavery in Brazil
events.text: Princess Isabel signs the Golden Law on 13 May, freeing c. 700,000 people without compensation or support.

source.label: Wikipedia — Lei Áurea

events.title: Anglo-Aro War
events.text: British forces captured Arochukwu on 28 December 1901, reportedly destroying the Long Juju shrine and ending the Aro Confederacy.

source.label: Wikipedia — Anglo-Aro War

events.title: 'Slaves in the Family' wins National Book Award
events.text: Edward Ball's history of his family's rice plantations and the c. 4,000 people they enslaved won the National Book Award for nonfiction.

source.label: Edward Ball — Slaves in the Family

events.title: Benin's apology and Cotonou conference
events.text: President Mathieu Kérékou apologised for Africans' role in the slave trade and hosted a reconciliation conference in Cotonou with diaspora and European delegates.

source.label: PBS — Noble Desire: A Time for Healing (Benin reconciliation conference)

events.title: France's Taubira Law
events.text: France recognised the slave trade and slavery as crimes against humanity, the first such national law.

source.label: University of Edinburgh MMOE — Loi Taubira (2001)

events.title: Farmer-Paellmann sues Aetna, FleetBoston and CSX
events.text: A federal suit in Brooklyn sought reparations from companies said to have profited from slavery; it was dismissed in 2004–05.

source.label: Business & Human Rights Resource Centre — Lawsuit chases companies tied to slavery

events.title: JPMorgan Chase and Wachovia apologise
events.text: Disclosures under Chicago's ordinance reveal predecessor banks held or took enslaved people as collateral; both banks apologise.

source.label: CNN Money — Wachovia apologizes for slavery ties

events.title: Bank of America apologises
events.text: Under Chicago's disclosure ordinance, Bank of America reported predecessor transactions involving enslaved people and CEO Ken Lewis expressed regret.

source.label: Chicago Sun-Times (via insideARM) — Bank of America admits ties to slavery (2005)

events.title: Brown University's Slavery and Justice report
events.text: Brown publishes its examination of the university's and Brown family's ties to slavery and the slave trade.

source.label: Brown University — Slavery and Justice report (2006)

events.title: Nigerian chiefs urged to apologise
events.text: The Civil Rights Congress of Nigeria asked traditional rulers to apologise for their ancestors' role in the slave trade; the chiefs declined.

source.label: Irish Times — Say sorry for slavery, Africans told (2009)

events.title: Compensation borrowing finally repaid
events.text: The last gilts into which the 1835 compensation borrowing had been consolidated were redeemed in 2015; a February 2018 HM Treasury tweet presenting this as a 'fact' drew criticism and was deleted. How much of the original debt was still outstanding is unknown (Full Fact).

source.label: Full Fact — What we know about the government loan to pay slave owners compensation

events.title: Cameron's Jamaica visit and the Duff link
events.text: UCL researchers identified a compensated slave-owner, Sir James Duff, as a distant cousin of David Cameron, who rejected reparations on his visit.

source.label: UCL News — David Cameron faces demands for slavery reparation

events.title: Valongo Wharf becomes a World Heritage Site
events.text: UNESCO inscribes Rio's slave-landing wharf as the most important physical trace of African arrival in the Americas.

source.label: UNESCO — Valongo Wharf Archaeological Site

events.title: López statue removed
events.text: Barcelona removes the statue of slave trader Antonio López, Marquis of Comillas.

source.label: Catalan News — Barcelona removes slave trader statue

events.title: Ghana's Year of Return
events.text: Ghana marked 400 years since 1619 with a diaspora homecoming campaign centred on the coastal castles.

source.label: Oxford Business Group — Homeward bound: Year of Return campaign (Ghana 2020 report)

events.title: Clotilda wreck identified
events.text: The Alabama Historical Commission confirms the wreck of the Clotilda in the Mobile River.

source.label: NBC News — America's last slave ship could offer a case for reparations

events.title: Glasgow signs £20m reparative justice deal
events.text: After its 2018 report, the University of Glasgow agreed with the University of the West Indies to raise £20m over 20 years.

source.label: World Economic Forum — University of Glasgow will pay £20 million in slavery reparations

events.title: Colston statue toppled; corporate apologies
events.text: Protesters toppled Edward Colston's statue in Bristol on 7 June; within days Lloyd's of London, Greene King and the Bank of England apologised for historic slavery links.

source.label: Wikipedia — Statue of Edward Colston

events.title: De Pury statue painted red; Zurich study
events.text: Neuchâtel's de Pury statue is vandalised after a removal petition (July), and a UZH study exposes Zurich's slavery investments (September).

source.label: Swissinfo — Switzerland joins debate about removing controversial memorials

events.title: Amsterdam apologises
events.text: Mayor Femke Halsema apologised on 1 July 2021 for the city government's active involvement in colonial slavery.

source.label: DutchNews — Amsterdam mayor apologises for slavery past

events.title: Amsterdam and Rotterdam apologise
events.text: Amsterdam's mayor apologises on 1 July and Rotterdam's on 10 December for their city governments' roles in slavery.

source.label: Amsterdam Open Research — Amsterdam city council apologizes

events.title: Evanston pays first local reparations; H.R. 40 clears committee
events.text: Evanston began its cannabis-funded housing reparations in March, and the House Judiciary Committee approved H.R. 40 25–17 in April.

source.label: Human Rights Watch — Historic progress on US slavery reparations bill

events.title: Harvard commits $100 million; Barbados weighs Drax claim
events.text: Harvard published its Legacy of Slavery report in April, and in November Barbados reportedly considered seeking reparations from Richard Drax.

source.label: The Harvard Crimson — Harvard Legacy of Slavery report

events.title: Church fund and family apologies
events.text: The Church Commissioners pledged £100m (January); the Trevelyan family apologised in Grenada (February) and the Gladstone family in Guyana (August).

source.label: Civil Society — Church Commissioners pledges £100m to atone for links to chattel slavery

events.title: Dutch king apologises
events.text: After 2022 apologies by ABN AMRO, DNB and PM Rutte, King Willem-Alexander apologised on 1 July 2023 for slavery and his ancestors' part in it.

source.label: DutchReview — King Willem-Alexander apologises for the Netherlands' role in slavery

events.title: Porto hospital censors slavery artwork
events.text: The Hospital Conde de Ferreira closes part of an installation asking how many enslaved people a psychiatric hospital is worth.

source.label: Hyperallergic — Portugal hospital removes artwork about its slavery ties

events.title: Citi and HSBC publish reviews; California task force reports
events.text: Citi found predecessors likely profited indirectly from slavery, HSBC named five predecessor banks with direct links, and California's task force issued its final report.

source.label: Citigroup — Re-examining Citi's historical connections to slavery

events.title: Portuguese president on reparations
events.text: Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa says Portugal must 'pay the costs' of slavery; the government rejects reparations.

source.label: The EastAfrican — Portugal must 'pay costs' of slavery

events.title: Hermitage locates enslaved cemetery; UMD reports on Calvert
events.text: The Hermitage announced it had found the burial ground of people Jackson enslaved, and UMD's 1856 Project documented Charles B. Calvert's enslavement of 52 people.

source.label: AP (via News4Jax) — Hermitage burial site found

events.title: Yale apologises
events.text: Yale issued a formal apology alongside David Blight's 'Yale and Slavery: A History'.

source.label: Yale News — Yale vows new actions to address past ties to slavery

events.title: Tinubu estate administrator claims presidential descent
events.text: The administrator of Madam Tinubu's estate publicly calls President Bola Tinubu a direct descendant; no genealogical evidence has been published and the claim is disputed.

source.label: Leadership (Nigeria)

events.title: Berlin's Nettelbeckplatz renamed
events.text: The Wedding square named for slave-ship mate Joachim Nettelbeck becomes Martha-Ndumbe-Platz, after Dortmund's 2024 renaming.

source.label: Wikipedia (de) — Joachim Nettelbeck (Seemann)
